unit-13.15ig66ldeci: The anchor is what makes the web a web: About us. The href can be an absolute URL, a relative URL (about.html, ../index.html, /blog/post-1, resolved against the current page's address, just like paths in a file system), or a fragment (#contact) that jumps to the element whose id is contact. Make the link text meaningful ("Read the report", not "click here"), because screen reader users often list all links out of context. Add target="_blank" rel="noopener" to open in a new tab safely.
unit-13.2e0pu7rdp1h: Images use . The alt attribute is the text alternative: shown if the image fails, read aloud by screen readers, and used by search engines. Describe the content or purpose; use alt="" for purely decorative images. Giving width and height lets the browser reserve space so the page does not jump when the image loads. Images are fetched with their own request, so large images slow a page down.
unit-13.wqqnjgs9cf: Everything the page refers to by URL (links, images, scripts, stylesheets) works the same way. You will see in the examples below that the editor's frame has no network, so we use text and shapes, and data URLs in a few places.

unit-13.r8pmeit8v5: HTML gives content structure and meaning, CSS presentation, JavaScript behaviour.

unit-13.248jr6ok7ks: Use semantic landmark elements instead of anonymous divs

unit-13.942is7eu3g: Two elements have no meaning of their own: <div> (a block container) and <span> (an inline container). They are useful hooks for CSS, but a page built only of divs tells browsers, search engines and assistive technology nothing. HTML has semantic elements that name the role of a region:
unit-13.18o30w59bkj: These landmarks let a screen reader user jump straight to the navigation or the main content, much as sighted people scan a page layout. They also help search engines. The rule is: if there is an element whose meaning fits, use it; use div only when nothing else does.
unit-13.1q5w6n3kzdq: A <table> is for tabular data, not for page layout (that was a bad old habit; CSS does layout, Lesson 13.4). Rows are <tr>; cells are <td> and header cells <th>. Group them with <thead>, <tbody> and <tfoot>, add a <caption> that names the table, and use scope="col" or scope="row" on headers so assistive technology can announce "Grade, row Ada" for each cell. colspan and rowspan let a cell cover several columns or rows.
unit-13.150sybercn5: A form collects input and sends it to a server (or, as you will do from Lesson 13.7, to JavaScript). The <form> element wraps the controls; its action is the URL to send to and method is get (data goes in the URL, for searches) or post (data goes in the request body, for changes and anything private).
unit-13.1v7shcz1s7p: The workhorse is <input>, whose type decides the control: text, email, password, number, date, checkbox, radio, range, color, file, submit. Others: <textarea> for several lines, <select> with <option> for a drop-down, and <button type="submit">. Each control that sends data needs a name attribute: the name is the key and the value is what the user entered, so submitting becomes ?email=ada%40example.org&plan=pro (the percent encoding from Lesson 11.7). Radio buttons that share a name form a group of which one can be chosen.
unit-13.268n2xr5068: Every control needs a label. <label for="email">Email</label> with <input id="email"> links them. Clicking the label focuses the input, and a screen reader announces the label when the control is reached. The alternative is to wrap the input inside the label. A placeholder is not a label: it vanishes as you type.
unit-13.18d54fak0ip: The browser can check input before sending, with no JavaScript: required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, step, pattern="[0-9]{4}" (a regular expression), and the type itself (type="email" must look like an address). A form with a failing control will not submit and the browser shows a message. The CSS pseudo-classes :valid and :invalid can style the state, and JavaScript can ask input.checkValidity().
unit-13.2c7p0bovtu5: Choosing the right type is free usability: type="email" brings the right keyboard on a phone, type="number" a number pad, type="date" a date picker. Add autocomplete="email" so browsers can fill in known values.
unit-13.2fmnry3t49q: Never trust client-side validation. Anyone can bypass the browser (turn off JavaScript, send the request by hand, as Unit 11 showed). Validation in the page is for the user's convenience; the server must check everything again (Lesson 13.9).
unit-13.188atb0w0qb: About one person in five has a disability that affects how they use the web: blindness or low vision, deafness, limited movement, dyslexia, or a broken arm for a month. Accessibility (often written a11y, "a" + 11 letters + "y") means building pages that work for all of them. It is also good engineering: the same techniques help search engines, voice assistants, and everyone on a poor connection or bright sun. In many countries it is the law for public services.
unit-13.13k3jy82c5u: A few habits cover most of it:
unit-13.i3349syvdb: Use semantic elements (headings in order, lists, landmarks, buttons for buttons and links for links).
unit-13.1x7061h1nbp: Give every control a label and every meaningful image alt text.
unit-13.1q5fr82733u: Make everything work with the keyboard: Tab moves through links and controls in the order of the page, Enter or Space activates. Do not remove the focus outline without replacing it. A <div onclick> cannot be reached by keyboard, a <button> can.
unit-13.29c792odr9i: Do not use colour alone to carry meaning (a red border for errors; add text), and keep enough contrast between text and background.
unit-13.1z9hkqrcg03: Where HTML has no element for it, ARIA attributes (aria-label, aria-expanded, role) describe custom widgets. The first rule of ARIA: use a real HTML element if one exists; ARIA only changes what is announced, not how it behaves.

unit-13.1tjgwcj6gsc: You already know Python well. JavaScript (JS) does the same jobs with different spelling, so this lesson goes quickly by comparing the two. JavaScript runs in every browser, so it is the language of the front end, and with Node.js it also runs servers (Lesson 13.9). Despite the name it has nothing to do with Java.
unit-13.eygnvq1ggz: Code in this lesson runs in a worker without a page: output comes from console.log(...). Statements end with ; (optional but recommended), blocks use { } rather than indentation, and conditions go in parentheses:
unit-13.28eze1hqzp7: Comments are // like this or /* like this */. Strings use 'single', "double" or backtick quotes; backticks allow ${expression} inside and multi-line text.
unit-13.ea75kyl4u9: Declare variables with const (cannot be reassigned; use it by default) or let (can be). Old code uses var, which has confusing scoping; do not use it. Both const and let are block scoped: they exist only inside the nearest { }.
unit-13.2cqj2ak71qq: The types: number (one type for integers and floats, a 64-bit float like Python's float, so 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3), bigint (123n), string, boolean, undefined (a variable with no value yet), null (deliberately empty), symbol, and object (everything else, including arrays and functions). typeof 5 is "number". There is no int division: 7 / 2 is 3.5; use Math.floor(7 / 2) or Math.trunc.
unit-13.22op7yan6yh: Equality. JavaScript has two equal operators. == converts types first and gives bizarre results (0 == "0" true, "" == 0 true, null == undefined true). Always use === and !==, which compare value and type with no conversion.
unit-13.1p19agayjvg: Truthiness. In conditions these values are falsy: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", [] and {} (unlike Python, where an empty list is falsy). Operators && and || return one of their operands, so name || "guest" is a default value, and ?? is a stricter default that only replaces null and undefined. Optional chaining user?.address?.city gives undefined instead of an error when a link is missing.
unit-13.2dhu4bidhlo: Functions are values: store them, pass them as arguments, return them (just like Python). Arrow functions are the short form used for callbacks (items.map(x => x * 2)); with a single expression the return is implicit. Missing arguments are undefined rather than an error, and extra ones are ignored. Rest parameters gather the rest: function sum(...nums) { ... }, and spread unpacks: Math.max(...numbers).
unit-13.j2kk9fzr80: A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the place where it was created, even after that place has finished:
unit-13.197d830pnq8: n is private: only the returned function can reach it. Closures are how JavaScript hides state, and the engine behind callbacks, event handlers (Lesson 13.7) and, later, framework hooks (Lesson 13.8).
unit-13.1av15n3s85o: An array is Python's list: [1, 2, 3], indexed from 0, with .length, .push(x), .pop(), .slice(a, b), .includes(x), .indexOf(x), .join(", "). Negative indexes do not work: use arr.at(-1) for the last element. An object is Python's dictionary: { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, read with obj.name or obj["name"], with keys that are strings. Objects are the basis of JSON (Lesson 13.6): JSON.stringify(obj) and JSON.parse(text).
unit-13.1f6y94mm8n4: Destructuring pulls values out concisely, and spread (...) copies:
unit-13.hbzs4vprmo: Prefer making a new array or object over changing the old one (immutability): it is easier to reason about and is exactly what UI frameworks expect.
unit-13.2g73ynzdbj1: The array methods replace most loops: map transforms each element, filter keeps some, reduce folds into one value, plus find, some, every, sort, flat and forEach.
unit-13.3i19h37w8m: Beware: sort() with no argument sorts as text ([10, 9, 1].sort() is [1, 10, 9]); pass a comparator (a, b) => a - b. And sort changes the array in place.
unit-13.27dgbxr7t66: class is syntax over JavaScript's prototype system; constructor is __init__, this is self (but always written explicitly inside methods, and its value depends on how the function is called, which is a classic source of confusion; arrow functions keep the this of where they were written). extends and super give inheritance. Files can be modules: export function f() {} and import { f } from "./f.js".
unit-13.dinn2se6y1: Errors use throw new Error("message") and try { ... } catch (e) { ... } finally { ... }, like Python's try/except. Many JavaScript mistakes do not throw at all: a missing property is undefined, "5" * 2 is 10, "5" + 2 is "52". A value of NaN ("not a number") from bad arithmetic quietly spreads through calculations; check with Number.isNaN(x).

unit-13.1wfykeoc3q8: A web page has one thread running your JavaScript. If it stopped to wait for a server for two seconds, the whole page, including scrolling and clicking, would freeze. So JavaScript never waits: anything slow (a network request, a timer, reading a file, a click) is started, and the program carries on. When the slow thing finishes, a callback is queued to run.
unit-13.1w9rwt54qjf: The machinery is the event loop. It repeats: take the next waiting task from the task queue (a timer firing, a click, a response arriving), run it to completion, then run all queued microtasks (promise reactions), then let the browser redraw, then take the next task. A task is never interrupted: while your function runs, nothing else does, so a long while loop freezes the page (this is the concurrency of Unit 10, using one thread and cooperation instead of preemption).
unit-13.1nns8sei5kw: prints A, D, C, B. First the synchronous code (A, D), then the microtask (C), and only then the timer task (B), even with a delay of 0. In this unit's runner timers use a virtual clock: setTimeout(f, 5000) runs promptly, but in the correct order relative to other timers.
unit-13.1nzqqlq50e: The old style is the callback: setTimeout(done, 1000). Nesting callbacks inside callbacks (to do step 2 after step 1 after step 0) gets deep and tangled, called callback hell, and error handling is awkward. Promises fix that.
unit-13.12dhly1kold: A promise is an object representing a value that will exist later. It is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error). Once settled it never changes.
unit-13.1x3ple5jogl: new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }) runs your function immediately; call resolve(value) or reject(error) when done. You consume one with .then(onValue), .catch(onError) and .finally(cleanup). Each of these returns a new promise, so they chain flat instead of nesting:
unit-13.44iwhbh2p9: A value returned from a then becomes the next step's input; a thrown error skips ahead to the next catch. Combinators run promises together: Promise.all([a, b, c]) waits for all (and rejects at once if any rejects), Promise.allSettled waits for all and reports each result, Promise.race takes the first to settle, and Promise.any the first to succeed.
unit-13.2buu2y6tb3m: async/await is syntax that lets promise code read like ordinary step-by-step code:
unit-13.11d5loi0amb: An async function always returns a promise. Inside it, await somePromise pauses that function (not the thread; other tasks keep running) until the promise settles, then gives the fulfilled value or throws the rejection, so ordinary try/catch handles errors. Common mistakes:
unit-13.1dpjgzuyvs6: Forgetting await: you get a promise object instead of the value.
unit-13.1z93mdt6w7z: Awaiting in a loop when requests are independent. for (const id of ids) await load(id) runs them one after another; await Promise.all(ids.map(load)) runs them together, which is much faster.
unit-13.1km1t7udgj5: An async function that throws and whose promise nobody awaits produces an unhandled rejection, an error that appears only in the console.
unit-13.s48x63dmnr: Talking to servers: fetch and JSON
unit-13.27r1c7vqrzs: fetch(url, options) makes an HTTP request (Lesson 11.7) and returns a promise of a response. It resolves as soon as headers arrive and rejects only on network failure; a 404 or 500 is still a successful fetch, so always check response.ok (status 200 to 299). Then read the body with await response.json() (parse JSON), or .text().
unit-13.g6sj918vfg: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the text format APIs use to exchange data: objects {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false, null. Keys and strings need double quotes; no comments, no trailing commas. JSON.stringify(value) turns a value into text (functions and undefined are dropped; Date becomes a string) and JSON.parse(text) turns it back, throwing SyntaxError on bad input. A deep copy trick is JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)); the modern way is structuredClone(x).
unit-13.21fard69ofi: In this lesson's runner fetch talks to a pretend server in memory with these routes: GET /api/users (a list of two users), GET /api/users/1 and /api/users/2 (one user, 404 for others), POST /api/users (returns the body plus id: 3, status 201), GET /api/slow (answers after 500 ms) and GET /api/fail (a network error). Real browsers also enforce the same-origin policy: a page may only read responses from its own origin unless the server allows others with CORS headers (Lesson 13.9).
unit-13.15frijmvy2q: Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promises), then timers, even with a delay of zero.

unit-13.2805izesatp: Three independent waits. Awaiting them one by one takes the sum; Promise.all takes the longest. The virtual clock lets us measure.

unit-13.2fy8imdshxp: An event is something that happened: a click, a key press, a form submission, a page finishing loading, the mouse moving. You register a listener, a function the browser calls (it is a callback, as in Lesson 13.6):
unit-13.1mtkp9z5weq: The event object says what happened: event.type, event.target (the element that was the source), event.currentTarget (the element the listener is on), event.key for keyboard events, event.clientX/Y for the mouse. unit-13.cqs32mqkdf: Default actions. Some events do something on their own: a link navigates, a form submit reloads the page. event.preventDefault() cancels that, which is what you want when JavaScript handles the form: form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => { e.preventDefault(); ... }).
unit-13.2dcchwm7dhw: Bubbling. After the target handles an event it bubbles up through its ancestors, so a click on a button inside a list also reaches the list and the document. This enables event delegation: one listener on the parent handles all its children, including ones added later:
unit-13.105emq8e2ay: event.stopPropagation() stops the bubbling (use sparingly). Remove a listener with removeEventListener using the same function reference.

unit-13.kyz7let4m: The last lesson ended with a pattern: keep state in data and write a render() that builds the page from it. In a big application you would write thousands of lines of createElement calls, keep many render functions in step, and decide which parts of the page to update when something changes. A framework (React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Solid) automates this. They differ in detail but share the same ideas:
unit-13.x91nocvp: The UI is a function of state. You describe what the page should look like for the current data. The framework makes the real page match.
unit-13.1cjdlu0u8tg: Components. A page is a tree of small, reusable pieces (a button, a card, a login form), each taking inputs (props) and perhaps keeping its own state.
unit-13.1baumu8iwuf: One-way data flow. Data flows down from parents to children as props; events flow up as function calls. That makes it easy to find why something changed.
unit-13.dmukbdhgi7: Efficient updates. When state changes the framework compares the new description with the old one and changes only the parts of the DOM that differ.
unit-13.1ennp7sifkg: In this lesson there is no page to draw on, so you will build these ideas as pure JavaScript functions that produce HTML text or plain objects, which also makes them easy to test. Everything here is a simplified version of what a real framework does; the point is that you understand the machine, not that you write your own.
unit-13.2342i9nv7vp: A virtual node is a plain object describing an element: its tag, attributes and children. A helper h (for "hyperscript") makes them short:
unit-13.12abeclduyh:
Nothing is drawn: tree is just data you can print, test, copy and compare. (React's JSX,
    ...
inside JavaScript, is a notation that turns into exactly these h calls.) To show it you write a function that renders the tree, here to an HTML string:
unit-13.535by83zcx: Because rendering is a function of data, the same tree can be drawn into the DOM, sent from a server as HTML (server-side rendering), or turned into a native phone screen.
unit-13.22aj8zth6q9: Escaping. Any text that goes into HTML must have &, <, >, " and ' replaced by & < > " '. Frameworks do this automatically for text children, which is why they are safe by default, and why escape hatches such as React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML carry that name.
unit-13.15sq8n2xm3k: A component is a function that takes props and returns a tree. Components return trees that contain other components, which composes the page:
unit-13.110aif85tqi: A component that only turns props into output, with no hidden state and no side effects, is pure: the same props always give the same result. This makes components easy to test (call the function, check the tree) and easy to reason about. Real frameworks add local state (React's useState, Vue's ref), effects (running code after rendering, such as fetching data), and keys: a unique key on each list item so the framework can tell which item is which after a reorder.
unit-13.18nxhfnmgby: Composition over inheritance. Components are built by nesting and by passing children, not by class hierarchies. A Card component takes children and wraps them; a Button takes onClick as a prop. This is the same idea as passing a function as an argument, from Lesson 13.5.
unit-13.i393pks7kf: State shared by many components lives in a store. The smallest useful store holds state, lets code subscribe to changes, and changes only through named actions:
unit-13.2c5ut36eguj: A reducer is a pure function (state, action) => newState that never changes the old state but returns a new one: { ...state, count: state.count + 1 }. This is the heart of Redux and of the Elm architecture. The cycle is one way: the view shows state; the user acts; the event dispatches an action; the reducer makes new state; subscribers re-render. Because every change is an action in a list, you can log them, undo by replaying fewer, and find bugs by reading the sequence.
unit-13.wb7pk21mrf: Replacing the entire page on every key press would lose the cursor position and scroll position, restart animations and be slow. So frameworks compare the old tree with the new tree and produce a small list of changes to apply to the real DOM. This is called diffing (React calls the tree the virtual DOM and the process reconciliation).
unit-13.1qeryn10ucx: A simple diff walks both trees together:
unit-13.g93ypqdg1p: no old node: create the new one; no new node: remove the old one;
unit-13.26qe36mg8wb: different tag (or one is text and one is an element): replace it;
unit-13.6uokifkpeu: same tag: update the changed attributes, then diff the children pairwise.
unit-13.22cf7xyvi8o: Comparing arbitrary trees optimally is slow (cubic), so frameworks use two assumptions that hold for UIs: elements of different types produce different trees, and a key marks which children are stable across renders. This reduces the work to one pass. Newer frameworks (Svelte, Solid) skip the diff and generate code that updates exactly the parts that depend on each piece of state, but the goal is the same: describe the UI for the current state and let the machine do the minimal DOM work.

unit-13.bni9973sxl: From Unit 11 you know a web server is a program listening on a port that reads an HTTP request and writes an HTTP response. At heart it is a function from request to response. In Node.js (JavaScript outside the browser) with the popular Express framework:
unit-13.22hbw1rssy4: Each such handler is a route: a method (GET), a path pattern (/api/users/:id, where :id is a parameter) and a function. The server matches the incoming request to the first route that fits, runs its handler, and sends what the handler produced. To keep this lesson runnable we will build the same machinery from plain objects: a request is { method, path, headers, body } and a response is { status, headers, body }. The code you write is the real shape of a back end; only the network is missing.
unit-13.6wn141rkqq: The back end does what the browser cannot be trusted to do: store data permanently (in a database, Unit 12), enforce rules, keep secrets (API keys, password hashes), and decide who is allowed to do what. Anything running in a browser can be inspected and changed by its user; the server is the only place where rules are enforced.
unit-13.lr9dgmd0e0: REST is a convention for web APIs. Things are resources named by nouns in the URL; the HTTP method says the action:
unit-13.xj0mc2m27c: GET must be safe (no change), and GET, PUT and DELETE idempotent (doing it twice equals once; Lesson 11.7). Choose status codes honestly: 400 the client sent something invalid, 401 not logged in, 403 logged in but not allowed, 404 no such thing, 409 conflict (duplicate), 422 valid syntax but unacceptable data, 429 too many requests, 500 the server failed. Errors should be JSON with a message: { "error": "name is required" }. Plural nouns, no verbs in paths (POST /api/orders, not /api/createOrder), and a version prefix (/api/v1) you can keep stable for clients.
unit-13.183ou008etu: Responses are usually JSON, with Content-Type: application/json. Large collections are paginated (?page=2&limit=20), and filtered with query parameters (?role=admin).
unit-13.1z0fetzkcms: Many things must happen for every request: log it, parse JSON, check the login, add headers, catch errors. Copying that into each handler would be a mess. Middleware is a function that sees the request on the way in and may change it, answer it itself, or pass it on by calling next(). Middleware form a chain; each can run code before and after the rest:
unit-13.w5r0p4t72: requireAuth stops the chain by responding without calling next(), so the protected handler never runs. Order matters: the logger goes first, the error handler last. A good mental model is the layers of an onion with the handler at the centre.
unit-13.szsj20odzk: Validate everything that arrives, on the server, even though the page already validated (Lesson 13.2). Check that required fields exist, types are right (a number is a number), lengths and ranges are sane, and reject the rest with 400 or 422. Treat the body as hostile. Prefer an allow-list: copy only the fields you expect ({ name, email }), never Object.assign(user, req.body), otherwise a client can send { "isAdmin": true } (a mass assignment attack).
unit-13.12tl25tytca: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Passwords are never stored: store a slow salted hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 from Lesson 11.9) and compare hashes. After login the server gives the browser a session identifier in a cookie, or a signed token such as a JWT, that the browser sends with each request (HTTP has no memory, so every request must carry proof). Cookies for sessions should be HttpOnly (scripts cannot read them), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite=Lax or Strict. Always use HTTPS.
unit-13.1gk9duzky65: Check authorization on every request for every resource: it is not enough that a user is logged in; GET /api/orders/12 must verify that order 12 belongs to this user, or any user could read any order by changing the number (an insecure direct object reference, a leading real-world vulnerability).
unit-13.rh7ucuzzyn: Cross-site scripting (XSS). An attacker gets their JavaScript to run on your page, usually because user text was put into HTML unescaped. The script can read the page, steal tokens, and act as the user. Defence: escape output (frameworks do it for you), never use innerHTML with untrusted text, and add a Content-Security-Policy header that restricts where scripts can come from.
unit-13.1vkkhbz1u1n: SQL injection (Lesson 12.9). Defence: parameterised queries, never string concatenation.
unit-13.1jx7z9czuhw: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF). You are logged in to your bank in one tab; a malicious page in another makes your browser send POST /transfer to the bank, and the browser helpfully attaches your cookie. Defence: SameSite cookies, a secret CSRF token that the attacker's page cannot know, and checking the Origin header.
unit-13.idl6mmajqc: Same-origin policy and CORS. Browsers stop a page from reading responses from a different origin (scheme + host + port), so a malicious site cannot read your email through your logged-in session. A server that really wants to share an API with another site says so with headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com. CORS is a rule enforced by the browser to protect users; it does not protect your server from direct requests (curl ignores it). Never answer * to credentialed requests.
unit-13.1b898trquue: Brute force and abuse. Rate limiting (the token bucket from Lesson 11.8), account lockouts, and slow password hashes.
unit-13.tsca921gl8: Secrets and dependencies. Never put keys in front-end code or in the repository; load them from environment variables. Keep dependencies updated, since a vulnerable library is your vulnerability.
unit-13.pp3jjln7oz: Security is a mindset: assume every input is hostile, give each part the least power it needs, and defend in layers so one mistake is not fatal.
unit-13.y9t1rei64n: Routes are method, path pattern and handler. A path like /api/users/:id captures a parameter.
unit-13.m18hrtpogq: Each middleware gets next(). The logger runs first, auth may stop the chain, and the handler runs last.
unit-13.t8sgapvrpe: Return the problems found. Copy only the allowed fields, so extra fields like isAdmin are ignored.
unit-13.2c793mtrb2h: Example 4: Escaping output to stop XSS
unit-13.12ez70z706w: A comment that contains a script tag, stored and later shown. Escaped, it is just text.
unit-13.nihapn94om: Being logged in is not enough. The server must check that the resource belongs to the user.
unit-13.1gc47tm7pc1: Example 6: CORS and the same origin
unit-13.icc33b41kc: An origin is scheme, host and port. A server opts in to other origins with a header.
unit-13.9s5gy87s10: Anything from a browser can be forged. Validate and authorize on the server every time.
unit-13.2bwwirnyq3j: Being logged in does not mean you may read every record. Check ownership.
unit-13.1yvmqsu0fux: Returning 200 with an error message in the body breaks clients and caches. Use 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors.
unit-13.spv4a228wm: Building SQL or HTML by concatenating input
unit-13.1qv9p4e6d6c: Use parameterised queries and escape output.
unit-13.13olp43zju7: CORS only tells browsers whether another site's page may read a response. Anyone can still call your server directly.
unit-13.1ig8gw348mb: A server is a function from request to response; routing picks the handler by method and path, with parameters.
unit-13.1dacuibroi4: REST names resources with nouns and uses methods and honest status codes: 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 500.
unit-13.1fp4y42zc48: Middleware wrap handlers for logging, authentication, validation and errors; order matters.

unit-14.og0m5inmuz: Explain how software engineering differs from programming and name the stages of the life cycle

unit-14.1sl90hopeth: Until now you have written programs that you alone understood, ran a few times, and finished. Software engineering is what changes when software is large, used by other people, built by a team, and has to keep working and changing for years. Surveys of real projects find that most of the cost of software is not writing it the first time but maintaining it: fixing bugs, adding features, adapting to new systems. Code is read far more often than it is written, usually by someone who does not remember (or never knew) why it was written that way. That person is often you in six months.
unit-14.184huw6ujvf: So engineering is about managing things that do not matter in a 50-line script:
unit-14.1ejqmkvdmmq: Complexity. No one can hold a million lines in their head, so we split systems into parts with clear interfaces (Lessons 14.4 to 14.6).
unit-14.2btx608g5le: Change. Requirements change while you build. A design that cannot change is a liability.
unit-14.19a7sralfju: People. Teams need shared understanding, shared tools and agreed ways of working (Lessons 14.2, 14.8 and 14.9).
unit-14.151xkhg295v: Quality and risk. Bugs cost money, and in some software (aircraft, medical devices, banks) they cost lives. Testing, review and monitoring are how we gain confidence (Lessons 14.3, 14.7 and 14.8).
unit-14.180m7pjmmsb: The classic failures are instructive. A software error crashed the first Ariane 5 rocket 37 seconds after launch in 1996, when a number converted from 64-bit float to a 16-bit integer overflowed (Lesson 1.2's overflow, at a cost of about half a billion dollars). A flaw in the Therac-25 radiation machine killed patients. Healthcare.gov launched in 2013 and could not handle the traffic. Most large projects that fail do so not because the code is hard but because nobody agreed what to build, the scope kept growing, or problems were discovered too late.
unit-14.24ezssaa52r: Whatever the method, building software goes through the same activities:
unit-14.11iqn9h1ev2: Requirements: find out what the users and the business need.
unit-14.1nldyj54qke: Design: decide the structure: parts, interfaces, data, technology.
unit-14.5txhnka0im: Verification: check it works (testing, review). Verification asks "did we build it right?" (does it meet the spec) and validation asks "did we build the right thing?" (does it meet the user's need).
unit-14.vtrfr32cft: Maintenance: fix, improve and adapt, usually the longest and costliest phase.
unit-14.19zhyloldyy: The methods differ in how they order and repeat these. In the waterfall model each phase finishes before the next starts, with documents handed over at each step. It is predictable and easy to manage when requirements are stable and well understood, and when mistakes are very expensive to fix after the fact (a bridge, a satellite). Its weakness is that you learn what is wrong only at the end, when changing it costs the most. The cost of fixing a defect grows steeply the later it is found.
unit-14.f08n6zg0sf: Agile methods (the 2001 Agile Manifesto: individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, responding to change) run the whole cycle in short loops. Teams deliver a small working piece every one to four weeks, get feedback, and adjust. Scrum organises this into fixed-length sprints: a planning meeting chooses work from a prioritised backlog; the team meets briefly each day; at the end it demonstrates working software (a review) and discusses how to improve (a retrospective). Kanban instead limits the number of tasks in progress on a board with columns such as To Do, Doing, Done. Most modern teams are agile in some form, usually with the engineering practices of Lessons 14.3 and 14.8 (automated tests, continuous integration) underneath, because short cycles only work if releasing is cheap and safe.
unit-14.12bdde63ufw: A requirement says what a system must do or be. Two kinds:
unit-14.1xyfwvud2n2: Functional requirements are behaviours: "A student can enrol in a course", "The system emails a receipt".
unit-14.1k38k7h0htl: Non-functional requirements (quality attributes) are how well: performance ("search results in under 300 ms for 95% of requests"), availability, security, usability, accessibility, privacy, maintainability. They are often the ones that decide the architecture, and the ones most often forgotten.
unit-14.1yt9lntam4k: Good requirements are specific, testable and agreed. "The system should be fast" cannot be checked; "95% of page loads finish in under 2 seconds on a 4G phone" can. Vague requirements are the main source of arguments at the end of a project.
unit-14.15gkvxqdm7: Agile teams write requirements as user stories: one sentence from the user's point of view, As a <role>, I want <goal> so that <benefit>, e.g. "As a student, I want to see my timetable so that I know where to go." The "so that" matters: it tells the team the real need, which may have a better solution than the one the requester imagined. Good stories are INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
unit-14.1pf7pabbwc7: Each story gets acceptance criteria: concrete conditions that must hold for it to count as done, often written as Given / When / Then scenarios: Given I am logged in as a student with two enrolments, When I open my timetable, Then I see both classes in time order. These are the seed of automated tests (Lesson 14.3) and settle the "is it finished?" argument. A shared definition of done (code reviewed, tests pass, documented, deployed) applies to every story.
unit-14.t83n5rsru0: There is never enough time to build everything, so teams prioritise. A simple method scores each item's value (what it is worth to users or the business) against its effort and works on the highest value-for-effort first. MoSCoW sorts items into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time, which is a useful way to negotiate a fixed deadline: the musts are protected, the coulds are what you drop when you run late.
unit-14.c31inn36ao: Estimating is hard: people are consistently optimistic (the planning fallacy), and the unexpected always happens. Agile teams estimate in story points, a relative size (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13: roughly Fibonacci, because bigger items are less certain) rather than hours, comparing each story to ones they have already done. A team's velocity is the number of points it actually completes per sprint, measured from experience. From the velocity and the remaining backlog you can forecast: remaining points / velocity, rounded up, is the number of sprints left, and with an average of the last few sprints it is a more honest estimate than any plan made in advance. Report a range, not a single date.
unit-14.12zsxu8867g: A burndown chart plots the points remaining against time; the ideal line falls evenly to zero and the actual line shows whether you are ahead or behind. A line that goes up means work was added (scope creep) or found (it is not a failure to be honest about this). Remember the warning known as Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. Velocity is for planning, not for judging people, because teams will inflate points to look fast.
unit-14.1emkxz65ttb: A user story has a fixed shape, so a program can pick it apart. Regular expressions (Unit 2) do the work.

unit-14.1vkv0vlnihz: Understand version control from the inside by building a tiny Git: content-addressed objects, commits that form a graph, branches as movable labels, and a three-way merge. Knowing the model makes every Git command predictable.
unit-14.2fxj9xlk485: Explain why teams use version control and what a commit, branch and merge are
unit-14.1oeiv91741y: Describe how Git stores snapshots as content-addressed objects using hashes
unit-14.z9gefg1zq3: Walk a commit graph to find history and common ancestors
unit-14.1lg32gekl9z: Perform a three-way merge and recognise a conflict
unit-14.26hhiyo1oy5: Choose sensible branching and commit habits
unit-14.l3b4arba05: Version control records every change to a set of files, who made it and why, so you can go back, compare, and work in parallel. Without it, teams email files named final_v3_REAL.docx and overwrite each other's work. With it you get a history you can search (who changed this line and why?), safe experiments on branches, and a way to merge the work of many people. Git is the dominant system. It is distributed: every developer holds the full history, so you can commit offline and there is no single point of failure. Services such as GitHub add a shared copy, pull requests and review on top.
unit-14.288425iwpi: Git stores snapshots, not differences. A blob holds one file's contents, a tree lists file names with the blob (or sub-tree) each points to, and a commit points to a tree plus its parent commit(s), an author and a message. Each object is stored under its hash, a fingerprint computed from its contents (Git uses SHA-1, moving to SHA-256; Unit 11 covered hashing). This is content addressing: identical content always has the same name, so Git stores it once, and changing even one byte gives a completely different hash. Because a commit's hash includes its parent's hash, history is tamper-evident: altering an old commit changes every hash after it.
unit-14.gh2xcrm2s1: Commits form a directed acyclic graph (Unit 7): each points back to its parent, and a merge commit has two parents. A branch is just a named pointer to a commit, and HEAD points at the branch you are on. Making a commit moves that pointer forward. This is why branches are so cheap: creating one writes 41 bytes.
unit-14.2ckjcn2oejp: A feature branch lets you work without disturbing main. When it is ready you merge it back. If main has not moved, Git just slides the pointer forward (a fast-forward). If both sides changed, Git does a three-way merge: it finds the merge base (the latest common ancestor of the two commits) and compares each side with it. For each file (or line): if only one side changed it, take that change; if both changed it identically, take it; if both changed it differently, that is a conflict and a human must choose. Comparing against the base is what lets Git tell "I changed it" from "they changed it", which a plain two-way comparison cannot.
unit-14.29wyx4vpsi2: Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a straight history, rewriting them (so never rebase commits others have pulled). git pull is fetch plus merge. A pull request asks for your branch to be reviewed and merged.
unit-14.hngv7s9jl: Commit small and often, each commit one logical change that builds and passes tests, with a message saying why: a short summary line, a blank line, then details.
unit-14.q83t6zsb3u: Branch per task, keep branches short-lived, and merge to main often; long-lived branches make painful merges.
unit-14.xsgfea7kxm: Never commit secrets (keys, passwords) or generated files; use .gitignore. Anything pushed should be treated as public forever.
unit-14.1vgkvbcdt2q: Review before merging; protect main so changes arrive by reviewed pull request with passing checks.
unit-14.gg8si2708k: Pull before you push, and read git status and git diff before committing.
unit-14.1251dkxwq6w: A tiny object store: the key is the hash of the content, so equal content is stored once.
unit-14.8bt6pfm65c: A commit is a message and a parent; a branch is a name pointing at a commit.
unit-14.1qmvf8mt2vr: The merge base is the nearest commit reachable from both branches. Collect one side's ancestors, then walk the other.
unit-14.lovmjs9v79: Example 4: Three-way merge of one file
unit-14.2bro783v7h0: Each side is compared with the base. A conflict only arises when both sides changed the same thing differently.
unit-14.2g7a4dxyye8: Deleting a key in a later commit does not remove it from history. Rotate the key and keep secrets out of the repository.
unit-14.1g4hanebn4u: Small commits with a reason make history searchable and changes revertable.
unit-14.1zrubugwadc: Rewriting commits others already pulled forces everyone to untangle diverged histories.
unit-14.1lpygvkkw9l: Version control records history and lets people work in parallel; Git is distributed.
unit-14.q2n3wyewvz: Git stores snapshots as content-addressed objects: blobs, trees and commits named by their hashes.
unit-14.ppe83q7a76: Commits form a graph; a branch is a movable pointer to a commit.
unit-14.14fvgqqikt: A three-way merge compares both sides to their merge base and conflicts only when both changed the same thing differently.
unit-14.24wf45vr6au: Commit small, branch per task, review changes, never commit secrets.
unit-14.1tlii56xhqw: Learn why and how to test software automatically: the testing pyramid, unit tests with arrange/act/assert, test doubles (stubs, fakes and mocks), test-driven development, and what coverage does and does not tell you. You will build a miniature test framework to see how tools like pytest work.
unit-14.1aicxq3y4kv: Explain the kinds of tests and the testing pyramid
unit-14.y5fqt1fcxz: Write unit tests in arrange, act, assert form with edge cases
unit-14.jdz647fmtq: Use a stub or mock to isolate code from slow or random dependencies
unit-14.ycappt0bd3: Apply the red, green, refactor cycle of test-driven development
unit-14.9eqhhbs280: Explain what coverage measures and why it is not proof of correctness
unit-14.1cbvuz4n6z8: Testing can show that bugs exist, never that none do, but good tests give confidence to change code. Every exercise in this course has been checked by automated tests, and professional teams do the same on a larger scale: when a developer changes one function, thousands of tests re-run in minutes to catch regressions, old behaviour that broke. Without them, each change is a gamble and teams become afraid to touch old code.
unit-14.1k6pimsewud: The testing pyramid describes a healthy mix. Many fast unit tests check single functions or classes in isolation. Fewer integration tests check that parts work together (code with a real database). Very few end-to-end tests drive the whole system like a user (a browser clicking through checkout). Lower tests are fast, cheap and pinpoint failures; higher tests are slow, brittle, and prove the whole thing works. An upside-down pyramid, mostly slow end-to-end tests, gives long waits and flaky results.
unit-14.23ff03v8715: A good test is small, fast, deterministic and checks one behaviour. The pattern is Arrange, Act, Assert: set up the inputs and objects, call the code, check the result. Name tests for the behaviour (test_empty_cart_total_is_zero), so a failure tells you what broke.
unit-14.6fo1cb55j6: Choose cases deliberately: the normal case, the boundaries (empty, one item, the maximum, just either side of a limit), and error cases (invalid input must raise the right exception). Most bugs live at the edges. A test should fail for one reason and never depend on the order of other tests, the clock, the network or randomness.
unit-14.11w149c5lgz: Frameworks such as unittest and pytest supply the plumbing: they find test functions, run each in isolation, catch the exceptions raised by failing assert statements, and report. They also give fixtures (shared set-up) and parametrised tests (one test, many inputs).
unit-14.2flb3bt422h: Code often depends on things that are slow, random or outside your control: the clock, a payment API, a database. A test double replaces such a dependency during a test. A stub returns fixed answers. A fake is a simple working version (an in-memory dictionary instead of a database). A mock also records how it was called, so the test can check that send_email was called once with the right address. Doubles only work if the code lets you pass the dependency in (dependency injection: give the function the clock, instead of having it call time.time() itself), which is one reason testable code tends to be well-designed code (Lessons 14.4 and 14.5).
unit-14.1o95s8twb2q: Beware over-mocking: a test full of mocks checks that the code calls what you told it to, not that the system works, and breaks whenever the implementation is refactored. Prefer real objects or fakes where they are fast, and mock only at the boundaries.
unit-14.w283cci5xn: Test-driven development (TDD) repeats a tight cycle: red (write a small failing test for the next behaviour), green (write the simplest code that passes it), refactor (clean up with the tests as a safety net). It leads to testable designs, tiny steps and a test for every behaviour.
unit-14.1xbk8dcpj40: Coverage is the share of lines (or branches) executed by the tests. Low coverage tells you code is untested; high coverage does not tell you it is tested well, because a test can run a line without checking anything. Treat coverage as a way to find gaps, not a goal. Other techniques extend testing: property-based testing generates many random inputs and checks rules that must always hold (sorting twice equals sorting once), mutation testing deliberately breaks the code to see whether the tests notice, and fuzzing throws malformed input at a program to find crashes. Tests are code too: keep them readable, because they are also living documentation of what the system does.
unit-14.t1i879nlim: This is the heart of pytest: find functions starting with test_, run each, and record failures.

unit-14.1ysl4x5wg9c: They pass today and fail tomorrow. Inject the dependency or fix the seed.
unit-14.261j8102yy3: Empty input, boundaries and errors are where the bugs are.
unit-14.ppqkl3ycay: A line can run without being checked. Use coverage to find untested code, not as proof.
unit-14.zbcqg1ntnx: Tests tied to the implementation break on every refactor and prove little.
unit-14.2e5fc5hfwqo: Automated tests catch regressions and make changing code safe; the pyramid favours many fast unit tests.
unit-14.smc52r7w99: Arrange, act, assert; test normal cases, boundaries and errors, deterministically.
unit-14.1vo38iyd5cz: Stubs, fakes and mocks replace dependencies, which works best when dependencies are injected.
unit-14.dy7sg20kw2: TDD cycles red, green, refactor; coverage finds gaps but does not prove quality.
unit-14.jw089hfj0j: Learn what makes code easy to change: cohesion and coupling, the SOLID principles, DRY and YAGNI, and refactoring, which improves structure without changing behaviour. You will see a messy function become clean through small, safe steps.
unit-14.1babfr6peb2: Define cohesion and coupling and say which to maximise or minimise
unit-14.5ozpxc6r0n: Explain the SOLID principles with an example of each
unit-14.yj4kry4grr: Refactor code in small steps while keeping behaviour the same
unit-14.18u5iejm8j9: Use dependency injection and interfaces to reduce coupling
unit-14.12764njfm46: Working code is the minimum. The real question is how hard it will be to change next month. Good design keeps the cost of change low as the system grows. Two ideas measure it. Cohesion is how closely the parts of one module belong together: a Invoice class with total() and add_item() is cohesive; one that also sends email and formats HTML is not. Coupling is how much one module depends on the details of another: if changing the database forces edits in 40 files, coupling is high. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling. Hiding details behind small, stable interfaces (abstraction and encapsulation from Unit 4) is the main tool.
unit-14.14kh6fvetjh: Other slogans capture the same wisdom. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): each piece of knowledge should live in one place, so a fix is made once. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): do not build for imagined future needs, since you will guess wrong and pay for the complexity. KISS: the simplest design that works is best. Beware the opposite error too: merging two things that only look alike creates false coupling.
unit-14.2f3wh87hr5r: Five guidelines for object-oriented design, from Robert Martin:
unit-14.gjukwn1uf6: S, Single Responsibility. A class should have one reason to change. A Report that calculates figures and prints them changes when either the maths or the layout does. Split it.
unit-14.1gzzroe6354: O, Open/Closed. Software should be open for extension, closed for modification: add new behaviour by adding new code (a new class), not by editing a growing if/elif chain.
unit-14.f2v61o4vl8: L, Liskov Substitution. Anywhere a base type is expected, a subtype must work without surprises. A Square that breaks a Rectangle's promise that width and height are independent violates this.
unit-14.2149xrka7m0: I, Interface Segregation. Prefer several small interfaces to one large one, so classes are not forced to implement methods they do not use.
unit-14.21y5e5n2qqc: D, Dependency Inversion. High-level code should depend on abstractions, not concrete details. The checkout logic should depend on "a payment method", not on one provider's library, and receive the real one from outside (dependency injection), which also makes it testable (Lesson 14.3).
unit-14.1evp4re7tsv: These are guides, not laws. Applied mechanically they give needless layers; used with judgement they keep code flexible. Python adds its own flavour: functions are objects, so often a function passed in replaces a whole class hierarchy.
unit-14.v268bsr08z: A code smell is a surface sign of a deeper problem: a very long function; a long list of parameters; duplicated code; a class that knows too much about another (feature envy); a giant if/elif chain switching on type; magic numbers (if status == 3); vague names; deep nesting; comments that explain confusing code instead of fixing it.
unit-14.1o3s44jm2hj: Refactoring improves structure without changing behaviour. The rules: have tests first (Lesson 14.3), make small steps, and re-run the tests after each one. Common moves: extract function (give a block a name), rename, replace magic number with a constant, replace conditional with polymorphism or a lookup table, inline a needless helper, introduce parameter object (group related arguments). Because each step is tiny and tested, you can always stop, and the code is never left broken. Refactor continually as part of normal work, not in a big rewrite; rewrites usually take longer than expected and lose the hard-won fixes in the old code.

unit-14.7fxm24des5: Layers of interfaces for a 50-line script add noise. Use judgement and YAGNI.
unit-14.mu9iyfntr: Improve code in small, tested steps instead.
unit-14.1twzzd9y4ac: Aim for high cohesion and low coupling; hide details behind small interfaces.
unit-14.geof3ojjri: DRY, YAGNI and KISS keep design honest.
unit-14.29pzvywtphe: SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
unit-14.162v5zx9lv9: Refactoring changes structure not behaviour, in small steps protected by tests.
unit-14.2e6fewczo0f: Learn the reusable solutions experienced engineers recognise: Strategy, Observer, Factory, Decorator, Singleton, Adapter and Iterator. You will see what problem each solves, how it looks in Python, and when not to use it.
unit-14.245fyeodusr: Explain what a design pattern is and what it is not
unit-14.6wwsi50gqe: Implement Strategy, Observer, Factory and Decorator in Python
unit-14.2e229bw1rlr: Recognise Adapter, Singleton and Iterator and their trade-offs
unit-14.1kh8c47lqd0: Choose the simplest tool for a problem, often a function instead of a class
unit-14.19vrfwaqywt: A design pattern is a named, proven solution to a problem that keeps recurring in software design. The classic catalogue is the 1994 book Design Patterns by the "Gang of Four", which describes 23, grouped as creational (how objects are made), structural (how they are combined) and behavioural (how they interact). A pattern is not a library you import; it is a shape you recognise and adapt. Their biggest value is vocabulary: "make that a strategy" or "it is an observer" conveys a whole design in four words. They also embody the principles of Lesson 14.4.
unit-14.286t4wp2945: Two cautions. Patterns solve specific problems; using them where there is none ("pattern fever") makes code more complicated. And many patterns exist to work around limits of languages like Java in 1994. In Python, where functions are objects and you have first-class functions, closures, decorators and duck typing, a pattern often shrinks to a dictionary or a function.
unit-14.21sfbjkoq9j: Strategy makes an algorithm swappable. Instead of an if/elif choosing how to sort or price, the caller passes in the behaviour (a function or object). It follows the Open/Closed principle and is dependency injection in miniature.
unit-14.ltqjn1zwax: Observer (publish/subscribe) lets one object notify many others when something happens without knowing who they are: a button calls its registered listeners; a stock price updates every chart. The subject keeps a list of subscribers and calls each on an event. It decouples producers from consumers, and is the basis of GUI events, the web's addEventListener (Unit 13) and message systems. The risks are surprise (who reacted?) and forgetting to unsubscribe.
unit-14.lu14g2ymms: Iterator gives uniform access to the items of a collection without exposing its structure. Python builds it into the language: for works on anything with __iter__, and generators (yield) make custom iteration easy and lazy.
unit-14.4087de56qd: Factory puts "which concrete class to create" in one place: make_shape("circle", 2) returns a Circle, and callers do not need to know the class names. Adding a type changes only the factory (or a registry it reads).
unit-14.1l53lgbl8n5: Singleton ensures only one instance exists (a configuration, a connection pool). It is the most overused and criticised pattern, as it is global state in disguise, making testing hard. In Python a module is already a singleton, which is usually enough.
unit-14.1hjynw8bs2h: Decorator adds behaviour to an object or function by wrapping it, with the same interface. Python's @decorator syntax is exactly this: @log_calls, @cache, @login_required wrap a function with extra behaviour (timing, retry, access control) without editing it. Adapter wraps an object with an incompatible interface so it fits the one you expect: a thin class that makes a third-party API look like your own Payment interface, which also protects the rest of the code from changes in that library.
unit-14.d5at7wqszd: The sorting rule is chosen by the caller instead of an if/elif chain.
unit-14.20kfrg5hvco: Subscribers register; the subject notifies all of them without knowing who they are.
unit-14.san3cjjxbm: Callers ask for a shape by name; only the registry knows the classes.
unit-14.27b5dhntjpl: Wrap a function to add behaviour (counting calls) without changing it.
unit-14.101gxip1xgw: A third-party class has a different interface; the adapter makes it look like ours.

unit-14.1utzcpjhavi: Writing a class where a function would do
unit-14.flnam1tltl: In Python a strategy is usually just a function.
unit-14.1rve0g9team: Stale subscribers keep objects alive and run code nobody expects.
unit-14.137p5dk33qh: Patterns are named solutions to recurring design problems and a shared vocabulary.
unit-14.s2a9umkc99: Strategy swaps algorithms, Observer broadcasts events, Iterator walks items lazily.
unit-14.ubehclbvue: Factory centralises object creation; Singleton is global state and best avoided; Decorator and Adapter wrap to add behaviour or fix interfaces.
unit-14.wedzci8w3a: In Python, functions and dictionaries often replace whole class hierarchies.
unit-14.q1df5fuv9r: Learn how large systems are organised: layers, modules and boundaries, monolith versus microservices, the dependency rule, APIs between components, and how to record and weigh architectural trade-offs.
unit-14.v13v5i2jcn: Explain what architecture is and why it is about hard-to-change decisions
unit-14.sm22cegvvo: Describe layered, client-server, event-driven and microservice styles with trade-offs
unit-14.1de7qz9x75h: Enforce a dependency rule between layers and detect violations
unit-14.4kpz7qan1b: Explain coupling through APIs and the value of stable interfaces
unit-14.1fa5mzvifjn: Record a decision with its context and consequences
unit-14.kh0m8n1gvu: Software architecture is the set of big decisions about how a system is divided into parts and how those parts communicate, the decisions that are expensive to change later. Choosing a database, splitting into services, deciding what runs on the client or server: these shape what the system can do easily and what it can barely do. It is mostly about quality attributes (Lesson 14.1): performance, scalability, security, reliability, maintainability. There is no best architecture, only trade-offs against your requirements. A team of three building a prototype and a bank processing millions of payments need different answers, and the right answer for the first is usually the simpler one.
unit-14.wuq01zvckx: The central tool is modularity: divide the system so that each part has a clear job and a small public interface hiding its internals (information hiding). Good boundaries let teams work in parallel and replace one part without disturbing the rest. Bad boundaries create a big ball of mud where everything depends on everything.
unit-14.1jv3pdi9p81: Layered architecture arranges code in horizontal layers, each depending only on the one below: presentation (UI), business logic (rules), data access (database). The dependency rule is that dependencies point one way (down, or inward toward the business rules), so you can swap the UI or database without rewriting the rules, and test the rules with no database at all. A layer that reaches around its neighbour (the UI querying the database directly) breaks the structure.
unit-14.1t23ylvgivs: Client-server splits a system between many clients and a server holding shared data and logic (Unit 9, Unit 13). Event-driven architecture has components publish events and others react (the observer pattern at system scale, Lesson 14.5), often through a message queue: producers and consumers are decoupled in time and knowledge, but the flow is harder to follow and debug. Pipes and filters passes data through a chain of transformations (like Unix pipes, Unit 8).
unit-14.1bg2kd95hjq: A monolith deploys everything as one unit: simple to build, test and run, and often right for a small team. Microservices split the system into many small independently deployed services, each with its own data, talking over the network. Benefits: teams deploy independently, parts scale separately, a fault can be isolated. Costs: network calls are slow and fail (Unit 9), data is spread across services, testing and operating are far harder. Many teams adopt microservices too early; a well-structured modular monolith can be split later if needed.
unit-14.1rkhrxpmnkd: Components talk through APIs: a documented contract of what you can ask and what you get back. Stable, versioned APIs let each side change independently; breaking an API breaks everyone using it. Design them so the common thing is easy, the contract is explicit (inputs, outputs, errors), and old callers keep working (backward compatibility). Prefer to expose what a component does, not how it stores things.
unit-14.24u9ke7ebun: Every choice trades one quality for another: caching speeds reads but risks stale data; splitting services scales better but adds network failure; strict security adds friction. Architects write architecture decision records (ADRs): short notes giving the context, the decision and its consequences, so later teams understand why. Diagrams help (boxes for components, arrows for dependencies; the C4 model draws them at four zoom levels), but code and ADRs are the real record. Finally, architecture erodes as quick fixes add forbidden dependencies, so teams automate checks, like the dependency checker below, to keep the structure honest.

unit-14.18ku3lqtpaq: Learn how to find bugs systematically and how to build software that keeps working when things go wrong: the scientific method of debugging, logging levels, retries with backoff, idempotency, timeouts and circuit breakers, and the measures teams use to define reliability.
unit-14.1orm4c9lgxs: Debug by reproducing, isolating and testing hypotheses
unit-14.1mtc3eqe1ip: Use logging levels and structured messages instead of print
unit-14.6rsldiuazb: Implement retries with exponential backoff and explain why idempotency matters
unit-14.ufq5o0uuoh: Explain timeouts, circuit breakers and graceful degradation

unit-14.17qa1x4yrej: Debugging is not guessing and changing things until it works. It is the scientific method. Reproduce the bug reliably, ideally as a failing automated test (Lesson 14.3), which also becomes the regression test afterwards. Isolate it by narrowing down: which input, which function, which version? Bisecting (halve the search space repeatedly, like binary search in Unit 7) is the key technique: git bisect finds the commit that introduced a bug by testing commits half-way between known good and bad. Form a hypothesis ("the list is empty when it reaches line 20"), test it by printing a value, using a debugger breakpoint or reading carefully, and revise. Explaining the problem aloud to someone (or a rubber duck) is surprisingly effective, since it forces you to state your assumptions, and the bug is usually in one of them.
unit-14.w2qgb2piko: Read the error message and stack trace from the bottom: the last line says what went wrong, the frames above say where it was called from. Change one thing at a time. When you find the cause, ask whether the same mistake exists elsewhere, fix the cause and not the symptom, and add the test.
unit-14.gijpp9ogfc: When software runs on a server, you cannot attach a debugger. You rely on logs: a record of what happened. Use a logging library rather than print: it adds timestamps, severity levels (DEBUG detailed, INFO normal events, WARNING odd but handled, ERROR a failed operation, CRITICAL the system is in trouble), and lets you route and filter output. Log enough to reconstruct what happened: what operation, which ids, what failed and why. Do not log secrets or personal data. Structured logs (key=value or JSON) are easy for machines to search. A correlation id attached to every message for one request lets you follow it across services. Too much logging buries signals and costs money; too little leaves you blind.
unit-14.g1ecaiy8y2: Monitoring goes further: metrics (counts, rates, latencies) are graphed over time, and alerts notify a person when something is wrong. Tracing follows one request across many services. Together these are called observability: being able to ask new questions about a running system.
unit-14.doeuy8shnd: In any system with many parts and networks (Unit 9), failures are normal: servers crash, calls time out, disks fill. Reliable software expects this.
unit-14.1xye677nk81: Timeouts: never wait forever for another service. Set a limit.
unit-14.1jswim9wpb5: Retries: a transient failure (a dropped packet) often succeeds on the second try. Use exponential backoff: wait 1 s, then 2, then 4, with a little random jitter, so thousands of clients do not retry at the same moment and overload a struggling server. Cap the attempts.
unit-14.1udrto5o94p: Idempotency: an operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Retrying is only safe for those. "Set the balance to 100" is idempotent; "add 10" is not, so a retried payment can charge twice. Give each request a unique idempotency key, which the server remembers, to make it safe.
unit-14.ifget6p9pb: Circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling the broken service for a while ("open" the circuit), fail fast, then cautiously try one request ("half-open") to see if it recovered. This protects both sides.
unit-14.eclpq6ch8c: Graceful degradation: when a part fails, keep the rest useful (show cached data, hide the recommendations) instead of an error page.
unit-14.fvq9u9nl44: Teams define reliability with numbers: a service level objective (SLO), such as "99.9% of requests succeed each month". 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month; 99.99% allows about 4. The gap is the error budget: while it lasts, ship features; when it is spent, focus on stability. After an incident a team holds a blameless post-mortem: it asks what in the system and process allowed the mistake, not who made it.

unit-14.11ayoipzc8f: Binary search over versions finds the first bad one in about log2(n) tests, which is what git bisect does.

unit-14.1ollopywzkb: Learn how teams keep quality high as code grows: code review, style and linting, measuring complexity, continuous integration and delivery pipelines, deployment strategies, and managing technical debt.
unit-14.nq7jsb6vog: Explain what code review, linting and static analysis catch
unit-14.1gns2shvxms: Compute cyclomatic complexity of a function from its syntax tree
unit-14.1kl41hkwofh: Describe a CI/CD pipeline and its stages
unit-14.1n77zdkwkwy: Compare deployment strategies such as blue-green, canary and feature flags
unit-14.mz8en4ybbq: Explain technical debt and decide when to pay it down
unit-14.xydbvg6dm1: Quality is maintained by habit and by tools. Code review: before a change is merged, a teammate reads it. Reviews catch bugs, spread knowledge, and keep the style consistent; the best reviews are kind, specific and about the code, not the person. Keep changes small so they can be reviewed well.
unit-14.ctwb7czxo9: A style guide (Python's is PEP 8) removes pointless arguments, and a formatter such as Black applies it automatically. A linter (flake8, ruff) reads the code without running it and flags likely mistakes: unused variables, undefined names, suspicious patterns. Static analysis goes further and a type checker (mypy) uses type hints (Unit 4) to find mismatches before the code runs. All of these run automatically on every change, so review time goes to design and logic rather than commas.
unit-14.2eff28h2b8f: Metrics can point to trouble spots, but only point. Cyclomatic complexity counts the independent paths through a function: start at 1 and add 1 for each decision (if, elif, for, while, except, each and/or, and each branch of a conditional expression). Under about 10 is comfortable; much higher means a function is hard to test (each path needs a test case) and hard to understand. It is a prompt to refactor (Lesson 14.4), not a score to chase.
unit-14.j165ita1c: In continuous integration (CI), every push automatically triggers a server to build the project and run the tests, linters and checks, and reports pass or fail within minutes. Developers merge to the main branch often (at least daily) so problems surface while the change is small and fresh, instead of in a painful "integration week" before release. A broken main branch is fixed first, before anything else.
unit-14.qeilwej0m5: Continuous delivery extends the pipeline so every change that passes can be released at the push of a button; continuous deployment releases it automatically. A typical pipeline has stages: build (compile or package), test (unit, then integration), analyse (lint, security scan), deploy to staging (a copy of production), deploy to production. Each stage gates the next; the early stages are fast so developers get feedback quickly. Builds should be reproducible: the same input gives the same output, with dependencies pinned. This very project builds its web and desktop apps this way.
unit-14.bvd6x8r8o0: Release safely: blue-green runs two identical environments and switches traffic from old (blue) to new (green), allowing instant rollback. Canary releases send the new version to 1 to 5% of users first and watch the metrics before widening. Feature flags ship code switched off and enable it for chosen users, separating deploying from releasing. Always have a rollback plan, and make database changes (migrations) backward-compatible so old and new code can run together.
unit-14.27vuop65g90: Technical debt is a metaphor: a quick, imperfect solution gets the feature out faster now, but, like a loan, charges interest: every later change in that area is slower and riskier. Some debt is a sensible choice (a prototype to test an idea); the danger is debt nobody tracks. Sources include rushed code, missing tests, outdated dependencies, and designs that no longer fit (the architecture of Lesson 14.6 eroding).
unit-14.od96z1ih7y: Manage it deliberately: keep a visible list, prioritise by the interest it costs (code you change every week, or that causes incidents, matters more than code nobody touches), and pay it down steadily, for example by the boy scout rule (leave the code a little cleaner than you found it) and a fixed share of each sprint. Refuse the opposite trap too: endless polishing delays the value users are waiting for. Dependencies carry debt as well: update them regularly in small steps, because skipping years makes upgrading a huge risk, and watch for known security flaws in them (the supply-chain risk of Unit 11).

unit-14.xv78h5xwf7: Code ships dark and is turned on for chosen users.

unit-14.12lhvtk7gfz: Complexity and coverage are signals. Targeting the number invites gaming.

unit-14.1aitufbil13: Reviews, formatters, linters and type checkers catch problems early and automatically.

unit-14.ztb3w9dfs5: Technical debt is a deliberate trade-off that must be tracked and paid down by interest.
unit-14.2khfedticm: Learn how software is built by people working together: planning a project with dependencies and the critical path, estimating with three-point (PERT) estimates, working well in teams, documentation, and the ethical and legal responsibilities of an engineer, including licences, privacy and bias.
unit-14.27vmvdx2vkm: Compute a project schedule and critical path from tasks and dependencies
unit-14.joufv6emt2: Use three-point (PERT) estimates to express uncertainty
unit-14.1x4g0tkfcrt: Describe habits of effective teams: communication, documentation and code ownership
unit-14.6mg0upi01w: Distinguish common open-source licences and explain privacy duties
unit-14.25rgo3k9jzw: Apply a professional code of ethics to realistic dilemmas
unit-14.2f8jpbnqsfy: A project is a set of tasks, each with a duration and some dependencies (tasks that must finish first). Drawn as a graph (Unit 7) this is a precedence network. Its most useful result is the critical path: the longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish. Its length is the shortest possible project duration, because nothing can finish sooner than the longest chain. Tasks on that path have no slack: any delay to them delays the whole project. Tasks off it have slack, time they can slip without harm. Managers focus on the critical path: protect it, shorten it by splitting or parallelising the work, and add people with care. Adding staff to a late project often makes it later, because newcomers must be taught and communication grows with team size (Brooks's law: with n people there are n(n-1)/2 communication paths).
unit-14.2fdmk492lo: Compute it with two passes: a forward pass finds the earliest each task can start (after all its dependencies finish) and finish; a backward pass finds the latest it can without delaying the end. The difference is the slack.
unit-14.177fm21kq2e: A single number hides how unsure you are. Three-point estimation asks for an optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P) duration. The PERT formula gives the expected value (O + 4M + P) / 6 and a standard deviation (P - O) / 6. For a whole project of independent tasks along the critical path, add the expected values and add the variances (the squares of the deviations), so the total deviation is the square root of their sum. Then a range such as "expected 40 days, about 95% likely to finish within 40 + 2 x 3.2 = 46 days" is an honest commitment. Estimates improve by comparing with similar finished work, breaking work into small pieces, and tracking actual against estimate. Beware the 90% done syndrome, and commitments pressed on people as promises: estimates are not deadlines.
unit-14.1dfpxpsdla9: Most project trouble is about people, not code. Effective teams share a few habits: a clear goal and shared ownership of the code (anyone may fix anything, with review); psychological safety, meaning people can raise problems or admit mistakes without being punished; frequent, direct communication; and written decisions. Documentation should be proportionate: a README that gets a newcomer running in ten minutes, decision records (Lesson 14.6), API docs generated from the code, and comments that explain why, not what. Code that needs a comment to say what it does should be clearer instead. Pair programming and mob programming spread knowledge; code review does too. Avoid the bus factor of one: if only one person understands something critical, you are one resignation away from trouble.
unit-14.2ergbr97yp3: Code you write belongs to someone and others may only use it under a licence. Permissive licences (MIT, BSD, Apache 2.0) allow almost any use, including in closed products, if you keep the notice. Copyleft licences (GPL) require that software built on the code be released under the same terms; the AGPL extends this to software offered over a network. Code with no licence is not free to use. You must follow the licences of your dependencies, and generated or copied code carries obligations too. Open source is a huge benefit but also a responsibility: maintainers are often unpaid, and vulnerabilities in widely used libraries affect everyone.
unit-14.1eipiob2q1q: Software handles personal data, so engineers have duties: collect only what you need (data minimisation), protect it (Unit 11), get meaningful consent, let people see and delete their data, and obey laws such as the EU's GDPR. Algorithms can embed bias: a model trained on past hiring decisions may repeat past discrimination, and a face-recognition system tested mostly on one group performs worse on others. Accessibility is an ethical requirement too, since software that excludes disabled users is simply incomplete.
unit-14.1a6lxego8vp: Professional bodies such as the ACM publish a code of ethics: contribute to society and avoid harm, be honest, respect privacy, give credit, and take responsibility. When you are asked to build something harmful or deceptive, "I was told to" is not a defence; the Volkswagen emissions scandal (software that detected tests and cheated them) ended in prison sentences for engineers. Raise concerns, document them, and know where you will draw the line.

unit-14.18sgvwtvqxk: No licence means no permission, and copyleft code can force your project's licence.
unit-14.rt5m97p4im: Data you hold can leak or be misused. Collect only what you need.
unit-14.161n6nzzaeu: Models learn the biases in their data. Test across different groups.
unit-14.1q7fyttj6ja: The critical path is the longest dependency chain and sets the shortest possible project length.

unit-15.utk4c1tqsn: Meet the vocabulary of the theory of computation: alphabets, strings and languages, where a "problem" is the question of whether a string belongs to a set. Learn the proof techniques you will use for the rest of the unit: direct proof, contradiction, induction and the counting and diagonal arguments.
unit-15.1j3cv4qgrm: By the end you will be able to:
