unit-15.1f7toxv9d6b: What the theory of computation asks
unit-15.t1muxrvukh: Two big questions sit behind everything in this unit. What can computers do at all? (Computability: some problems have no program, however clever or powerful the machine.) What can they do efficiently? (Complexity: some problems have a program but not one that finishes before the universe ends.) The surprise is that these questions have precise, provable answers. To get there we strip computing to its core: a machine reads a finite input, follows fixed rules, and says yes or no.
unit-15.27ts0397c8x: Proving things about "all possible programs" needs a precise model. We study a ladder of ever more powerful models: finite automata (no memory beyond a state), pushdown automata (one stack), and Turing machines (unlimited tape). Each rung can solve problems the one below cannot, and the top rung is believed to capture everything any computer can do. This is the content of the Church-Turing thesis (Lesson 15.6).
unit-15.zazccp3uw9: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, written Σ (sigma). Σ = {0, 1} is the binary alphabet; Σ = {a, b, ..., z} the lower-case letters. A string is a finite sequence of symbols from Σ; its length |w| is the number of symbols. The empty string ε (epsilon) has length 0 and is not the same as "nothing": it is a string, just a short one. Concatenation joins strings: if x = 01 and y = 10 then xy = 0110, and εx = x. The set of all strings over Σ is Σ*. Over {0, 1} there are 2^n strings of length n, so Σ* is infinite but countable: you can list it, shortest first, and within a length alphabetically (shortlex order): ε, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, ...
unit-15.22e7k8u1sor: A language is any set of strings over Σ, that is, any subset of Σ*. {0, 01, 011} is a language; so is "all binary strings with an even number of 1s", "all valid Python programs", and "all English sentences". Because languages are sets we can combine them: union (A ∪ B), intersection, complement (strings not in A), concatenation AB (a string from A followed by one from B), and the Kleene star A* (zero or more strings from A, in a row).
unit-15.etdrwdhd11: Here is the key idea: every yes/no problem is a language. "Is this number prime?" is the language of binary strings that encode primes. "Does this program have a bug?" is the language of buggy programs. A decision problem asks whether a given string is in the language, and a machine that answers correctly for every string decides the language. Everything in this unit is about which languages can be decided by which machines, and at what cost.
unit-15.xbk5txypwj: Theory is proof-driven, so the toolkit matters. A direct proof starts from assumptions and reasons forward. Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of what you want and derives something impossible (the classic: √2 is irrational). Proof by induction shows a claim holds for every natural number n: prove the base case (usually n = 0 or 1) and the inductive step (if it holds for n then it holds for n + 1); the dominoes then fall. A variant, strong induction, assumes the claim for all smaller values. Induction is how we prove things about strings and programs, because they are built up step by step: "a string over {0, 1} of length n has exactly 2^n possible values" follows because each new symbol doubles the count.
unit-15.1koxnleo9y1: A counting argument shows something exists by showing there are more candidates than ways to handle them (the pigeonhole principle: put n + 1 pigeons in n holes and some hole has two). It underlies the pumping lemma (Lesson 15.4). Finally, diagonalisation, due to Georg Cantor, shows some infinite sets are strictly bigger than others. Suppose you could list all infinite binary sequences s₁, s₂, s₃, ...; build a new sequence whose n-th digit is the opposite of the n-th digit of s_n. It differs from every listed sequence in at least one place, so it is not in the list, a contradiction. So the infinite binary sequences are uncountable, while the strings and the programs (which are finite strings) are countable. That gap, more languages than programs, is the heart of Lesson 15.7: most languages cannot be decided by any program at all.

unit-15.ydcotsxa1l: Explain what a DFA can and cannot recognise
unit-15.194cda2p2qz: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) reads a string one symbol at a time, left to right, and moves between a fixed, finite set of states. At the end it either accepts or rejects. It has no memory other than which state it is in, which is why it can only "remember" a bounded amount of information about what it has read. Many real devices are DFAs: a turnstile (locked, unlocked), a vending machine, the lexer of a compiler (Unit 6), a traffic light, the protocol state of a network connection (Unit 11).
unit-15.1izfp1xxy4o: Formally, a DFA is five things (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F):
unit-15.sa6v7cy4o5: Q, a finite set of states;
unit-15.hvug727uks: δ (delta), the transition function δ: Q  times  Σ  to  Q, which says exactly one next state for each (state, symbol);
unit-15.2gi0p7sv3p1: F ⊆ Q, the set of accepting (final) states.
unit-15.1gdyyw8sdhh: The word deterministic means that for every state and symbol there is exactly one move, so a given input always follows one path. The DFA accepts w if the path from q₀ reading w ends in a state in F. The set of all accepted strings is the language of the DFA, L(M). A language recognised by some DFA is called a regular language. In a diagram, states are circles, accepting states have a double circle, the start state has an arrow into it, and each transition is an arrow labelled with a symbol. In Python we store δ in a dictionary from (state, symbol) to the next state.
unit-15.1w8xbx7r85a: The art of DFA design is to decide what the machine must remember and give each distinct piece of information its own state. For "binary strings with an even number of 1s" we only need the parity so far: two states, even and odd, and a 1 flips between them. For "strings that end in 01" we must remember the last symbols that could start such an ending: no progress, last symbol was 0, last two were 01. For "strings whose value as a binary number is divisible by 3" we remember the remainder so far (0, 1, 2); reading a bit b turns the value v into 2v + b, so the new remainder is (2r + b) mod 3. Divisibility by any fixed number needs only that many states.
unit-15.lnebcpixlw: Make the DFA total: every state must have a move for every symbol. If a string can no longer be accepted, send it to a dead state (a trap) that loops on every symbol. Check your design on small inputs, including the empty string.
unit-15.fw99n00vjq: DFAs combine neatly. The complement (strings the machine rejects) is built by swapping accepting and non-accepting states, which works only because the DFA is total and deterministic. Union and intersection use the product construction: run two DFAs at the same time on the same input, using pairs of states (p, q). The pair is accepting for union if either state accepts, for intersection if both do. So regular languages are closed under complement, union and intersection: combine regular languages this way and you stay regular.
unit-15.1mwmrwmbcy9: Different DFAs can accept the same language, so we ask for the smallest. Two states are equivalent if no string can tell them apart (every string leads both to accepting or both to rejecting). Minimisation removes states that cannot be reached from q₀ and merges equivalent ones. The standard method, partition refinement, starts with two groups (accepting, non-accepting) and keeps splitting any group whose members send the same symbol to different groups, until nothing changes. The result is the unique smallest DFA (up to renaming) for the language, which makes it possible to test whether two DFAs are equivalent.
unit-15.ybt91ikn: What a DFA cannot do is count without bound. No DFA recognises 0ⁿ1ⁿ (n zeros then n ones), because that needs to remember n, and a machine with k states runs out of memory for n > k. The pumping lemma in Lesson 15.4 turns this idea into a rigorous proof.
unit-15.1r0tdtil05l: The transition function is a dictionary. This DFA accepts binary strings with an even number of 1s.
unit-15.23m1w5y5ob6: States are remainders. Reading a bit b turns the value v into 2v + b.
unit-15.umncnzac66: Flip which states accept. This works because the DFA is total and deterministic.
unit-15.yqogy90r2c: Run two machines at once. States are pairs; the accept rule decides union or intersection.
unit-15.ii085lto6r: Partition refinement: start by splitting accepting from non-accepting and refine until stable.
unit-15.1s6zm0h0smn: A DFA must have a move for every state and symbol. Send hopeless inputs to a trap state.
unit-15.1c27ec466x5: Swapping accepting states only works if the machine is total. Add the dead state first.
unit-15.1f6qgdtatsu: Using one state per input seen
unit-15.gx78mj55so: A DFA's states are a fixed finite set. Decide what must be remembered and give each distinct situation one state.
unit-15.mij2u1ls1e: A DFA cannot check that the number of 0s equals the number of 1s, since that needs unbounded memory.
unit-15.1t14z0duzyj: A DFA is (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): finitely many states, exactly one move per state and symbol, and no other memory.
unit-15.14l5ajtdfxt: The language of a DFA is the set of strings that end in an accepting state; such languages are called regular.
unit-15.2e3ot03j8fg: Design by deciding what must be remembered; add a dead state to make the machine total.
unit-15.k2pxp4ih1: Regular languages are closed under complement (flip accepting states) and union and intersection (product construction).
unit-15.y17dyy7hh9: Minimisation merges equivalent states and gives the unique smallest DFA; DFAs cannot count without bound.
unit-15.5h6tu8bvdm: Learn nondeterminism: machines that may have several possible moves, or none, and accept if any path leads to acceptance. You will simulate NFAs by tracking sets of states, add epsilon moves, convert an NFA to a DFA with the subset construction, and see that nondeterminism adds convenience but not power.

unit-15.23bo0dqqbqt: Explain why the number of DFA states can grow exponentially
unit-15.kzqzksutrx: A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) relaxes the DFA rules: from a state, reading a symbol, the machine may have zero, one or several possible next states. It accepts a string if there exists at least one sequence of choices that ends in an accepting state. It is not a real machine that guesses: it is a way of describing a language compactly. Imagine that at every choice the machine clones itself and follows all options at once; if any clone ends in an accepting state, the input is accepted.
unit-15.8s5838aoxd: NFAs make some languages much easier to describe. "Binary strings whose third symbol from the end is 1" needs only four NFA states: stay in the start state reading anything, guess that this 1 is the third from the end, then check that exactly two more symbols follow. A DFA must remember the last three symbols and needs eight states. In general a language of this shape needs about 2ⁿ DFA states but n + 1 NFA states.
unit-15.ibsy86vdvq: Formally an NFA is (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) as before, but the transition function returns a set of states: δ: Q  times  Σ  to  P(Q) (the power set of Q). An empty set means "no move": that clone dies. Missing transitions need no dead state.
unit-15.1659eolenox: To run an NFA on a computer we do not guess: we track the set of all states the machine could be in. Start with {q₀}. For each input symbol, replace the set by the union of everything reachable by that symbol from any state in it. Accept if the final set contains an accepting state. This is the clone idea made concrete, and it costs at most |Q| work per step, so simulating an NFA is as fast as a DFA up to a factor of |Q|.
unit-15.1b199vngjoy: Epsilon transitions (ε-moves) let an NFA change state without reading any input. They make it easy to glue machines together: to accept "A or B" add a new start state with ε-moves to the starts of both. To simulate them, take the ε-closure of a set: all states reachable by following ε-arrows any number of times (a graph search, Unit 7). Take the closure at the start and after each symbol.
unit-15.1itwgr35ngk: NFAs are no more powerful than DFAs: every NFA has an equivalent DFA. The subset construction makes it: each state of the new DFA is a set of NFA states. The start state is the ε-closure of {q₀}. The transition from a set S on symbol a is the ε-closure of everything reachable from any member of S by a. A set is accepting if it contains an NFA accepting state. We only build the sets we can actually reach. Our simulation above does exactly this step by step; the construction just records the answers in a table.
unit-15.755qa493xt: The price is size. An NFA with n states can need up to 2ⁿ DFA states, and for some languages (like "the n-th symbol from the end is 1") this blow-up cannot be avoided. So NFAs are exponentially more concise but exactly as expressive: the class of languages is still the regular languages. Conversely a DFA is already an NFA, so the two models recognise the same languages. This equivalence will be used in Lesson 15.4 to turn regular expressions into machines, and you will meet the same idea again whenever a problem says "there exists a choice such that..." (Lesson 15.8's NP is the nondeterministic version of polynomial time).

unit-15.4febp03rd9: You met regular expressions as a practical tool in Unit 2. Here they are a mathematical object. A regular expression over an alphabet Σ is built from just three operations:
unit-15.h2j8g4xao: Union R|S (or R + S): strings matching R or S.
unit-15.1x7xx31mbui: Concatenation RS: a string matching R followed by one matching S.
unit-15.1wf6t1a7o4a: Star R*: zero or more strings matching R, in a row.
unit-15.2cp7usuti7a: The base cases are a single symbol a, the empty string ε, and the empty set ∅ (matches nothing). Everything else in practical regex syntax, like R+ (= RR*), R? (= R|ε), character classes [abc] (= a|b|c) and . (any symbol), is shorthand for these. A regular expression denotes a language: (0|1)*1 is "all binary strings ending in 1"; 0*10*10* is "exactly two 1s".
unit-15.1fat6opt3y4: The central theorem is Kleene's theorem: a language is regular (recognised by a DFA or NFA) if and only if some regular expression denotes it. Three kinds of description, DFAs, NFAs and regular expressions, are the same thing in three clothes. To prove it we convert in both directions; we show the useful direction, regex to NFA, next.
unit-15.7bzdzwc4kh: Thompson's construction builds an NFA (with ε-moves) from a regular expression, one operator at a time, and each piece has one start state and one accept state. A symbol a is two states joined by an a arrow. For R|S, add a new start with ε-arrows to the starts of R and S, and ε-arrows from both accept states to a new accept. For RS, ε-link R's accept to S's start. For R*, add ε-arrows letting you skip R or loop back to its start. The NFA has at most about twice as many states as the expression has symbols and operators, so building it is cheap, and simulating it with sets of states (Lesson 15.3) matches a string in time proportional to the string times the expression size. This is how fast regex engines such as RE2 and grep work. The direction back, from a DFA to a regular expression, works by eliminating states one at a time, replacing arrows with expressions.
unit-15.l6ffc39nwr: A neat alternative to building machines is Brzozowski derivatives: the derivative of a language L with respect to a symbol a is the set of strings w such that aw is in L. For regular expressions it is computed by simple rules (e.g. the derivative of R|S is the union of the derivatives, and of RS depends on whether R matches the empty string), giving a very short matcher: to test w, take the derivative for each symbol in turn and finally check whether what is left accepts ε. The expression is the state of the DFA.
unit-15.26jorhee0en: Finite memory has limits. The pumping lemma captures why. If L is regular, there is a number p (the pumping length, at most the number of states in some DFA for L) such that every string w in L with |w|  greater than or equal to  p can be split into three parts w = xyz with (1) |y|  greater than or equal to  1, (2) |xy|  less than or equal to  p, and (3) x yⁱ z is in L for every i  greater than or equal to  0. The reason is the pigeonhole principle (Lesson 15.1): reading p symbols visits p + 1 states, so a state repeats, and the loop between the repeats (the part y) can be skipped or repeated any number of times without changing whether the string is accepted.
unit-15.8fy3yzoyfk: To use it, argue by contradiction: assume L is regular with pumping length p, pick a cunning string in L of length at least p, show that every legal split xyz can be pumped out of L. The classic example: L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ}. Take w = 0ᵖ1ᵖ. Since |xy|  less than or equal to  p, y lies entirely within the 0s, so xy²z has more 0s than 1s and is not in L. Contradiction, so L is not regular. The lemma is a necessary condition only: it can prove a language non-regular but never that one is regular. Other non-regular languages: balanced parentheses, palindromes, {1^(n²)}, and the strings with equal numbers of 0s and 1s. The next lesson adds a stack to recognise some of them.
unit-15.1uonp1tfgk4: Beware: practical "regex" libraries (Python's re, Perl) add backreferences ((a*)\1), which match non-regular languages like ww, and they use backtracking, which can take exponential time on bad patterns ("catastrophic backtracking", a real source of denial-of-service bugs). Theoretical regular expressions need no such tricks and always run in linear time.

unit-15.brl7ztjbde: A DFA cannot match nested brackets, but programming languages are full of them (Unit 6 wrote a parser for exactly this). A context-free grammar (CFG) generates strings from rules (also called productions). It has variables (non-terminals, like S), terminals (the symbols of the strings, like 0, 1, (), a set of rules A  to  w meaning "A can be replaced by the string w" (made of variables and terminals), and a start variable. A derivation starts with the start variable and repeatedly replaces a variable by the right side of one of its rules until only terminals remain. The strings so derivable form the grammar's language.
unit-15.5czvf2t22v: Example: S  to  0S1 | ε generates ε, 01, 0011, 000111, ..., which is exactly {0ⁿ1ⁿ}, the language that no DFA can recognise. Each use of the rule wraps one more 0 and 1 around the middle. Balanced parentheses: S  to  (S)S | ε. Arithmetic: E  to  E+T | T, T  to  T*F | F, F  to  (E) | n encodes that * binds tighter than +, because * sits deeper in the grammar. Languages with such a grammar are context-free languages; the regular languages are a proper subset (a regular grammar only ever puts a variable at the end of the right side).
unit-15.wg5xzogni1: A derivation can be drawn as a parse tree: the root is the start variable, each node's children are the symbols on the right side of the rule used, and the leaves read left to right spell the string. Parsers in compilers build exactly these trees. A grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees, as E  to  E+E | E*E | n does for n+n*n (is it (n+n)*n or n+(n*n)?). Ambiguity is a problem for languages that must have one meaning, and it is why real grammars encode precedence in layers like the one above. Some context-free languages are inherently ambiguous and every grammar for them is.
unit-15.hwqjwsozlq: The machine matching context-free languages is the pushdown automaton (PDA): an NFA with a stack. On each step it reads an input symbol (or none), looks at the top of the stack, and may push or pop. To recognise {0ⁿ1ⁿ} push a marker for each 0, pop one for each 1, and accept if the stack ends empty exactly when the input does. Balanced brackets work the same way. The stack gives it unbounded memory, but only last-in first-out, so it can match nesting, not arbitrary cross-referencing. It cannot recognise {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, or {ww}: a stack that counts the a's and b's together is emptied by the time it reads the c's. The equivalence theorem says PDAs recognise exactly the context-free languages. Deterministic PDAs are weaker than non-deterministic ones (unlike finite automata): palindromes need the machine to guess the middle.
unit-15.2963qn16qwy: A pushdown automaton is a good picture for how a program's call stack matches nested calls, and why recursive-descent parsers handle nested constructs.
unit-15.xbb2he5onl: To parse in general we use Chomsky normal form (CNF): every rule is either A  to  BC (two variables) or A  to  a (one terminal), plus possibly S  to  ε. Every context-free grammar can be converted to CNF (remove ε rules, unit rules, split long right sides, replace terminals inside longer rules by variables). With CNF, the CYK algorithm (Cocke, Younger, Kasami) decides membership by dynamic programming (Unit 8): for each substring, find the set of variables that can derive it. Substrings of length 1 come from the A  to  a rules. A longer substring from position i of length l is derivable from A if for some split point k there is a rule A  to  BC with B deriving the left part and C the right. The answer is whether the start variable derives the whole string. It takes big O of n³ · |G| time for a string of length n, fast enough for natural language fragments but too slow for large programs, which is why programming languages use restricted grammars (LL, LR) parsed in linear time.
unit-15.ers2up4cmf: Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and star, but not under intersection or complement (the intersection of {aⁿbⁿc*} and {a*bⁿcⁿ} is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, which is not context-free). A pumping lemma for context-free languages exists too, with two pumped parts, and is used to prove languages like {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} are not context-free. Here we need a more powerful machine: the Turing machine of the next lesson.

unit-15.1fxfcmj9ojk: In 1936 Alan Turing asked what it means to compute and answered with a deliberately simple machine, imitating a person with a pencil and unlimited paper. A Turing machine (TM) has a tape: an endless row of cells, each holding one symbol; the input is written on it, and the rest is blank (_). A head sits on one cell and can read it, write a symbol, and move one cell left or right. A finite controller holds the current state and a table of rules: in state q, reading symbol a: write b, move L or R, and go to state q'. The machine starts in the start state with the head on the first input symbol. It halts when it enters the special accept or reject state. If it never enters either, it runs forever.
unit-15.hj3pg5mc4x: Formally a TM is (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject): states, input alphabet, tape alphabet (which includes the blank and anything the machine writes), a transition function δ: Q  times  Γ  to  Q  times  Γ  times  {L, R}, a start state and two halting states. Compared with a DFA it has two powers added: it can write, and it can go back, so its memory is the whole tape and does not run out. A configuration is a snapshot: the tape contents, the head position and the state. A computation is a sequence of configurations, and tracing one by hand shows how little is going on at each step.
unit-15.24nt8jm1bv6: Three outcomes are possible for an input: the machine accepts, rejects, or loops. A language is Turing-recognisable (recursively enumerable) if some TM accepts exactly its strings (it may loop on others). It is decidable (recursive) if some TM accepts its strings and rejects all others, always halting. The difference matters hugely in the next lesson.
unit-15.19x5ylig7rz: Programming a TM feels like writing assembly, but the ideas are familiar. To decide {0ⁿ1ⁿ} (which a DFA cannot) we could cross off one 0 (writing X), travel right to the first 1 and cross it off (writing Y), go back left, and repeat; accept if only X's and Y's remain, reject if the counts differ. For {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, which no PDA can recognise, the same idea works with three markers. To add 1 to a binary number, go to the right end, then walk left turning 1s into 0s until you find a 0 (or the blank) and turn it into 1. A TM can copy, compare, add and multiply by repeating such moves, and "use a marker to remember where I was" is its version of a variable.
unit-15.1ni457pgb4p: Variants do not add power. A TM with several tapes, a tape that is infinite in both directions, a head that may stay put, or non-determinism (several rules for one situation) can each be simulated by the plain one-tape, deterministic machine, usually with a polynomial or at worst exponential slowdown. This robustness is evidence that the model is natural. Different formalisms invented independently, including Church's λ-calculus, Gödel's recursive functions, Post's rewriting systems, random-access machines, and every real programming language (given unlimited memory), turn out to compute exactly the same functions.
unit-15.d1lmz1dfk5: The Church-Turing thesis says: anything that can be computed by an effective step-by-step procedure can be computed by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a theorem, because "effective procedure" is an informal notion and cannot be proven equal to a formal one, but no counter-example has ever been found in ninety years, and every new model has matched it. So when we show that no TM can solve a problem, we conclude that no program in any language, on any computer, ever can.
unit-15.16f845zu9d5: Turing's other great idea: a TM is described by a finite table, so it can be written as a string and given as input to another machine. A universal Turing machine U takes a description ⟨M⟩ of a machine and an input w, and simulates M on w. That is a programmable computer: the program (⟨M⟩) is data. Every interpreter, virtual machine and operating system is a universal machine in this sense (Unit 6 compilers, Unit 10 processes). It also sets up the self-reference at the heart of the next lesson: a machine can be asked questions about machines, including itself.
unit-15.14mgtsk92h2: A rule table maps (state, symbol) to (new state, symbol to write, direction). The tape is a dictionary so it can grow either way.
unit-15.82buqg1le9: Mark a 0 with X, find the matching 1 and mark it Y, return to the left, repeat.
unit-15.1svw9mhkvkg: A machine that moves right forever on blanks never halts. The step limit stops our simulator.
unit-15.1rrlg63vgdw: A rule table is just a dictionary, so one program can run any other. This is a universal machine in miniature.
unit-15.2a9zfe9nzb5: Thinking a TM halts on every input
unit-15.d6fbnrvpf5: It may loop forever. Deciding requires halting on all inputs; recognising does not.
unit-15.1detuy1ek57: The tape is unbounded. A real computer has finite memory, so it is a very large finite automaton; the TM is the idealisation.
unit-15.1yan6wn8fl3: Thinking the Church-Turing thesis is a proven theorem
unit-15.dow2gbq4fm: It links an informal idea (effective procedure) to a formal one. It has never been contradicted but cannot be proved.
unit-15.lkqang8qsy: Assuming extra tapes make a TM more powerful
unit-15.1cayg9ejmu0: They only change speed (by a polynomial factor), never what is computable.
unit-15.njr62pkepr: A Turing machine has a finite controller, an unbounded tape and a head that reads, writes and moves; it accepts, rejects or loops.
unit-15.2e6xc8h1vez: Decidable languages have a TM that always halts; recognisable languages only need acceptance to halt.
unit-15.dqvbdti77y: Extra tapes, two-way tape or non-determinism do not add computing power.
unit-15.1mygwj9ls1y: The Church-Turing thesis: anything effectively computable is computable by a Turing machine.
unit-15.rdu5x15oz4: A universal Turing machine runs any machine from its description: programs are data.
unit-15.o976s5qgjz: Prove that some well-defined problems can never be solved by any program. You will see why programs can be counted but problems cannot, prove the halting problem undecidable by diagonalisation, use reductions to show other problems undecidable, and meet Rice's theorem and the limits of program analysis.
unit-15.1ns5mzp7eta: Explain why there are more problems than programs
unit-15.133r9vj4nqs: Prove that the halting problem is undecidable
unit-15.1ib2fu2e1n5: Use a reduction to transfer undecidability to another problem
unit-15.1388byj21eq: State Rice's theorem and what it means for tools such as bug finders
unit-15.1pxheymvnyl: Distinguish decidable, recognisable and unrecognisable problems
unit-15.16vgjx3vltz: Every program is a finite string over a fixed alphabet, so the set of all programs is countable: list them in shortlex order (Lesson 15.1). But a problem is a language, a set of strings, and there are uncountably many sets of strings (the same diagonal argument as for infinite binary sequences: a language is just an infinite 0/1 table saying which strings are in it). So there are vastly more problems than programs. Therefore some languages, in fact almost all of them, are not decidable by any program. This counting argument is non-constructive: it proves unsolvable problems exist without naming one. To name one we need to point to a specific problem and prove it unsolvable.
unit-15.mir3tql6xa: The halting problem asks: given a program P and an input x, will P halt on x or run forever? It would be wonderful to have such a checker: it would catch every infinite loop before you ran the code. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no program can do it.
unit-15.1pmu9pq61g4: Suppose, for contradiction, there were a function halts(P, x) that always returns True/False correctly. Then write this new program:
unit-15.2npwqcxce2: Now ask: what does D(D) do? If halts(D, D) says True ("D halts on D"), then D loops forever, so the answer was wrong. If it says False ("D loops on D"), then D returns immediately, so the answer was wrong again. Either answer is wrong, so halts cannot exist. The proof is a diagonalisation: line up all programs against all inputs in a table of halts/loops, and D does the opposite of the diagonal. The same self-reference lies behind Gödel's incompleteness theorem and the liar paradox ("this sentence is false").
unit-15.5tt8lutsql: The halting problem is recognisable: simulate P on x and accept if it halts. If it halts you find out; if it does not, you wait forever. So it is recognisable but not decidable. Its complement (does P run forever?) is not even recognisable: if it were, we could run both recognisers at once and decide halting.
unit-15.4lx6b56vo1: Once one problem is undecidable, others follow by reduction: to show B is undecidable, show that a decider for B would let you build a decider for the halting problem (A). Write A  less than or equal to  B ("A reduces to B"): a computable function turns every instance of A into an instance of B with the same answer. If A is undecidable and A  less than or equal to  B then B is undecidable. Example: "does program P ever print Hello?" is undecidable, because we can turn "does P halt on x?" into "does this modified program print Hello?" by running P on x and printing Hello only after it finishes. Other undecidable problems: whether two programs compute the same function; whether a program has a bug; whether a program ever reaches a given line; whether a program is a virus; whether a grammar is ambiguous; Hilbert's tenth problem (does a polynomial equation have an integer solution?); and the tiling of the plane by given tiles.
unit-15.cv6g6ayrdh: Rice's theorem says this is no accident: every non-trivial question about what a program does (its behaviour, not its text) is undecidable. Non-trivial means some programs have the property and some do not. So no tool can perfectly decide "this program never crashes", "this code is dead", "this program sorts correctly". Real tools get around it by being approximate: they may refuse or give up (a compiler's type checker rejects some good programs, a linter reports false alarms and misses things), or they check only syntactic properties, or they run with timeouts. Complete correctness checking is out of reach in general, which is why testing, careful design and proofs on restricted programs (Unit 14) matter.
unit-15.e0z0v7hu82: Note what is still computable: a bounded version is decidable. "Does P halt on x within a million steps?" can be answered by simulation. And one can sometimes prove termination for particular programs; the theorem says no method works for all of them.
unit-15.fzwbxw3gx4: Programs of length n over a small alphabet are finite in number, but the number of languages grows far faster.
unit-15.1e98hzds67a: Example 2: Halting is recognisable but not decidable
unit-15.1pt2l3h4woq: Simulating with a step budget answers 'halts within k steps'. A 'No' only means 'not yet'.

unit-15.102vb4r694t: From 'does P halt on x?' to 'does P' print Hello?', so a Hello-detector would solve halting.
unit-15.idj6ngld9m: Even a single input hides trouble: this loop's termination is an open problem for all n (the Collatz conjecture).
unit-15.18fznmvsbk7: Believing a smarter checker could solve the halting problem
unit-15.1t2huxcnikr: The proof covers every possible checker, however clever. Practical tools approximate or restrict the programs they accept.
unit-15.ck2y87epzz: Confusing undecidable with unsolvable on instances
unit-15.sh04n0bxkz: Individual programs can often be proved to halt or loop. What is impossible is one method that works for all of them.
unit-15.1nldyjne5ht: Treating a long-running program as one that never halts
unit-15.13orv8w8k4f: Running longer is the only way to find out, and you may never learn the answer. A time limit gives 'unknown'.
unit-15.2ch5rnvbbw9: To prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable A to B (A  less than or equal to  B), not the other way round.
unit-15.izej8pu2r4: Programs are countable but languages are not, so most problems are not solvable by any program.
unit-15.6tnzl6p176: The halting problem is undecidable: a program D that does the opposite of the predicted behaviour of D on itself contradicts any checker.
unit-15.12obav79ml0: Halting is recognisable (simulate and wait) but its complement is not.
unit-15.v1tvixp87j: Reductions transfer undecidability; Rice's theorem makes every non-trivial semantic property of programs undecidable.
unit-15.221krpk6zb3: Bounded versions such as halting within k steps are decidable, and practical tools work by approximation.
unit-15.29780a23fvf: Move from "can it be solved?" to "how fast?". You will define running time as a function of input size, meet the class P of efficiently solvable problems and the class NP of problems whose answers can be checked quickly, work with certificates and verifiers, and understand the P versus NP question.
unit-15.1y533c5yhe7: Define time complexity and explain polynomial versus exponential growth
unit-15.1u494b7708e: Define P and NP using deciders and verifiers
unit-15.fxgk4khd0f: Write a polynomial-time verifier for problems such as SAT, subset sum and Hamiltonian path
unit-15.2av6x8a99wb: Explain why checking can be easier than finding
unit-15.eely63jp74: State the P versus NP question and what it would mean to answer it
unit-15.1jlgpmjue5: Some solvable problems are solvable only in theory: a program exists but would not finish before the sun burns out. We measure the running time of a Turing machine (or any program, since they all simulate each other with only polynomial slowdown) as a function of the input size n: the longest running time over all inputs of that length (the worst case, as in Unit 4). We care about how it grows, so we use Big-O: a polynomial algorithm takes big O of nᵏ steps for some constant k; an exponential one takes something like 2ⁿ.
unit-15.n6qcvufl6a: The difference is dramatic. At a billion steps a second, an n² algorithm handles n = 100,000 in about 10 seconds, but a 2ⁿ algorithm handles n = 60 in over 30 years and n = 100 in more time than the age of the universe. Doubling the speed of a computer lets a 2ⁿ algorithm handle only one more input symbol. So polynomial time is the working definition of "efficient". This is a convention, and a rough one (n¹⁰⁰ is not practical, and some exponential algorithms are fine on real data), but it is robust: polynomial time is the same for every reasonable machine model (the extended Church-Turing thesis), and polynomials are closed under composition, so calling an efficient subroutine a polynomial number of times is efficient.
unit-15.1yssdt466at: P is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time. Sorting, shortest paths (Unit 8), connectivity, primality testing (proved in P in 2002), matching, linear programming and 2-colouring a graph are all in P.
unit-15.22sy9uk0ff3: Many important problems seem to have no polynomial algorithm but share a special feature: if someone shows you a solution, you can check it quickly. A certificate (or witness) is such a proof of a "yes" answer, and a verifier is a polynomial-time algorithm that checks a candidate certificate against the input. NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) is the class of decision problems that have a polynomial-time verifier, equivalently, solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic machine that guesses the certificate (the NFA idea of Lesson 15.3 applied to time: "there exists a choice such that..."). Examples:
unit-15.oysbkw5eyj: SAT (satisfiability): is there an assignment of true/false to the variables that makes a Boolean formula true? Certificate: the assignment; verification: evaluate the formula.
unit-15.2apztect558: Subset sum: does some subset of these numbers add up to the target? Certificate: the subset.
unit-15.13g5s41fb2l: Hamiltonian path: is there a path through a graph visiting every vertex exactly once? Certificate: the path (the vertex order).
unit-15.tsi64oo19d: Clique: does the graph contain k vertices all pairwise adjacent? Vertex cover, graph colouring with 3 colours, travelling salesperson (is there a tour of length at most L?), the knapsack decision version, and integer factoring (does n have a factor below k?) are in NP as well.
unit-15.1znfb7k9zml: Every problem in P is in NP (a verifier can ignore the certificate and just solve the problem), so P ⊆ NP. The great open question is whether P = NP: can every problem whose solutions are quick to check also be quickly solved? Almost everyone believes not: finding a proof seems harder than checking one, finding a needle harder than recognising it, writing a symphony harder than recognising a good one. But after more than fifty years nobody has proved it, and it is one of the seven Clay Millennium Problems with a million-dollar prize. If P = NP then breaking most cryptography (Unit 16), optimal scheduling, protein design and mathematical theorem finding would all be efficiently solvable; the world would change.
unit-15.270zdnpm7en: Brute force always works for problems in NP, since there are finitely many candidate certificates: try them all. SAT with n variables has 2ⁿ assignments; subset sum with n numbers has 2ⁿ subsets; Hamiltonian path has up to n! orderings. That is exponential time, so NP ⊆ EXPTIME. The truth for each problem lies somewhere between P (known fast algorithm) and exponential (known only slow). For many, we have clever algorithms (dynamic programming for subset sum with small numbers, Unit 8; SAT solvers that handle millions of variables on real inputs) but nothing that is polynomial in the worst case.
unit-15.23w0ue9tvt2: Two warnings about the definitions. First, NP means "verifiable quickly", not "not polynomial": it contains P. Second, the definition covers only yes answers: proving that a formula is unsatisfiable has no obvious short certificate. The class of problems whose "no" answers have short certificates is coNP; whether NP = coNP is also open. Between P and NP there are suspected "intermediate" problems such as graph isomorphism and integer factoring, which are not known to be in P and are not believed to be NP-complete (Lesson 15.9). Finally, complexity classes exist for space too: PSPACE contains problems solvable using a polynomial amount of memory, however long they take, such as many two-player game positions. The known chain is P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME, with P  not equal to  EXPTIME proven, so at least one of these inclusions is strict, but we don't know which.
unit-15.2fq8gcu7tx8: How long would n steps, n^2, n^3 and 2^n take at a billion steps per second?
unit-15.2boda7ugvl8: Checking an assignment is easy: evaluate each clause. Finding one by brute force tries all 2^n.

unit-15.q7f7js1xdz: 2-SAT clauses force implications, so propagation solves it in polynomial time. This simple solver is a tiny taste.
unit-15.pkxenoy9rb: NP means nondeterministic polynomial time, or quickly verifiable. P is inside NP.
unit-15.el2sdfk180: Exponential algorithms are fine for small inputs. And practical SAT solvers handle huge instances that follow structure.

unit-15.184pmihtie2: Running time is measured against input size; polynomial time is the working notion of efficient, exponential time is not.
unit-15.2f6b1v3tn0s: P: problems decidable in polynomial time. NP: problems whose yes-answers have short certificates a polynomial verifier can check.
unit-15.xyvspkrop2: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME; whether P = NP is the most famous open problem in computer science.
unit-15.1tqkxuoj0cx: Brute force over certificates solves any NP problem in exponential time; no polynomial method is known for SAT, Hamiltonian path or subset sum.
unit-15.os9s2gnro9: Subset sum with small numbers is solvable by dynamic programming (pseudo-polynomial), which does not resolve P vs NP.
unit-15.1fuayr8e7mp: Learn how problems are shown to be as hard as any in NP, using polynomial-time reductions, and how to reduce 3-SAT to independent set, clique and vertex cover. Then learn what engineers do when a problem is NP-complete: exact search with pruning, approximation algorithms, heuristics and special cases.
unit-15.1sxyzng7br3: Define polynomial-time reductions, NP-hard and NP-complete
unit-15.1er3ejwufun: Explain the Cook-Levin theorem and why SAT is the first NP-complete problem
unit-15.1dldbyy2fba: Reduce 3-SAT to independent set, and independent set to clique and vertex cover

unit-15.1ep2bkycsbq: Inside NP there are problems that are, in a precise sense, the hardest. A polynomial-time reduction from A to B (written A  less than or equal to ₚ B) is a function, computable in polynomial time, that converts every instance x of A into an instance f(x) of B such that x is a yes-instance of A if and only if f(x) is a yes-instance of B. If we could solve B fast, we could solve A fast: convert, then solve. (Compare the reductions of Lesson 15.7, which only asked for computability.) A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it, and NP-complete if it is also in NP. An NP-complete problem is therefore a hardest problem in NP: a fast algorithm for any one of them would solve every problem in NP fast, and so would prove P = NP. Conversely, if P  not equal to  NP, none of them has a polynomial algorithm.
unit-15.1opvpx5v690: How do we get the first one? The Cook-Levin theorem (1971) proved SAT is NP-complete. The idea: any problem in NP has a polynomial-time verifier running on a Turing machine; the machine's computation, a table of tape contents over time, can be described by a huge Boolean formula that is satisfiable exactly when the verifier can be made to accept, so the formula encodes "there is a certificate that makes the machine accept". Once SAT is known to be hard, new problems are shown hard by reducing a known hard problem to them. In 1972 Richard Karp did this for 21 problems, and now thousands of problems in scheduling, packing, routing, logic, games and biology are known to be NP-complete.
unit-15.tfxq6wg4xn: 3-SAT restricts SAT to formulas in which every clause has exactly three literals. It is still NP-complete (any clause can be broken into three-literal clauses with extra variables), while 2-SAT is in P (Lesson 15.8). It is the usual starting point.
unit-15.morflk4ah7: 3-SAT  less than or equal to ₚ Independent Set. An independent set of size k in a graph is k vertices with no edge between any two of them. Given a 3-SAT formula with m clauses, build a graph with a triangle for each clause (one vertex for each of its three literals) and add an edge between every pair of vertices labelled by complementary literals (x and ¬x). Ask for an independent set of size m. An independent set can take at most one vertex from each triangle (they are connected), so size m means exactly one literal per clause; the extra edges forbid choosing both x and ¬x. Setting the chosen literals true gives a satisfying assignment, and a satisfying assignment gives one true literal per clause, which gives the independent set. So the formula is satisfiable iff the graph has an independent set of size m.
unit-15.1kdr4v99i5g: The rest follow easily. Independent set  less than or equal to ₚ Clique: a set is independent in G exactly when it is a clique in the complement graph (edges and non-edges swapped). Independent set  less than or equal to ₚ Vertex cover: a vertex cover is a set of vertices touching every edge, and S is independent exactly when all the vertices outside S form a vertex cover, so a graph has an independent set of size k iff it has a vertex cover of size n  minus  k. These facts mean that Clique, Independent Set and Vertex Cover are all NP-complete, three faces of the same problem.
unit-15.chiwtl78a8: NP-completeness is not a reason to give up; it tells you which expectations to drop. Engineers use several strategies.
unit-15.jp2kz49ef2: Exact search with pruning. Backtracking explores the space of choices but abandons a branch as soon as it cannot succeed. For SAT, DPLL assigns variables one at a time, simplifies the formula, and uses unit propagation (a clause with one remaining literal forces that literal). Modern SAT solvers extend this with clause learning and run on formulas with millions of variables, routinely solving hardware verification, planning and scheduling problems that look impossible by theory, because real instances have structure.
unit-15.1uh8ew0an68: Approximation algorithms run in polynomial time and give a provably near-optimal answer. Vertex cover has a simple 2-approximation: repeatedly pick any edge that is still uncovered and add both endpoints; the result is at most twice the optimal size, because the picked edges share no vertices (a matching) and any cover needs one endpoint of each. Some problems cannot be approximated well unless P = NP (general travelling salesperson), while others have schemes getting arbitrarily close.
unit-15.2ftftels4zp: Heuristics and local search (greedy choices, hill climbing, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms) give good answers with no guarantee; common in practice (Unit 17 meets related ideas).
unit-15.2d06yfcdfz6: Special cases. Restricting the input often makes it easy: 2-SAT, bipartite graphs, trees, small numbers (Lesson 15.8's dynamic programming), or a small parameter k (fixed-parameter tractable: vertex cover is solvable in big O of 2ᵏ · n).
unit-15.1wnpo5yz89n: Change the problem. Settle for an average-case, probabilistic or "good enough" answer.
unit-15.1ifuv78x711: A last remark: hardness can be a feature. Cryptography (Unit 16) relies on problems believed hard on average, like factoring. But note that factoring is not known to be NP-complete, and the cryptography needs hardness for typical instances, which is a stronger thing than worst-case NP-hardness.
unit-15.7o4n7srddw: A triangle per clause, plus edges between complementary literals. Satisfiable iff an independent set of size m exists.

unit-15.1173db6j46r: The same vertex sets give answers to three different problems.
unit-15.6rjatjd96w: Assign variables, simplify, and backtrack. Unit clauses force their literal.
unit-15.25cs1q5zgpt: Pick an uncovered edge and take both endpoints. The answer is never more than twice the optimum.

unit-15.10t4fpjtj7u: Always go to the closest unvisited city. Fast, and often decent, but it can be far from optimal.
unit-15.22tlbq577t2: To show B is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem A to B (A  less than or equal to  B), turning A's instances into B's.
unit-15.1dkwix82f3b: It means no known polynomial algorithm for the worst case. Many instances are easy, and approximations and SAT solvers work well in practice.
unit-15.1rbitqeyf33: Forgetting that a reduction must preserve the answer
unit-15.pxo96m87qj: The transformed instance must be a yes-instance exactly when the original is, in both directions.
unit-15.1aotxw9d0yw: An approximation algorithm has a proven guarantee on the answer's quality; a heuristic has none.
unit-15.nj0ws2kzlo: A  less than or equal to ₚ B means a polynomial-time conversion that preserves yes/no answers. NP-complete problems are in NP and every problem in NP reduces to them.
unit-15.9raw6z8ecd: Cook-Levin: SAT is NP-complete. 3-SAT, independent set, clique and vertex cover are NP-complete through chains of reductions.
unit-15.1xgq0rcorhs: A fast algorithm for any NP-complete problem would prove P = NP.
unit-15.2gol5hq7504: Coping strategies: pruned exact search (DPLL), approximation with guarantees (vertex cover 2-approximation), heuristics, special cases, small parameters.
unit-15.ex3zmwl7yx: Hardness is a worst-case statement; real instances and relaxed goals are often tractable.

unit-16.2171kt6hvuq: Learn to think about systems the way both an attacker and a defender do. You will learn the core security goals (confidentiality, integrity, availability), how to describe assets, threats and attackers, how to rank risks, how to reason with attack trees, and why password strength is really about entropy.

unit-16.1ur0mgb6jz8: What security is and is not
unit-16.1b4ee2wnmwc: Security is about making a system behave correctly in the presence of an adversary: someone who is trying to make it misbehave. Most of this course asked whether code does what you intended for ordinary inputs. Security asks what happens when someone chooses the input, the timing, the network messages, or the dependencies specifically to hurt you. A program that works perfectly for friendly users can be completely broken against a hostile one. Defenders must close every hole; an attacker needs one.
unit-16.6nuvkhps4g: We describe goals with three words, the CIA triad. Confidentiality: only authorised people can read the data (a stolen medical record breaks it). Integrity: data and programs cannot be changed without authorisation, or the change is detected (a tampered bank balance breaks it). Availability: the system works when needed (a denial-of-service attack or ransomware breaks it). Related goals: authentication (proving who someone is), authorisation (what they are allowed to do), accountability or non-repudiation (logs that prove who did what), and privacy. No system is perfectly secure, and security always costs convenience, money or speed, so the real question is secure enough against which attackers, at what cost?
unit-16.2b93ttkh58s: Two principles to remember throughout this unit. Kerckhoffs's principle: a system should stay secure even if everything about it except the key is public. Secrecy of design ("security by obscurity") is fragile; well-reviewed open designs with secret keys are not. Defence in depth: use several independent layers (firewall, authentication, encryption, monitoring), so that one failure is not the end. Also least privilege (give each person and program only the access it needs), fail safe (when something goes wrong, deny access), and keep it simple (complexity is where bugs, and therefore vulnerabilities, live).
unit-16.1g0u7bcvd58: You cannot defend against threats you have not thought of. Threat modelling is the habit of asking four questions at design time: What are we building? What can go wrong? What will we do about it? Did we do a good job? Start by listing the assets (what is worth protecting: customer data, passwords, uptime, reputation), the actors (users, administrators, attackers inside and outside), and the attack surface: every place where an attacker can interact with the system, such as network ports, web forms, APIs, file uploads, USB ports, third-party libraries and employees. Reduce the attack surface and you reduce risk: turn off unused services.
unit-16.27pr3j06qpp: A checklist for "what can go wrong" is STRIDE, six kinds of threat: Spoofing (pretending to be someone else), Tampering (changing data), Repudiation (denying having done something), Information disclosure (leaking data), Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege (gaining rights you should not have). Walk through each part of the design and ask which of the six applies. Draw trust boundaries on your diagram, lines where data crosses from less trusted to more trusted (the internet to your server, a user's browser to your database): everything crossing a trust boundary must be validated.
unit-16.1bhl4gce7dq: Not every threat deserves the same effort. A simple risk estimate is likelihood times impact, scored on small scales; handle the highest first. For each, choose a response: mitigate (add a control), avoid (remove the feature), transfer (insurance, a trusted provider), or accept (knowingly live with it). Attackers vary too: a curious teenager, a criminal group after money, an insider, a state agency. A defence that stops the first does nothing against the last, so match defences to the realistic attacker.
unit-16.p9a5ezsn20: An attack tree puts the attacker's goal at the root and lists ways to achieve it as children. An OR node needs only one child to succeed; an AND node needs all of them. Attach a cost to each leaf. The cheapest successful attack follows the cheapest child at every OR node and the sum of the children at every AND node. That cheapest path is the weak link: spend on strengthening it, because strengthening the strong parts changes nothing. A bank vault with a steel door and a cheap lock on the back window is only as safe as the window.
unit-16.21uv1jlj3hn: Passwords show the same logic in numbers. A secret chosen uniformly from N possibilities has entropy log₂(N) bits; each extra bit doubles the attacker's work. A random 8-character password from 94 printable characters has about 52 bits; a random 4-word passphrase from a 7776-word list has about 52 bits; an 8-character password a human chooses ("Summer2024!") has far less, because humans are predictable and attackers try likely guesses first (dictionaries, leaked-password lists, common patterns). Brute-force time is about N/2 guesses on average divided by the guess rate, and the rate depends on how the password is stored (Lesson 16.3): billions per second against a fast hash, a few per second against a deliberately slow one. This is why length and unpredictability matter more than complexity rules, and why password managers that generate random passwords are good advice.
unit-16.j0womvvukh: Likelihood and impact on a 1 to 5 scale. Risk is their product. Rank, then decide on a response.

unit-16.200zvt5k6hg: Entropy measures unpredictability: each bit doubles the attacker's work, so length and randomness matter.
unit-16.2ax7liua5bq: Learn how secret-key encryption works and how it fails. You will build the one-time pad, see why reusing a key is fatal, build a small Feistel block cipher, compare modes of operation (ECB, CBC, CTR), and add authentication with a MAC. Everything is a toy for learning: real systems use vetted libraries, never homemade ciphers.
unit-16.2f8mx9kitpv: Explain encryption, keys, ciphertext, Kerckhoffs's principle and the goal of semantic security
unit-16.2dgbhyadh6c: Implement XOR stream encryption and show why key reuse breaks the one-time pad
unit-16.1xlk1nfh6n9: Build a Feistel network and explain block ciphers like AES
unit-16.2dxs3i09ep4: Compare ECB, CBC and CTR modes and explain nonces and IVs
unit-16.1ov5la89aba: Combine encryption with a MAC to detect tampering and explain why you must not roll your own crypto
unit-16.2fqvscnef03: Encryption turns readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using a key; decryption reverses it. In symmetric (secret-key) encryption the same key encrypts and decrypts, so the two parties must share the key in advance (Lesson 16.4 solves how). By Kerckhoffs's principle (Lesson 16.1) the algorithm is public and only the key is secret.
unit-16.1ue0j64mwqx: The simplest cipher that is perfectly secure is the one-time pad: XOR the message, bit by bit, with a truly random key as long as the message, used once. XOR is its own inverse ((m ⊕ k) ⊕ k = m, Unit 9), so the same operation decrypts. Claude Shannon proved in 1949 that with a random, never-reused key the ciphertext tells an eavesdropper nothing about the message, since every plaintext of that length is equally likely. The catches are practical: the key must be as long as all the data, random, shared securely, and never reused. Use the key twice and c₁ ⊕ c₂ = m₁ ⊕ m₂: the key cancels out, leaving the XOR of the two plaintexts, which leaks structure (known words, "crib dragging", spaces in text). This two-time-pad mistake has broken real systems, including Soviet cables in the 1940s and the WEP wifi protocol.
unit-16.l3we9zlhr2: Practical stream ciphers replace the long random key with a short key stretched into a long keystream by a pseudo-random generator, then XOR it with the message. The same rule applies: never use the same key and nonce (a number used once) together twice. Modern examples are ChaCha20 and AES in counter mode.
unit-16.uenpl5f7wp: A block cipher encrypts a fixed-size block (AES: 128 bits) under a key, as a keyed permutation: each key picks one scrambling of all possible blocks, undoable with the key. A good block cipher has confusion (each ciphertext bit depends on the key in a complicated way) and diffusion (changing one plaintext bit flips about half the ciphertext bits, the avalanche effect). It gets there by repeating a simple round many times, mixing in a different round key each time.
unit-16.uu9mcro8w5: A Feistel network (used in DES) is a neat way to build an invertible cipher from any round function, even a non-invertible one. Split the block into halves L and R. In each round: L' = R and R' = L ⊕ F(R, roundkey). To decrypt, run the same rounds with the round keys in reverse order, and the halves swap back. Because the function F is only ever XORed in, it never needs to be inverted. AES uses a different structure (a substitution-permutation network) but the same principle: many rounds of simple steps give a complex scrambling.
unit-16.njvyq4u52b: Key length sets the brute-force cost: a k-bit key has 2ᵏ possibilities. DES's 56-bit key was broken by 1998 and is obsolete; 128-bit AES is considered safe against any foreseeable brute force (2¹²⁸ is more than the number of atoms in a few thousand Earths), and 256-bit keys cover even quantum speed-ups. Real attacks target implementation mistakes, keys, and modes, not the cipher itself.
unit-16.f6t3vp6mbt: A block cipher handles one block; real messages are longer, so we need a mode of operation. The naive ECB (electronic codebook) mode encrypts every block independently with the same key: identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks, so patterns show through. (Encrypt a bitmap image in ECB and the picture's outline is still visible.) Never use ECB. CBC (cipher block chaining) XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting, and starts with a random initialisation vector (IV), so equal blocks differ. CTR (counter) mode encrypts a counter (nonce plus block number) and XORs the result with the plaintext, turning the block cipher into a stream cipher; it can be parallelised and needs no padding, but a repeated nonce under the same key is catastrophic.
unit-16.1idji1aj62m: Encryption alone gives confidentiality but not integrity. An attacker can flip ciphertext bits without knowing the key: in a stream cipher, flipping bit i of the ciphertext flips bit i of the plaintext (malleability), for example turning "pay 100" into "pay 900". So we add a message authentication code (MAC): a short tag computed from the message and a secret key, such as HMAC-SHA256. The receiver recomputes it and rejects any message whose tag does not match, comparing in constant time (hmac.compare_digest) so timing does not leak how many bytes matched. The safe pattern is encrypt-then-MAC: encrypt, then MAC the ciphertext (and the IV and any headers), and verify the MAC before decrypting. Modern libraries bundle this as authenticated encryption (AEAD), for example AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Rules to carry forward: use a vetted library; never invent your own cipher or protocol; always authenticate; never reuse a nonce; generate keys and IVs with a cryptographically secure random source (secrets, os.urandom), never random.
unit-16.jg0nk2vngc: XOR with a random key as long as the message. The same operation encrypts and decrypts.
unit-16.20t8l9ssik2: Example 2: Why you must never reuse a pad
unit-16.1agjqf3zb2u: Two ciphertexts under the same key XOR to the XOR of the two plaintexts. The key vanishes, and a guessed word reveals the other message.
unit-16.181h96rxef2: Each round swaps halves and XORs in a function of the other half. Decrypting uses the same code with reversed round keys.
unit-16.18scbgdorp1: Example 4: ECB leaks patterns, CTR does not
unit-16.12zlaeelww: Encrypt a message of repeating blocks with a toy keyed permutation in two modes and count distinct ciphertext blocks.
unit-16.gsz9gj4e9e: A MAC tag over the ciphertext lets the receiver reject tampered messages before decrypting.
unit-16.138d4e9fo88: With a stream cipher or CTR mode, a repeated (key, nonce) pair leaks the XOR of the plaintexts. Use a fresh nonce for every message.
unit-16.255nthagjup: Identical blocks give identical ciphertext. Use an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM.
unit-16.g6bl8suy12: An attacker can modify ciphertext in predictable ways. Always add a MAC or use AEAD.
unit-16.gsg78oxgre: Ciphers that look unbreakable to their authors are routinely broken by experts. Use well-reviewed libraries.
unit-16.28nwg6v15p5: It is predictable. Use secrets or os.urandom for anything secret.
unit-16.ycq4jaha19: Symmetric encryption uses a shared key; the one-time pad is perfectly secure but needs a random one-use key as long as the message.
unit-16.29whnf4bif3: Reusing a keystream leaks the XOR of the plaintexts, which is why nonces must never repeat.
unit-16.1hb2uw5vhcf: Block ciphers (like AES) are keyed permutations with confusion and diffusion; Feistel networks build them from any round function.
unit-16.6ab1rcpglc: Modes matter: ECB leaks patterns; CBC needs a random IV; CTR needs a unique nonce.
unit-16.1va9ucg3vtg: Add authentication (encrypt-then-MAC or AEAD), compare tags in constant time, use vetted libraries and secure randomness.
unit-16.1kkf95u1dtj: Learn what cryptographic hash functions guarantee and how they are used for integrity, fingerprints, Merkle trees and message authentication, and why passwords must be stored with a salted, deliberately slow key-derivation function instead of a plain hash.
unit-16.8bsqxqv0nr: State the properties of a cryptographic hash: preimage, second-preimage and collision resistance
unit-16.a9e6tduws9: Use SHA-256 and HMAC from Python's standard library and explain length-extension attacks
unit-16.eamwgss7u0: Build a Merkle tree and verify membership with a short proof
unit-16.mq3mdjhj4j: Explain why fast unsalted hashes are unsafe for passwords and how salts and slow KDFs help
unit-16.1kp7o0qq3lp: Implement and verify salted PBKDF2 password storage with constant-time comparison
unit-16.l8syvn4894: A cryptographic hash function maps any input to a fixed-size digest (SHA-256: 256 bits) and is built to be one way and unpredictable. You met hashing as a data-structure tool in Unit 7; the cryptographic version demands much more. Three properties:
unit-16.9h4hjofr12: Preimage resistance: given a digest h, it is infeasible to find any input that hashes to h. (Finding it takes about 2ⁿ guesses for an n-bit hash.)
unit-16.2fcsf78t2do: Second-preimage resistance: given an input x, it is infeasible to find a different x' with the same hash.
unit-16.4lwpndgb3e: Collision resistance: it is infeasible to find any two different inputs with the same hash. The birthday paradox makes this easier than preimages: collisions appear after about 2^(n/2) tries (23 people share a birthday more often than not, the same effect). So an n-bit hash gives only n/2 bits of collision resistance, which is why 128-bit MD5 and the 160-bit SHA-1 are broken for collisions (attackers have produced two different PDFs with the same SHA-1) and why SHA-256 or SHA-3 should be used today.
unit-16.5wy6rok986: Hashes also show the avalanche effect: changing one input bit flips about half of the output bits, so similar inputs have unrelated digests (Lesson 16.2). Uses: a checksum or fingerprint of a file (download integrity, git commit ids from Unit 14), commitments (publish the hash now, reveal the value later), digital signatures (sign the hash of a document, Lesson 16.4), and deduplication. A plain hash proves nothing about who made the data: anyone can recompute it. For that you need a key.
unit-16.172an2tagpj: A message authentication code is a hash with a secret key: only someone who knows the key can produce a valid tag. It is tempting to build one as H(key || message), but for hashes with the Merkle-Damgård structure (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2) this is vulnerable to length extension: an attacker who sees H(key || m) can compute H(key || m || padding || extra) without knowing the key, because the digest is the internal state at the end of m. The standard fix is HMAC, which hashes twice with the key mixed in two different ways: HMAC(k, m) = H((k ⊕ opad) || H((k ⊕ ipad) || m)). Use hmac.new(key, msg, "sha256") and compare tags with hmac.compare_digest. SHA-3 and BLAKE2 do not have the length-extension flaw.
unit-16.1m006kq51tj: A Merkle tree hashes data in a binary tree: each leaf is the hash of a block, and each parent is the hash of its two children. The single root commits to all the data: changing any block changes the root. To prove that one block belongs to the tree you need only the sibling hashes along the path to the root, about log₂ n hashes instead of all n blocks. Merkle trees underlie git (a hash DAG), BitTorrent, certificate transparency logs, Amazon's DynamoDB repairs and blockchains.
unit-16.2fu0uqehffe: A site must check passwords without keeping them, because databases get stolen. Never store passwords in plain text, and never use encryption (a stolen key unlocks everything). Store a hash instead and compare. But a fast, plain hash is still weak. An attacker with the stolen hashes can brute-force offline at billions of guesses per second on a GPU, trying common passwords first (dictionary attack), and the same hash for the same password lets them crack all users with the same password at once. Precomputed tables of hashes (rainbow tables) make cracking instant.
unit-16.1l3c1mkdv16: Two defences. A salt is a random value, unique per user, stored beside the hash and mixed into the input: H(salt || password). Equal passwords now produce different hashes, and precomputed tables are useless because the attacker must attack each user separately. (A salt is not secret.) Second, make each guess slow on purpose with a key-derivation function that repeats the work many times or needs lots of memory: PBKDF2 (many iterations of HMAC), bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2, the current recommendation. Tune the cost so that one check takes around 100 milliseconds: a legitimate login hardly notices, but the attacker's guess rate falls from billions per second to thousands. Store the algorithm, the cost, the salt and the hash together, so you can raise the cost later and upgrade old records when users log in. A pepper is a secret value mixed in and kept outside the database (in a key vault), adding a layer if only the database leaks.
unit-16.28hpp3y72ek: Defence beyond hashing: enforce a minimum length, check new passwords against lists of breached passwords, rate-limit and lock out repeated login failures, never tell attackers whether the username or the password was wrong, and offer multi-factor authentication (Lesson 16.7). Compare the stored hash to the computed one with hmac.compare_digest, not ==.

unit-16.1tj43xu3av8: Cryptographic hashes are one-way, second-preimage and collision resistant; collisions cost about 2^(n/2) because of the birthday effect.

unit-16.uq2pr2smqk: Passwords need a unique salt and a deliberately slow KDF (Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2) so offline guessing is expensive.
unit-16.nqc5kkcvl4: Use constant-time comparison, check against breached passwords and add rate limits and multi-factor authentication.
unit-16.tremcrmbh9: Solve the key-distribution problem: how can two strangers agree on a secret over a channel that anyone can read? You will implement Diffie-Hellman key exchange, textbook RSA encryption and signatures with toy numbers, see why small keys and unpadded RSA are insecure, and follow how certificates and the TLS handshake combine these tools.
unit-16.2czeohya3ss: Explain asymmetric cryptography, public and private keys, and why it complements symmetric encryption
unit-16.1maec5xk5od: Perform Diffie-Hellman key exchange with modular exponentiation
unit-16.1o0aygaljhu: Generate RSA keys, encrypt, decrypt, sign and verify with small numbers
unit-16.26c1xovszlt: Explain why key size, padding and hashing before signing matter
unit-16.18q2mwhmekw: Describe certificates, certificate authorities and the TLS handshake
unit-16.e8gy6mzug6: Symmetric encryption (Lesson 16.2) is fast and strong, but both sides need the same secret key first. How do you share it with a website you have never met, over a network where anyone can listen? Until the 1970s that seemed impossible. Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography solves it with two related keys: a public key that anyone may know and a private key that only the owner keeps. What one key does, only the other can undo. Its security rests on trapdoor one-way functions: maths that is easy in one direction and infeasible to reverse without a secret, such as multiplying two large primes (easy) versus factoring the product (hard, Unit 6 and Lesson 15.8), or computing powers modulo a prime (easy) versus finding the exponent, the discrete logarithm (hard).
unit-16.elqeuet9n5: Public-key operations are thousands of times slower than symmetric ones, so in practice they are used only to agree on a symmetric key and to sign; the bulk data is then encrypted with AES or ChaCha20 (hybrid encryption).
unit-16.814e9mg37n: In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a way for two people to create a shared secret in public. Everyone agrees on a large prime p and a generator g (both public). Alice picks a secret number a and sends A = gᵃ mod p; Bob picks a secret b and sends B = gᵇ mod p. Alice computes Bᵃ mod p, Bob computes Aᵇ mod p, and both get gᵃᵇ mod p, because exponents multiply. An eavesdropper sees p, g, A and B, but finding a from A is the discrete logarithm problem, infeasible for large p (2048-bit, or elliptic-curve versions with 256-bit keys). Python's pow(g, a, p) does fast modular exponentiation by repeated squaring (Unit 6).
unit-16.28bewo8dlch: Plain Diffie-Hellman is not authenticated: a man in the middle can run one exchange with Alice and another with Bob and relay (and read) everything. So the exchange must be combined with authentication, using signatures and certificates. Using fresh random a and b every session gives forward secrecy: if a long-term key is stolen later, old recorded sessions still cannot be decrypted.
unit-16.b0ghq22hth: RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 1977), recalled from Unit 6: pick two large secret primes p and q, publish n = pq and an exponent e (often 65537), and compute the private exponent d = e⁻¹ mod (p minus 1)(q minus 1). To encrypt a number m < n compute c = mᵉ mod n; to decrypt compute cᵈ mod n. It works by Euler's theorem; breaking it needs d, which needs the factors of n. Key sizes: 2048 bits minimum today, since factoring 512-bit numbers takes hours on a laptop and 768-bit ones were factored in 2009. Textbook RSA is insecure: it is deterministic (the same message gives the same ciphertext) and malleable (c·2ᵉ decrypts to 2m), so real systems add random padding (OAEP). Also never encrypt directly with tiny messages or tiny e.
unit-16.24so78zp9ez: Run the maths backwards and you get a digital signature: the owner computes s = H(m)ᵈ mod n with the private key; anyone checks sᵉ mod n == H(m) with the public key. A valid signature proves the message came from the key's owner (authenticity, non-repudiation) and was not altered (integrity). We sign the hash, not the message, so large messages are fine and certain forgeries fail; real systems use padding schemes (PSS) or modern curves (Ed25519).
unit-16.pwt4gv51lr: Remaining question: how do you know a public key belongs to the person you think? A certificate is a statement "this public key belongs to example.com" signed by a certificate authority (CA) whose own key your browser or operating system already trusts. CAs can themselves be certified by higher CAs, forming a chain of trust up to a root certificate. A browser checks the whole chain, the validity dates, that the name matches the site, and that the certificate is not revoked. This is public-key infrastructure (PKI). It is only as strong as its CAs: a compromised or careless CA can issue fake certificates, which is why certificate transparency logs (Merkle trees, Lesson 16.3) now publish every certificate.
unit-16.1sozusqv5br: TLS (the padlock in your browser, used by HTTPS from Unit 11) stitches it together. The client says hello with the ciphers it supports; the server replies with its certificate; both run an (elliptic-curve) Diffie-Hellman exchange, with the server signing its part to prove identity; from the shared secret they derive symmetric session keys; and from then on all data is encrypted and authenticated with an AEAD cipher. All this takes about one network round trip in TLS 1.3.
unit-16.1hnqoyj4nvg: pow(base, exponent, modulus) squares repeatedly and never builds a huge number.
unit-16.1o4pl3hn8ai: Both sides get the same secret; the listener sees only A and B.
unit-16.k7p4hczr3l: Key generation, encryption, decryption and a signature, with tiny primes. Never use numbers this small.
unit-16.1tc7af121nl: Factoring a 40-bit modulus by trial division takes moments. This is why real keys have 2048 bits or more.
unit-16.2g0b349qcwg: Example 5: Textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable
unit-16.154uy87muko: The same message always encrypts the same way, and multiplying a ciphertext multiplies the plaintext.
unit-16.1wywozqazbz: Walk from a certificate up to a trusted root, checking each signature with the issuer's key. Here a signature is simulated by a keyed hash.
unit-16.te5hxhnh9g: Use hybrid encryption: RSA or Diffie-Hellman to agree a key, then AES-GCM for the data, with proper padding.
unit-16.1hclbmgk40o: Trusting a public key without verifying whose it is
unit-16.1sj3iw4zq6j: Key exchange without authentication allows man-in-the-middle attacks. Certificates and signatures bind keys to identities.
unit-16.26aar11zr8: Small or reused keys and primes
unit-16.24sifg2fp1t: Use 2048-bit RSA or elliptic curves. Poor randomness in key generation has produced real breakable keys.
unit-16.3difsrr7f0: Sign a padded hash of the message, not the raw message, so forgeries fail.
unit-16.238cchet70e: Click-through on certificate warnings is how man-in-the-middle attacks succeed.
unit-16.hgvfwdx7ut: Public-key cryptography uses a public and a private key based on trapdoor problems such as factoring and discrete logarithms.
unit-16.1yy9a70uvbn: Diffie-Hellman creates a shared secret in public: both compute g^(ab); it needs authentication to stop man-in-the-middle attacks.
unit-16.r8vbzfjvmy: RSA encrypts with the public key and decrypts with the private key; signatures reverse the roles on a hash. Textbook RSA needs padding and large keys.
unit-16.24wdk1jinqc: Certificates signed by CAs bind public keys to names through a chain of trust; TLS uses them with key exchange and symmetric encryption.
unit-16.1ca3fpvv4ml: Hybrid encryption and forward secrecy are standard practice.
unit-16.8gnps2j19x: Understand the most common root cause of vulnerabilities: treating data as code. You will see how SQL and command injection and path traversal work in miniature, how parameterised queries, allowlists and safe path handling defend against them, and how buffer overflows break memory safety in C. Everything is explained for defence, with safe in-memory simulations.
