unit-16.26yebxkg8e3: Many of the worst vulnerabilities share one idea: a program builds a command out of pieces of text, and some piece comes from an attacker. If the attacker's text can change the structure of the command rather than just fill in a value, it is injection. The OWASP Top 10 list of web risks has had injection near the top for two decades.
unit-16.1h3i2dt38g7: SQL injection (Unit 12 warned about it): code builds "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'". A name such as x' OR '1'='1 closes the quote and adds a condition that is always true, returning every row; '; DROP TABLE users; -- can be even worse. The database cannot tell which characters the developer meant as code and which came from the user, because both arrived in one string. Command injection is the same with a shell: os.system("ping " + host) runs whatever follows a ; or && in host. Path traversal uses ../ in a file name to climb out of the intended folder and read files such as /etc/passwd. Cross-site scripting (Lesson 16.6) injects HTML and JavaScript into pages. The pattern is always the same: mixing untrusted data into a language that has control characters.
unit-16.1xcjdam50qr: The cure is to keep code and data separate so that data can never be interpreted as code.
unit-16.9vhtmfbof7: Parameterised queries (prepared statements): send the SQL text with placeholders (WHERE name = ?) and the values separately. The database parses the structure first, and the values are only ever values, never syntax, whatever characters they contain. This is the primary SQL injection defence; escaping by hand is error-prone. ORMs use it for you.
unit-16.26rgbx83gdo: Pass arguments as a list, not as one shell string: subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host]) has no shell, so ; means nothing. If a shell is unavoidable, quote with shlex.quote.
unit-16.19sefi7eurr: Validate input with an allowlist: define what is allowed (a hostname matches [A-Za-z0-9.-]{1,253}, an id is digits only, a role is one of three values) and reject everything else. Allowlists beat denylists (trying to list bad characters), because attackers find encodings you did not think of. Validate on the server, since browser checks can be bypassed. Validate type, length, range and format, and reject early.
unit-16.268fiw6y9e6: Canonicalise before checking: convert paths, URLs and Unicode to one standard form first, then check. For files, join the base folder with the user path, resolve .. and symlinks, then confirm the result still starts with the base folder.
unit-16.19vfik1tg7v: Least privilege: the database account used by the web app should not be able to drop tables or read other schemas, so a flaw costs less. Encode on output for the context where data lands (HTML, URL, SQL, shell).
unit-16.bsmsp8rnop: These layers cover each other's gaps: validation catches malformed input early, parameterisation protects the query even if validation has a hole, and least privilege limits the damage if both fail.
unit-16.yk83biw44u: In C (Unit 9) an array has no bounds check. Writing past the end of a fixed-size buffer overwrites whatever sits next to it in memory: other variables, a saved return address on the stack, function pointers. A buffer overflow such as strcpy(buf, user_input) with a 16-byte buf and a longer input lets an attacker overwrite the return address and redirect execution into their own code (stack smashing). Related bugs: use after free (using memory after releasing it), double free, integer overflow (a length computed as a * b wraps around to a small number, a small buffer is allocated, then a large copy overflows it), and format-string bugs (printf(user_input)). Memory-safety bugs have caused roughly 70% of serious vulnerabilities in large C and C++ projects at Microsoft and Google, and many famous attacks such as the Morris worm (1988) and Heartbleed (2014, an over-read that leaked server memory).
unit-16.2a18f11l6e0: Defences exist at several levels. Write in a memory-safe language (Python, Java, Go, Rust), where out-of-range access raises an error or is rejected at compile time; Rust adds ownership rules (Unit 10) that rule out use after free. In C use bounded functions (strncpy/snprintf, strlcpy), check every length, and compile with warnings, sanitizers (-fsanitize=address) and fuzzers (Lesson 16.8). Operating systems and compilers add mitigations that make exploits harder: stack canaries (a secret value before the return address, checked on return), ASLR (randomising addresses), non-executable stacks (NX/DEP), and control-flow integrity. None of them is a substitute for correct code, because attackers chain bypasses.

You will learn the same-origin policy, how cross-site scripting (XSS) and cross-site request forgery (CSRF) work and how to prevent them, how to protect sessions and cookies, how security headers such as Content-Security-Policy help, and how server-side request forgery and open redirects arise.

unit-16.19idjquuzp4: The browser as a security boundary
unit-16.284r9vwtep7: Your browser runs code from many sites at once, so it needs rules to stop one site from reading another's data. The core rule is the same-origin policy: a page's origin is the triple scheme + host + port (https://shop.example:443), and scripts from one origin may not read responses or the DOM of another. Requests can still be sent across origins (an , a form post, a link), which is why CSRF exists, but reading the response needs the other server's permission through CORS headers (Unit 13). Cookies follow a looser rule: they are attached to every request for their domain, whichever page triggered it.
unit-16.1n3fyxcd5vu: Remember that the client is not trusted. Anything the browser sends (form fields, headers, cookies, hidden inputs, JavaScript checks) can be forged by an attacker with a few lines of code. The server must enforce authentication, authorisation and validation itself.
unit-16.ycpigm1ui: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection (Lesson 16.5) where the target language is HTML or JavaScript. If a site puts user-controlled text into a page without encoding it, an attacker's text such as or becomes code that runs with the site's privileges in the victim's browser: it can read the page, steal the session cookie, make requests as the user, or rewrite the page. Stored XSS keeps the payload in the database (a comment, a profile name) so every visitor is hit; reflected XSS bounces it off a URL parameter in a link the victim is tricked into opening; DOM-based XSS happens entirely in client-side JavaScript that writes to innerHTML (Unit 13).
unit-16.1gwau9hxgoo: Defences. Encode output for its context: in HTML text convert & < > " ' to entities (html.escape); in an attribute always quote the attribute and encode; in a URL use percent-encoding; in JavaScript never splice data into script source (put it in a data attribute or JSON). Modern template engines escape by default, so do not disable that. In the browser prefer textContent to innerHTML. If you must allow some HTML (rich text), use a well-tested sanitiser with an allowlist of tags. Add a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) response header such as default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' that tells the browser to run scripts only from your own origin and to block inline scripts, a strong second layer. Mark session cookies HttpOnly so that scripts cannot read them even if XSS occurs.
unit-16.1mkykegpc1r: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) abuses the fact that browsers send cookies automatically. You are logged in to bank.example; you visit evil.example, which contains a hidden form that posts to bank.example/transfer. The browser dutifully attaches your session cookie, and the bank sees a legitimate-looking authenticated request. The attacker cannot read the response, but state-changing actions are enough.
unit-16.rfzhinrmnv: Defences. SameSite cookies: SameSite=Lax (now the browser default) or Strict stops cookies being sent on cross-site POSTs. CSRF tokens: embed a random, unguessable, per-session (or per-request) token in every form and require it back on each state-changing request; a forged cross-site form cannot know it. Check the Origin header as well. Never change state with a GET request. Re-authenticate or confirm for sensitive actions.
unit-16.1b6c2rvqu3o: A session lets the server recognise a returning user: after login it gives the browser a session id (a long, unguessable random value), usually in a cookie, and keeps the session data server-side; or it stores data in a signed cookie whose HMAC (Lesson 16.3) stops the user editing it. Cookie flags: Secure (only over HTTPS), HttpOnly (invisible to JavaScript), SameSite, a sensible expiry, and a narrow domain and path. Generate ids with a secure random source, regenerate the id on login (to stop session fixation, where an attacker plants a known id before the victim logs in), and destroy the session on logout. Use HTTPS everywhere, with HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) so browsers refuse plain HTTP.
unit-16.1w6alfqm4pw: A handful of response headers harden a site cheaply: Content-Security-Policy (limits where scripts and other resources load from), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (do not guess file types), X-Frame-Options: DENY or CSP frame-ancestors 'none' (stop clickjacking, where your site is loaded invisibly inside another page and the user is tricked into clicking it), Referrer-Policy, and Strict-Transport-Security. They cost nothing and block whole classes of attack.
unit-16.6rsxg7pi0h: Two more mistakes that come from trusting a URL. An open redirect (/login?next=https://evil.example) lets an attacker use your good domain to bounce victims to a phishing page; only redirect to relative paths or allowlisted hosts. Server-side request forgery (SSRF) happens when a server fetches a URL supplied by the user (a "fetch preview" feature): the attacker points it at http://localhost/admin or the cloud metadata address http://169.254.169.254/, reaching internal systems the attacker cannot touch directly. Defences: allowlist hosts and schemes, resolve the name and reject private, loopback and link-local addresses, do not follow redirects blindly, and use network-level egress limits. Parse URLs with a real parser (urllib.parse), never with string tricks: https://trusted.example@evil.example/ has the host evil.example.

unit-16.ul4cwxhod2: Who are you, and what may you do?
unit-16.1wb26q5wauo: Authentication (authn) answers "who is this?" and authorization (authz) answers "what may they do?". They are different checks, and many serious breaches are a correct login followed by a missing authorization check. Authentication evidence comes in factors: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone, a hardware key), something you are (a fingerprint). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines factors from different categories, so that stealing a password alone is not enough.
unit-16.1v0brumbcjy: Good practice for passwords follows Lesson 16.3: hash with a slow salted algorithm, check against lists of breached passwords, allow long passphrases, do not force frequent rotation, and give the same vague error for "no such user" and "wrong password" so attackers cannot enumerate accounts. Password reset flows are authentication too, and a weak one (a guessable question, a token that never expires) is a back door: reset tokens must be random, single use, short lived and tied to the account.
unit-16.1x9o67nzzde: A second factor often is a six-digit code. HOTP (HMAC-based one-time password, RFC 4226) computes HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter), takes 4 bytes chosen by the low nibble of the last byte (dynamic truncation), masks the top bit, and reduces modulo 10^6. TOTP (RFC 6238) is HOTP where the counter is floor(unix_time / 30), so the code changes every 30 seconds. The server and the authenticator app share the secret once (the QR code), and afterward both compute the same code independently with no network traffic. Servers accept a small window of neighbouring time steps for clock drift and reject a code that was already used.
unit-16.25haeh4k0uj: Phishing-resistant factors are better still. Passkeys / WebAuthn use public-key cryptography (Lesson 16.4): the device signs a challenge that includes the site's origin, so a fake site cannot relay it. SMS codes are the weakest, because phone numbers can be hijacked.
unit-16.71pz34t9jj: Even a good system is attacked by volume. Brute force tries every password; credential stuffing tries username and password pairs leaked from other sites, exploiting reuse; password spraying tries a few common passwords against many accounts. Defences are layered: rate limiting per account and per source address, exponential back-off or temporary lockout (careful: permanent lockout lets attackers lock out real users, a denial of service), CAPTCHA after repeated failure, MFA, and monitoring for patterns such as one address failing for many accounts. Compare secrets in constant time (Lesson 16.3).
unit-16.10lea1llqtf: Once you know who the user is, decide what they can do. Access control lists (ACLs) attach permissions to each resource. Role-based access control (RBAC) gives users roles (viewer, editor, admin), and roles carry permissions, which scales to large organisations. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) decides from attributes of the user, resource and context ("doctors may read records of patients in their own hospital, during a shift"). Apply the principle of least privilege: grant the minimum needed, deny by default, and check on every request on the server.
unit-16.26jnarmpzot: The classic flaw is broken access control, including the insecure direct object reference (IDOR): GET /invoice/1042 returns invoice 1042 to anyone logged in, because the code checked "is logged in" but not "does invoice 1042 belong to you?". Changing the number in the URL then exposes everyone's data. Always check ownership, never rely on hiding ids, and beware privilege escalation: a normal user reaching admin functions by calling the endpoint directly or setting role=admin in a request body (mass assignment).
unit-16.18rje1iifuq: Instead of a server-side session, an API may issue a token after login. A JSON Web Token (JWT) has three base64url parts, header.payload.signature; the payload carries claims such as sub (subject), exp (expiry) and role. The signature (HMAC or public-key) lets servers verify it without a database lookup, but pitfalls abound: always verify the signature and expiry, pin the allowed algorithm (an attacker once could set "alg":"none"), keep tokens short lived, and remember a JWT is only signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read it. Revoking a token before it expires needs extra machinery.
unit-16.xaidago2jh: OAuth 2.0 lets a user grant an app limited access to their account on another service without giving the app their password. In the authorization-code flow, the app redirects the user to the provider, the user logs in there and approves scopes (such as read:calendar), the provider redirects back with a one-time code, and the app exchanges it (with its client secret, or a PKCE verifier) for an access token. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top ("Sign in with ..."). The state parameter is a CSRF token for the redirect. Never put tokens in URLs that get logged.

unit-16.1tj1f4a5xiw: Use deny-by-default RBAC/ABAC, least privilege, and ownership checks to avoid IDOR and privilege escalation.

unit-16.fjc274765d: Learn habits that prevent vulnerabilities before they ship: least privilege, safe handling of secrets, careful error handling, dependency and supply-chain hygiene, fuzzing and security testing. You will build a secret scanner, a version checker for known-vulnerable packages, a hash-pinned dependency verifier and a tiny fuzzer.

unit-16.v3ft9impew: Keep secrets out of source code, logs and error messages

unit-16.12hnl99o1ss: Describe how security fits into the development lifecycle
unit-16.24b6o1gi91z: Security is easier to design in than to bolt on. Classic principles (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975) still guide us. Least privilege: every user, process and key gets only the access it needs, so a compromise of one part reaches little. Fail-safe defaults: deny unless explicitly allowed, and when something errors, fail closed rather than open. Defence in depth: several independent layers (validation, encoding, least-privilege database accounts, network rules, monitoring), so one failure is not fatal. Economy of mechanism: simple designs have fewer bugs. Complete mediation: check every access, every time. Separation of duties and open design: security must not depend on the design being secret (Kerckhoffs's principle, Lesson 16.2). Psychological acceptability: a control that people bypass because it is painful protects nobody.
unit-16.hrgj6r2jmm: Reduce the attack surface: every open port, endpoint, feature, dependency and permission is something to defend, so remove what you do not need. Validate at trust boundaries, keep code that handles untrusted input small and isolated, and prefer safe, high-level libraries and memory-safe languages (Lesson 16.5).
unit-16.17keu9i8krm: A secret is any value that grants access: passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys, database URLs. The most common leak is committing them to source control, where they stay in history forever and often end up public. Rules: keep secrets out of code, load them from the environment or a secrets manager, give each environment its own, scope them minimally, rotate them regularly, and revoke and rotate immediately when one leaks (assume it is already compromised: deleting the commit is not enough). Scan repositories automatically for secret patterns before they are pushed.
unit-16.16b2p3l3hvx: Also keep secrets out of logs, error pages and URLs. Detailed stack traces help attackers map your system, so show users a generic message plus an incident id, and log the details privately. Never log passwords or full card numbers; redact them. Limit what data you collect at all: data you do not hold cannot be stolen (Lesson 16.9 on privacy).
unit-16.lpy33tm4qd: Modern programs are mostly other people's code: a typical web app pulls in hundreds of packages through dependencies and transitive dependencies. A vulnerability in any of them is yours. In 2021 the Log4Shell flaw in a ubiquitous Java logging library let attackers run code on servers worldwide, and teams spent weeks just discovering where they used it. Attackers also target the supply chain directly: typosquatting (a malicious package named reqeusts), dependency confusion (publishing a public package with the same name as an internal one so the build fetches it), compromised maintainer accounts, and malicious build or CI steps.
unit-16.2c20qh8u132: Defences. Use a lockfile to pin exact versions so builds are reproducible; pin by hash where you can so a swapped file is detected; audit dependencies regularly (npm audit, pip-audit, GitHub Dependabot) and update promptly; prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies; review what a new package does; keep an SBOM (software bill of materials), a list of components, so you can answer "are we affected?" fast; protect CI secrets; and use signed releases and provenance (verifiable records of how an artifact was built). Version numbers follow semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), which is how advisories express "affected versions below 2.4.1".
unit-16.1krxzn70hmi: Finding bugs: testing, fuzzing and review
unit-16.198v69v6xnm: Security flaws are bugs, so the Unit 14 tools apply with a hostile mindset: unit tests for abuse cases (empty, huge, negative, Unicode, nested input), code review with a security checklist, static analysis (SAST) that scans source for dangerous patterns (such as string-built SQL), dependency scanning, and dynamic testing (DAST) that attacks a running app. Fuzzing feeds large numbers of random or mutated inputs to a program and watches for crashes, hangs or violated properties; coverage-guided fuzzers (AFL, libFuzzer) steer toward new code paths and have found thousands of real vulnerabilities. A property is a statement that must hold for every input ("decode(encode(x)) == x", "the result never contains <"), and checking properties on random inputs is property-based testing.
unit-16.i8puqfy80m: Security belongs in the whole lifecycle ("shift left"): threat-model the design (Lesson 16.1), write secure code, review, test, scan in CI, deploy with least privilege, monitor (Lesson 16.9), and have a vulnerability disclosure policy so researchers can report bugs responsibly. Always test only systems you own or have written permission to test.

unit-16.28mv3kpz659: Security belongs at every stage of the lifecycle, and testing is done only on systems you may test.
unit-16.174yyf4hhvm: Finish the unit by looking at security as an ongoing practice: logging and detecting suspicious behaviour, responding to incidents, protecting personal data and privacy, and the legal and ethical rules that govern security work. You will write log analysers, an anomaly detector, a data-minimisation and anonymisation toolkit, and a risk scorer.
unit-16.kd7tp5ljgn: Design useful, safe security logs and detect brute force and anomalies from them
unit-16.1kvppciofw6: Describe the stages of incident response and the value of backups and recovery drills
unit-16.1ri7xp67wga: Explain data minimisation, pseudonymisation and k-anonymity
unit-16.2foz0xlhfw8: Describe the rules of ethical security work: authorization, scope, responsible disclosure
unit-16.1v5245mgroe: Score and prioritise risks with likelihood and impact
unit-16.1dkjfecjvwd: No defence is perfect, so assume that some attack will succeed and plan to detect it quickly, respond, and recover. Prevention alone leaves you blind; studies regularly find that breaches go unnoticed for months. Detection depends on logging the right events: logins (success and failure), changes of permission, access to sensitive data, configuration changes, errors, and unusual volumes. Good logs are structured (JSON fields, not free text), carry a timestamp in a single timezone, a user and source address, and an event type; they go to a central, write-protected store so an intruder cannot erase their tracks; and they never contain passwords, tokens or full personal data (Lesson 16.8). Alerts need tuning: too many false alarms and people ignore them (alert fatigue), too few and attacks are missed.
unit-16.m7bb8i6ec6: Typical detections: many failed logins from one address (brute force) or one account failing from many addresses (spraying), a login from a new country minutes after one from another (impossible travel), a spike in data downloaded by one user, a new administrator account created at 3 a.m., and requests containing ' OR 1=1 or ../. Tools called SIEM (security information and event management) collect and correlate logs; IDS/IPS (intrusion detection/prevention systems) inspect network traffic; EDR watches endpoints; honeytokens are fake credentials or files that nobody legitimate touches, so any use is a strong alert.
unit-16.9f9rdhwawz: When something is found, follow a rehearsed plan, commonly the NIST stages: preparation (roles, contacts, tools, runbooks), detection and analysis (is it real, how big, what was touched?), containment (isolate the machine, disable the account, block the address, without destroying evidence), eradication (remove the malware, close the hole, rotate every secret that may have leaked), recovery (restore from clean backups, monitor closely), and lessons learned (a blameless post-mortem that fixes the process, not a hunt for someone to blame). Communicate clearly and early with affected users, and obey legal notification deadlines.
unit-16.27bp8hz4mw1: Resilience matters as much as defence. Backups follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two kinds of media, one off-site and offline or immutable, because ransomware encrypts or deletes whatever it can reach, including connected backups. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup, so practise recovery. Measure RTO (recovery time objective: how long can we be down?) and RPO (recovery point objective: how much data can we lose?). Keep systems patched, since most breaches use flaws that were already fixed.
unit-16.j095zrhy61: Security protects data from attackers, privacy governs what data we collect and how we may use it. Personal data (names, emails, addresses, locations, health, browsing history, device ids) belongs to the person, and laws such as the EU's GDPR and California's CCPA give them rights: to know what is held, to correct and delete it, to withdraw consent, and to take it elsewhere, while obliging organisations to collect only what they need for a stated purpose and to report breaches. Engineering principles: data minimisation (do not collect what you do not need, delete what you no longer need), purpose limitation, encryption at rest and in transit, access control and audit trails, and privacy by design.
unit-16.i3u4shnf5f: Removing names does not make data anonymous. Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with tokens (keeping a protected mapping); it reduces risk but the data can still be linked back. Re-identification attacks join "anonymous" records with other data: a famous study found that 87% of Americans are uniquely identified by just ZIP code, birth date and sex. k-anonymity requires every combination of identifying attributes (quasi-identifiers) to be shared by at least k people, usually by generalising (age 34 becomes "30-39", ZIP 80302 becomes "803**") or suppressing rows. Differential privacy goes further: it adds calibrated random noise to statistics so that the presence or absence of any single person barely changes the result.
unit-16.fqpg45zgj7: Security knowledge is dual-use: the same skills defend and attack. The rule is authorization. Testing a system you do not own, or exceeding the permission you were given, is a crime in most countries (for example the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and the UK Computer Misuse Act), however good your intentions. Professionals work under a written scope and rules of engagement: which systems, which techniques, which dates, who to call if something breaks. Penetration testers and red teams attack with permission; blue teams defend; bug bounty programmes invite researchers to test specified systems for rewards.
unit-16.2efi7qym8o8: If you find a vulnerability, practise responsible (coordinated) disclosure: report it privately to the owner, give a reasonable time to fix it (often 90 days), do not access more data than needed to prove the issue, do not publish exploits against unpatched systems, and never extort. Weigh the harms of your design choices: surveillance, bias, addictive patterns and weak protection of vulnerable people are security and ethics problems too. Codes of ethics such as the ACM Code of Ethics ask you to avoid harm, be honest, respect privacy and confidentiality, and take responsibility for your work.
unit-16.zh23wbtb4r: Finally, manage risk rationally. Risk = likelihood  times  impact. You cannot remove all risk, so rank threats (using your threat model from Lesson 16.1), fix the high-risk ones first, mitigate, transfer (insurance), accept or avoid the rest, and revisit as the system changes. Security is a process, never a finished product.

unit-17.1ayufmddobw: Begin Unit 17 with the oldest idea in AI: solving problems by searching. You will learn what an intelligent agent is, how to describe a problem as a state space, and how breadth-first search, uniform-cost search, greedy search and A* find paths, using mazes, puzzles and a heuristic you design yourself.
unit-17.1j3cv4qgrm: By the end you will be able to:
unit-17.ym6nwzy6gy: Describe an agent in terms of percepts, actions, environment and goals
unit-17.15811ba5vzx: Formulate a problem with states, actions, transitions, step costs and a goal test
unit-17.3bfv2l3p5d: Implement breadth-first and uniform-cost search and explain when each is optimal
unit-17.1j5hdt0f5rf: Design admissible heuristics and use them in A* search
unit-17.207ebf8qa83: Compare search strategies by nodes expanded, memory and solution quality
unit-17.rd8g37u8cj: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the study of building machines that do things that would need intelligence if a person did them: perceiving, reasoning, planning, learning, understanding language, and acting. The field began in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College, and its history is a cycle of optimism and disappointment. Early programs played checkers and proved theorems using search and logic. Later came expert systems (hand-written rules), then the statistical machine learning of the 1990s and 2000s, and since about 2012 deep learning, where large neural networks learn from huge data sets. Unit 17 follows that path from first principles, using nothing but plain Python.
unit-17.2n0eees5tg: A helpful unifying idea is the intelligent agent: something that perceives its environment through sensors (percepts) and acts on it through actuators (actions) to achieve a goal. A thermostat is a very simple agent, a chess program is a more capable one, a self-driving car is a very complex one. We judge an agent with a performance measure: how well does it achieve its goals? A rational agent picks the action expected to maximise that measure, given what it knows. Environments differ in ways that matter: fully or partially observable, deterministic or random, one agent or many, static or changing, discrete or continuous.
unit-17.1sfalzpqbb9: Many tasks reduce to search. We describe a problem by: an initial state; the actions available in each state; a transition model (which state results from an action); a goal test; and a path cost (usually a sum of step costs). Together these form a state space, a graph (Unit 7) whose nodes are states and whose edges are actions. A solution is a path from the initial state to a goal state, and an optimal solution has the lowest cost.
unit-17.22r4757q0hd: Search explores the graph from the start. It keeps a frontier of states discovered but not yet expanded, repeatedly picks one, checks the goal, and adds its neighbours. Different rules for picking from the frontier give different algorithms. We also keep an explored set so we never expand the same state twice, which stops infinite loops in graphs with cycles. We judge an algorithm on: completeness (does it find a solution if one exists?), optimality (is it the cheapest?), and its time and space use, measured in the number of nodes it generates. Two numbers describe the problem: the branching factor b (successors per state) and the depth d of the shallowest goal.
unit-17.jvb32eebav: Uninformed (blind) strategies know nothing about how close a state is to the goal. Breadth-first search (BFS) expands the shallowest state first, using a queue (Unit 7). It finds the path with the fewest steps, so it is optimal when all steps cost the same, but it stores about b^d nodes, which explodes quickly. Depth-first search (DFS) uses a stack and dives deep first. It needs little memory but can wander forever in an infinite space and does not find shortest paths. Uniform-cost search (UCS) generalises BFS to step costs: it always expands the frontier node with the lowest path cost so far (g), using a priority queue (a heap, Unit 7). It is optimal with any non-negative costs. This is Dijkstra's algorithm (Unit 8) seen as a search.
unit-17.zugr5uowxg: Mazes, route finding, solving a sliding-block puzzle, planning moves for a robot, and even the "word ladder" game (change one letter at a time) are all search problems, and the same few functions solve them once the problem is described as states, actions and goals. That is the power of the abstraction.
unit-17.blzx27pgfj: Informed search uses a heuristic h(n): an estimate of the remaining cost from state n to the goal. Greedy best-first search expands the node with the smallest h. It is fast but can be fooled and is not optimal. A* (A-star) expands the node with the smallest f(n) = g(n) + h(n): the cost so far plus the estimated cost to go. If h is admissible, meaning it never overestimates the true remaining cost, then A* with a tree search is optimal; with an explored set, you also need h to be consistent (h(n) is at most the step cost to a neighbour plus h(neighbour)), which is true for most natural heuristics. The better (larger, but still admissible) the heuristic, the fewer nodes A* expands.
unit-17.1zer6duq5rv: Good heuristics come from relaxing the problem: removing a rule so that the easier problem's exact cost is a lower bound. For a grid where you cannot go diagonally, ignoring the walls gives the Manhattan distance |dx| + |dy|. For the 8-puzzle, "tiles can jump anywhere" gives the number of misplaced tiles; "tiles slide through each other" gives the total Manhattan distance of tiles, which is larger and so prunes more. A* is the workhorse behind GPS route planning and game path-finding. With a heuristic of 0 it reduces to uniform-cost search; as the heuristic gets exact it expands only the optimal path.

unit-17.25jgpl2ptnx: Learn how a program plays two-player games perfectly or well. You will model a game as a tree, write minimax, speed it up with alpha-beta pruning, memoise repeated positions, limit the depth with an evaluation function, and solve combinatorial games such as Nim.

unit-17.mcpffxsi0s: Implement minimax and explain optimal play

unit-17.11dg2z4t2lm: In Lesson 17.1 the world just sat there while we searched. In a game, an opponent acts against us. We study two-player, turn-taking, zero-sum games with perfect information (both players see everything): tic-tac-toe, chess, checkers, Go, Connect Four. Zero-sum means one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, so we can describe the result as a single number, the utility (for example +1 for a win by the player called MAX, 0 for a draw, -1 for a win by the other player, MIN). MAX wants the number big, MIN wants it small.
unit-17.1q2hnl0xsmw: A game is defined by: the initial state, a function saying whose turn it is, the legal moves, the result of a move, a terminal test (is the game over?) and the utility of terminal states. Unfolding all possible moves gives the game tree: the root is the current position, edges are moves, leaves are finished games. Tic-tac-toe has fewer than 550,000 distinct game sequences, which a computer explores instantly; chess has around 10^120, more than the number of atoms in the universe, so it can never be explored completely.
unit-17.2b6ikofubaw: Minimax assumes both players play optimally. Every state gets a value: the utility MAX can force from there. At a terminal state it is the utility. At a state where MAX moves, the value is the maximum of the children's values (MAX picks their best); where MIN moves it is the minimum (MIN picks the move that is worst for MAX). The recursion unwinds from the leaves to the root, and the best move is the child with the best value. Minimax is a depth-first search, so it uses little memory (the depth of the tree), but its time is big O of b^m where b is the branching factor and m the maximum depth.
unit-17.1esqj03r7dc: For tic-tac-toe, minimax shows that with perfect play from both sides, the game is a draw. The value of the empty board is 0. Notice what minimax does not do: it does not try to trick a weak opponent. It plays the move that guarantees the best result against the best possible reply. Against a weaker opponent a different move might win more often, but it would risk more.
unit-17.13j6c4wrb0q: Minimax examines many positions that cannot affect the decision. Alpha-beta pruning returns exactly the same value but skips those branches. It carries two numbers down the tree: alpha, the best value MAX can already guarantee on the path so far (starts at -infinity), and beta, the best value MIN can already guarantee (starts at +infinity). If at some node alpha >= beta, the opponent would never allow the game to reach it, so the remaining children are pruned (not searched).
unit-17.c8h5tcn6ir: The saving depends on move ordering: examining good moves first produces more cutoffs. With perfect ordering, alpha-beta searches about big O of b^(m/2) nodes, so it can look twice as deep in the same time. Real programs order moves with heuristics (captures first in chess), and add an iterative deepening loop (search to depth 1, then 2, then 3...) that provides the best move so far when time runs out.
unit-17.22qtqqnb2g3: Evaluation functions, transposition tables and beyond
unit-17.98139yyj8r: For big games we cannot reach terminal states, so we stop at a depth limit and score the position with an evaluation function that estimates who is winning. In chess a simple one adds piece values (pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9) plus a bonus for mobility and king safety; in Connect Four it can count open lines. A good evaluation function is cheap and correlates strongly with the real result. Many positions can be reached by different move orders (transpositions), so programs store computed values in a transposition table (a dictionary, Unit 7); this is the same memoisation idea as dynamic programming (Unit 8).
unit-17.1vajrabwpwe: Some games can be solved with clever structure rather than search. In Nim-like games where players alternately remove objects and a player who cannot move loses, every position is either a winning position (the player to move can force a win) or a losing position. A position is winning exactly when some move leads to a losing position. For games with chance (backgammon) minimax is extended to expectiminimax. Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), which plays thousands of random games from a position and favours moves that win more often, powered the programs that beat top Go players (AlphaGo combined it with neural networks, Lesson 17.7). Chess engines such as Stockfish still rely on alpha-beta with strong evaluation. In 2017 AlphaZero learned chess, shogi and Go from scratch by self-play.

unit-17.19kcjv79fu3: Real-world agents never have perfect information. Learn how to reason with probabilities: conditional probability, Bayes' rule and the base-rate trap, a naive Bayes text classifier, updating beliefs about a coin, exact inference in a small Bayesian network, and Markov chains.

unit-17.gb0z8mew8z: A deterministic search (Lesson 17.1) assumes we know exactly where we are and what each action does. Real problems are different: sensors are noisy, a medical test can be wrong, an email might be spam, a robot is not sure where it is. Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty, and a probabilistic agent keeps a belief, a probability distribution over the possible states of the world, and updates it as evidence arrives. Unit 6 introduced the rules; we need three of them, and a fourth that grew out of them.
unit-17.sssj8vu3zs: The conditional probability of A given B is P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B): the chance of A once we know B happened. The product rule rearranges this to P(A and B) = P(A | B) P(B). Two events are independent if knowing one tells nothing about the other: P(A and B) = P(A) P(B). The law of total probability says that if B1, B2, ... partition the possibilities, then P(A) = sum of P(A | Bi) P(Bi): add up the ways A can happen.
unit-17.y6hubltivt: Since P(A and B) = P(A | B) P(B) = P(B | A) P(A), we get Bayes' rule:
unit-17.3q6an9h5ws: P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E)
unit-17.z4q13asee2: Read H as a hypothesis and E as evidence. P(H) is the prior (belief before the evidence), P(E | H) is the likelihood (how probable the evidence is if the hypothesis is true), P(E) is the evidence probability (often computed with total probability), and P(H | E) is the posterior, the updated belief. Bayes' rule turns the easy direction (how likely is a positive test if you are ill?) into the one we need (how likely are you ill if the test is positive?).
unit-17.11eulhscptm: The classic trap is the base-rate fallacy. A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it 90% of the time (sensitivity) and gives a false alarm 5% of the time (so specificity is 95%). If you test positive, what is the chance you are ill? Most people say about 90%. The true answer is only about 15%, because the 5% false alarms among the 99% healthy people outnumber the true positives among the 1% ill. Ignoring the prior (the base rate) gives wildly wrong conclusions in medicine, law courts and security alerts (Lesson 16.9). In practice we compare hypotheses using odds or the log of the probabilities.
unit-17.52bqwua4tw: Naive Bayes and learning from counts
unit-17.1l3wnbyyqpj: Suppose we want to classify an email as spam or ham from the words it contains. Bayes gives P(spam | words) proportional to P(spam)  times  P(words | spam). Modelling the joint probability of all words is hopeless, so naive Bayes makes a simplifying assumption: given the class, words are conditionally independent, so P(words | spam) = product of P(word | spam). The assumption is false (words come in phrases) yet the classifier works surprisingly well, and it is the basis of early spam filters.
unit-17.1xtx5arbg91: Training is just counting: P(spam) is the share of training emails that are spam, and P(word | spam) is the count of the word in spam emails divided by all word counts in spam. A word never seen in spam would get probability 0 and wipe out the whole product, so we use Laplace (add-one) smoothing: add 1 to every count and add the vocabulary size to the denominator. Multiplying many small numbers underflows to zero, so we add logarithms instead. To classify, compute each class's log-score and choose the larger. The same recipe works for sentiment, topic labelling and language identification.
unit-17.1xbumy20ohp: Bayes' rule is a recipe for learning from data. Take a coin of unknown bias p. Start with a prior over many candidate values of p (say 0.0, 0.1, ..., 1.0, all equally likely). After each flip, multiply each candidate's weight by the likelihood of the flip (p for heads, 1 - p for tails) and renormalise so the weights sum to 1. After a few flips the distribution concentrates near the true bias. This Bayesian updating is how a robot refines where it is, and how some sciences quantify evidence.
unit-17.eua3hjwua3: A Bayesian network represents a joint distribution compactly as a directed acyclic graph (Unit 7). Each node is a variable, with a table of its probability given its parents. The classic example has Burglary and Earthquake causing an Alarm, which makes John and Mary call. We answer queries by inference: P(Burglary | JohnCalls, MaryCalls) is found by summing the joint probability over the hidden variables (enumeration) and normalising. Exact enumeration is exponential in the number of variables, so real systems use smarter or approximate algorithms (sampling). A Markov chain models a state that changes randomly, where the next state depends only on the current one (the Markov property): weather, a web surfer following links (Google's PageRank), or the next word in text. Its transition matrix gives the probabilities, and repeated multiplication describes the state after n steps; many chains settle to a stationary distribution. A hidden Markov model (HMM) adds states that cannot be seen directly and observations that depend on them, and powered speech recognition for decades.

unit-17.1irs27xvku7: Traditional programming turns rules + data into answers. Machine learning (ML) flips this: it takes data + answers and produces the rules (a model) that can then be applied to new data. It is the right tool when the rules are too complicated to write by hand (recognising a face, translating a sentence) but plenty of examples exist. Arthur Samuel defined it in 1959 as giving computers "the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed", and Tom Mitchell's version is: a program learns from experience E for a task T if its performance P on T improves with E.
unit-17.15blpfms36z: The vocabulary: each example is a row with features (the inputs, such as height and weight) and, in supervised learning, a label or target (the answer we want to predict). Classification predicts a category (spam or ham, digit 0-9). Regression predicts a number (a house price). In unsupervised learning there are no labels and we look for structure, for example grouping similar customers (clustering, Lesson 17.8). In reinforcement learning an agent learns by trial and error from rewards (also Lesson 17.8). Training adjusts the model's parameters; settings we choose beforehand, such as k in k-nearest neighbours, are hyperparameters.
unit-17.g7u2l2bl76: The simplest classifier stores all the training examples and, for a new point, finds the k closest training points and takes a majority vote of their labels. This is k-nearest neighbours (k-NN). "Closest" needs a distance; the usual choice is the Euclidean distance sqrt(sum of squared differences of the features). The method is non-parametric (no formula is learned), "training" is just memorising, and prediction costs a pass over all stored examples. A very small k (k = 1) follows every quirk of the data, including mistakes; a very large k blurs the boundaries and drifts toward always predicting the commonest class. An odd k avoids ties in two-class problems.
unit-17.1j9udkeyv8l: k-NN depends entirely on the distance, so feature scales matter. If one feature is in the thousands (income) and another between 0 and 1 (a ratio), the large one drowns out the small one. The standard cure is standardisation: replace each value x with (x - mean) / standard deviation, giving every feature mean 0 and spread 1. The mean and standard deviation must be computed on the training data only and then applied unchanged to the test data.
unit-17.ioysypmsb2: A model that memorises the training data scores perfectly on it, which tells us nothing. What we want is generalisation: good performance on new data. So we hold some data back. Split into a training set (to fit the model), a validation set (to choose hyperparameters and compare models) and a test set, touched once at the very end for an unbiased estimate. A typical split is 60/20/20 or 80/20 after shuffling. When data is scarce, k-fold cross-validation splits it into k parts, trains on k-1 and tests on the remaining one, rotates, and averages the k scores.
unit-17.1uvl1rcgc8m: Overfitting means fitting noise: training accuracy is high but test accuracy is much lower; the model is too flexible for the amount of data. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to capture the pattern, poor on both sets. This is the bias-variance trade-off: simple models have high bias and low variance, complex ones the reverse, and the best model balances them. Remedies for overfitting include more data, simpler models, regularisation (Lesson 17.5) and early stopping. Data leakage is a subtle cheat: any information from the test set seeping into training (scaling with statistics from all the data, duplicates in both sets, a feature that secretly encodes the label) gives optimistic scores that vanish in production.
unit-17.awcf0r8ret: Accuracy, the fraction of correct predictions, can be badly misleading. If only 1 in 100 transactions is fraudulent, a "model" that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and completely useless. For a two-class problem we count a confusion matrix: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the cases we flagged, how many were real? Recall (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN): of the real cases, how many did we find? Precision and recall pull against each other (flag everything and recall is perfect while precision collapses), and the F1 score, their harmonic mean 2PR/(P+R), summarises them in one number. Which matters more depends on the cost of each error: a cancer screen wants high recall, a spam filter that hides real mail wants high precision. The same arithmetic as the base-rate effect of Lesson 17.3 applies.
unit-17.20trr2imndh: A good baseline guards against self-deception: compare any model with a trivial one (always predict the most common class, or the average). And always look at the data first: plot it, check for missing values and mislabelled rows, and ask whether the training data represents the situation where the model will be used, a theme that returns when we discuss bias and fairness (Lesson 17.9).

unit-17.11rabhofbwb: Regression predicts a number. The simplest model is a straight line, linear regression: ŷ = w·x + b, where w is the slope (weight) and b the intercept (bias), and ŷ ("y-hat") is the prediction. Given examples (x1, y1), ..., (xn, yn) which line is best? We need a loss function that scores how wrong a line is. The standard choice is the mean squared error (MSE): the average of (ŷi - yi)². Squaring makes errors positive, punishes big mistakes more than small ones, and gives a smooth bowl-shaped function of w and b with one bottom. Fitting the model means choosing the parameters that minimise the loss: the method of least squares (Legendre and Gauss, around 1800).
unit-17.zq7luarfhn: For one feature the minimum has a closed-form answer. With means x̄ and ȳ: w = Σ(xi - x̄)(yi - ȳ) / Σ(xi - x̄)² and b = ȳ - w·x̄. The numerator is the covariance of x and y, the denominator the variance of x. For many features there is also a matrix formula, the normal equation, but it costs a lot for big data, so we usually use a numerical method instead.
unit-17.mill4v05a: Gradient descent minimises any smooth loss by walking downhill. Imagine standing on a hilly landscape in fog: you feel which way the ground slopes and take a step downhill, then repeat. The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives (Unit 6 and calculus): it points in the direction of steepest increase, so we move the opposite way: parameter  from  parameter - η  times  gradient, where η (eta) is the learning rate, the step size.
unit-17.1pkhbrhjdw7: For one feature with MSE loss L = (1/n) Σ (w xi + b - yi)², the gradients are ∂L/∂w = (2/n) Σ (ŷi - yi) xi and ∂L/∂b = (2/n) Σ (ŷi - yi). Starting from w = b = 0 and repeating the update, the loss shrinks toward its minimum. The learning rate is a hyperparameter that needs care: too small and learning is painfully slow; too large and each step overshoots, the loss bounces around or diverges to infinity; a good value converges smoothly. Features on very different scales make the loss landscape a long narrow valley where gradient descent zig-zags, which is one more reason to standardise features (Lesson 17.4). On big data we use stochastic gradient descent (SGD): update from one example (or a small mini-batch) at a time, noisy but much cheaper per step, and the engine of neural-network training (Lesson 17.7). In general, one number tells you if gradient descent has converged: the loss stops decreasing. On a convex loss like MSE there is a single minimum, so the method always finds it; neural-network losses are not convex but descent still works well in practice.
unit-17.1fu7npk2cnu: With d features the model is ŷ = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wd xd + b, written as a dot product of the weight vector with the feature vector plus a bias. Everything extends naturally: the gradient for weight wj is (2/n) Σ (ŷi - yi) xij, and the bias is updated like a weight whose feature is always 1. Linear models can capture curves too if we supply nonlinear features: add x², x³ (polynomial regression) or products of features, and the model is still linear in its parameters.
unit-17.15jnrc8sk68: To judge a fit, the loss on test data (the test MSE) is the honest number. The coefficient of determination R² = 1 - (sum of squared residuals) / (total sum of squares about the mean) tells what fraction of the variation in y the model explains: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than always predicting the mean, and it can be negative on new data for a bad model. Always plot the residuals (errors): a pattern means the model is missing something. Beware that a correlation is not causation, and that a line fitted to a narrow range should not be extrapolated far outside it.
unit-17.1bh934hk2zd: A flexible model (for example a degree-9 polynomial through 10 points) can pass exactly through every training point and swing wildly between them: overfitting (Lesson 17.4). Regularisation discourages complexity by adding a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss. Ridge regression (L2) adds λ Σ wj², which shrinks weights toward zero; for one centred feature the solution is simply w = Σ xi yi / (Σ xi² + λ), so a bigger λ gives a smaller slope. Lasso (L1) adds λ Σ |wj|, which drives some weights exactly to zero and so selects features. The strength λ is a hyperparameter chosen with a validation set or cross-validation. Regularisation reflects a belief that simpler explanations are more likely right, a form of Occam's razor, and is also a Bayesian prior on the weights (Lesson 17.3). Stopping gradient descent early has a similar effect.
unit-17.h77iy56wp0: Regression extends in directions you will meet soon: logistic regression (Lesson 17.6) turns the output into a probability to classify, and a neural network (Lesson 17.7) stacks many such units with nonlinear functions between them.

unit-17.gut2zmml1h: In classification we predict a category. The simplest two-class model draws a straight line (a hyperplane in many dimensions) through the feature space and says "one side is class 1, the other is class 0". It computes a score z = w·x + b and predicts 1 when z  greater than or equal to  0. The line z = 0 is the decision boundary. Data that a line can split perfectly is linearly separable.
unit-17.14zsb1pck8c: The perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958, one of the earliest learning machines and the ancestor of neural networks) learns w and b with a mistake-driven rule. Go through the examples; if the prediction is right do nothing; if it is wrong, nudge the weights toward the correct answer: w  from  w + η (y - ŷ) x and b  from  b + η (y - ŷ), where y and ŷ are 0 or 1. The perceptron convergence theorem guarantees that if the data are linearly separable the rule finds a separating line in a finite number of updates. But if they are not, it never settles. The famous example is XOR (exclusive or): points (0,0) and (1,1) are class 0, (0,1) and (1,0) are class 1, and no single straight line separates them. Minsky and Papert pointed this out in 1969, which cooled interest in neural networks for years, until multi-layer networks (Lesson 17.7) solved it.
unit-17.zqhf1ebmzt: The perceptron says only "yes" or "no". Often we want a probability: "this email is 93% likely to be spam". Logistic regression (despite the name, a classifier) passes the linear score through the sigmoid (logistic) function σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)), which squashes any number into the range 0 to 1: σ(0) = 0.5, large positive z gives nearly 1, large negative z nearly 0. The output p = σ(w·x + b) is the model's estimate of P(class 1 | x). Predicting class 1 when p  greater than or equal to  0.5 uses the same boundary as before (z = 0), but now we also know how confident the model is.
unit-17.oc5j1hy7yd: We train it by maximising the probability of the observed labels, equivalent to minimising the log-loss (cross-entropy): L = -(1/n) Σ [ y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p) ]. A confident wrong answer (p = 0.01 when y = 1) costs a lot, a confident right one costs almost nothing. The beautiful fact is that the gradient is as simple as for linear regression: ∂L/∂wj = (1/n) Σ (p - y) xj and ∂L/∂b = (1/n) Σ (p - y). So the same gradient-descent loop (Lesson 17.5) trains it. For more than two classes, softmax generalises the sigmoid, giving one probability per class that sum to 1.
unit-17.6euxw20ser: The cut-off 0.5 is a choice. Lowering the threshold flags more cases: recall goes up and precision goes down (Lesson 17.4). A ROC curve plots the trade-off for every threshold, and its area (AUC) summarises how well the model ranks positives above negatives, independent of any one cut-off.
unit-17.1e2iv8jyoqh: A decision tree classifies by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about features, like a game of twenty questions: "Is income above 50?" "Is age below 30?" Each internal node tests a feature against a threshold, each branch is an answer, and each leaf gives a class. Trees are easy to read and explain, handle mixed feature types, and need no scaling, which is why they are popular in business and medicine.
unit-17.j406ptidrj: How do we pick the questions? We want splits that make the groups as pure as possible. Gini impurity of a group is 1 - Σ p_c², where p_c is the fraction in class c: 0 for a pure group, 0.5 for a 50/50 two-class mix. Entropy (Unit 6, information theory) is -Σ p_c log2 p_c and plays the same role; information gain is the entropy reduction from a split. The greedy CART algorithm tries every feature and every threshold (midpoints between sorted values), picks the split with the lowest weighted impurity of the two children, then recurses on each side, stopping when a group is pure, a maximum depth is reached, or too few examples remain. Leaves predict the majority class.
unit-17.2847482rhc0: Left unlimited, a tree keeps splitting until every training example is alone in a leaf: perfect training accuracy and badly overfitted (Lesson 17.4). Limiting depth, requiring a minimum leaf size, or pruning reduces this. A single tree is also unstable: a small change in the data can give a different tree. The remedy is an ensemble: train many trees on different random samples (bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating) and let them vote. A random forest adds randomness in the features each split may use. Averaging many noisy but different models cancels their individual errors, cutting variance, and forests and boosted trees (gradient boosting) remain among the best methods for table-shaped data. Other classic classifiers worth knowing are support vector machines (maximum-margin boundaries) and, from Lesson 17.3, naive Bayes.

unit-17.lxzd86m0dz: An artificial neuron, loosely inspired by brain cells, is the unit from Lesson 17.6: it takes inputs x, multiplies each by a weight w, adds a bias b, and passes the sum through an activation function f: output = f(w·x + b). A layer is many neurons looking at the same inputs, written compactly as a matrix of weights (one row per neuron). A neural network feeds the outputs of one layer in as the inputs of the next. The first layer is the input, the last the output, and any layers between are hidden layers. Computing the output for an input, left to right, is the forward pass.
unit-17.2cy3x432z: The activation function must be nonlinear. If it were the identity, a stack of layers would collapse into one linear function (a matrix times a matrix is a matrix), no more powerful than a line. Popular choices are the sigmoid 1/(1+e^-z) (output 0 to 1, used for probabilities), tanh (-1 to 1), and the ReLU (rectified linear unit) max(0, z), which is simple, fast, and the default in deep networks because it avoids the flat regions that slow sigmoid training. With a nonlinearity and enough hidden neurons, a network can approximate any reasonable function (the universal approximation theorem). XOR, which no single neuron could learn (Lesson 17.6), is solved by just two hidden neurons: one detects "at least one input on", another "both on", and the output subtracts them.
unit-17.2cb8jm3uxe1: Training means choosing the weights to minimise a loss on the training data (mean squared error for regression, cross-entropy for classification), by gradient descent (Lesson 17.5). A network may have millions of weights, so we need all the partial derivatives ∂L/∂w efficiently. Backpropagation (popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in 1986) computes all of them with one backward sweep using the chain rule of calculus: if L depends on p, and p depends on z, and z depends on w, then ∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂p  times  ∂p/∂z  times  ∂z/∂w.
unit-17.1r37jhtdcv8: For a network with one hidden layer, sigmoid units and squared-error loss on one example (y true, p output): the output "error signal" is δ_out = 2 (p - y) · p (1 - p), using that the sigmoid's derivative is σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 - σ(z)). The gradient for an output weight is δ_out  times  (hidden activation h_j). The error then flows back: each hidden unit receives δ_j = δ_out  times  w_j  times  h_j (1 - h_j) and its input weight gradients are δ_j  times  x_i. The recipe: (1) forward pass, saving every activation; (2) backward pass, computing each layer's δ from the layer after it; (3) update every weight by w  from  w - η ∂L/∂w. Repeating over the data many times (epochs), usually in mini-batches, drives the loss down. Frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow do the backward pass automatically (automatic differentiation); understanding it by hand once makes everything else less mysterious.
unit-17.294zkkc2frl: Practical issues: weights must start small and random (all zeros would make every hidden neuron identical, a symmetry that gradients never break); if gradients vanish (shrink to near zero through many sigmoid layers) or explode, learning stalls, which is why ReLU, careful initialisation, normalisation layers and residual connections matter; and as always, validation data and regularisation (dropout randomly switches neurons off during training, weight decay is ridge regression) fight overfitting. Optimisers such as momentum and Adam improve on plain SGD by smoothing and adapting the steps.
unit-17.4u9c8arpgs: Images have thousands of pixels, and connecting every pixel to every neuron would need huge numbers of weights while ignoring that nearby pixels are related. A convolutional neural network (CNN) slides a small grid of weights, a kernel or filter (for example 3 by 3), across the image, taking the dot product at every position. The same few weights are reused everywhere (weight sharing), so the layer detects a pattern, say a vertical edge, wherever it appears. Early layers learn edges and textures, later ones parts and whole objects. CNNs drove the 2012 breakthrough in image recognition (AlexNet) and are used for medical images, self-driving cars and more.
unit-17.utau4e9rfp: For classifying into many categories the output layer uses softmax: softmax(z)_i = e^(z_i) / Σ_j e^(z_j), which turns any list of scores into probabilities that sum to 1; the matching loss is the cross-entropy -log(p of the true class). Sequences (text, audio, time series) call for other architectures. Recurrent networks (RNNs and LSTMs) keep a memory as they read item by item. The transformer (2017) replaces recurrence with attention, letting every position look at every other position to decide what matters; it is the basis of the large language models of Lesson 17.9. Deep learning simply means networks with many layers, and its recent success rests on three things: huge data sets, fast GPUs (graphics chips that do many multiplications at once) and better training techniques. Networks are powerful but are black boxes that are hard to interpret, can be fooled by tiny adversarial changes to the input (a security concern, Unit 16), and learn the biases in their data (Lesson 17.9).

unit-17.nhkg3giyj9: In unsupervised learning the data come without labels and the goal is to discover structure. The most common task is clustering: grouping similar items, such as customers with similar buying habits, genes with similar activity, or news stories about the same event. Related tasks are dimensionality reduction (compressing many features into a few that keep most of the information, for visualisation or speed), density estimation, and anomaly detection.
unit-17.214jricsod3: k-means is the classic clustering algorithm. Choose the number of clusters k, then repeat two steps until nothing changes: (1) assign each point to its nearest centroid; (2) update each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it. Each round never increases the inertia, the sum of squared distances from points to their centroids, so the algorithm always terminates, but only at a local minimum: different starting centroids can give different answers, so practical versions (k-means++) choose spread-out starts and run several times. The method assumes round, similar-sized clusters, is sensitive to feature scale (standardise first, Lesson 17.4) and to outliers, and needs k in advance. A common guide is the elbow method: plot inertia against k and look for the bend where adding clusters stops helping much. Other approaches include hierarchical clustering (repeatedly merging the two closest groups, producing a tree called a dendrogram), DBSCAN (grows clusters from dense regions and labels isolated points as noise) and Gaussian mixture models. Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions in which the data vary most and projects onto the first few.
unit-17.15c07xxm0yr: Anomaly detection looks for rare items that differ from the rest: fraud, failing machines, intrusions (Unit 16). A simple method flags a value whose z-score (how many standard deviations from the mean) is large, say beyond 3. Anomalies can also be found by distance to neighbours, by cluster membership, or by how poorly a model reconstructs them. Because anomalies are rare there are few examples to learn from, so these methods are usually unsupervised and need human review.
unit-17.25dn55ibr5w: Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning by trial and error. An agent in an environment repeatedly observes a state s, chooses an action a, receives a numerical reward r and moves to a new state s'. There is no teacher giving correct actions, only the reward signal, which may be delayed (you learn you blundered in chess only at the end). The agent's behaviour is a policy π(s) that picks an action in each state, and its aim is to maximise the return: the total future reward, usually discounted by a factor γ (gamma, between 0 and 1) so that nearer rewards count more: G = r₁ + γ r₂ + γ² r₃ + ... RL trained game players (TD-Gammon, Atari agents, AlphaGo), controlled data-centre cooling, and fine-tunes language models from human feedback (Lesson 17.9).
unit-17.1vnaq74nf3: The first dilemma is exploration versus exploitation: use what you know works, or try something new that might be better? The multi-armed bandit isolates it: several slot machines ("arms") with unknown average payouts; to maximise winnings you must sample them to learn which is best but not waste pulls on bad ones. The epsilon-greedy strategy pulls the arm with the best estimated average most of the time, but with a small probability ε picks a random arm. The estimate is updated incrementally: Q  from  Q + (r - Q) / n, an average without storing the history.
unit-17.248feer3raj: Markov decision processes, value iteration and Q-learning
unit-17.gz83cy49wt: A Markov decision process (MDP) formalises sequential decisions: states, actions, a transition model P(s' | s, a), a reward function, and the Markov property (the future depends on the current state only, Lesson 17.3). The value V(s) of a state is the expected return from s when acting optimally. It satisfies the Bellman equation: V(s) = max over a of Σ P(s' | s, a) [ r + γ V(s') ]: the best action is the one with the highest expected immediate reward plus discounted value of where you land. If the model is known, value iteration solves it: start with V = 0 and apply the Bellman update to every state repeatedly until the values stop changing, then read off the policy: in each state choose the action that achieves the maximum.
unit-17.5nqeu0ppbg: Often the model is unknown; the agent only experiences transitions. Q-learning (Watkins, 1989) learns the action value Q(s, a), the expected return of taking a in s and then acting optimally, directly from experience with no model: after each step, Q(s, a)  from  Q(s, a) + α [ r + γ max over a' of Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) ]. The bracket is the temporal-difference error: the gap between what we predicted and what we got plus our estimate of the future. The learning rate α sets how fast we change. The agent acts ε-greedily so it keeps exploring, and as the Q-table converges, always choosing the action with the largest Q gives the optimal policy. A table is fine for hundreds of states; for huge ones (Atari screens, Go) deep Q-networks use a neural network (Lesson 17.7) to approximate Q, and policy-gradient methods learn the policy directly. RL needs a lot of trial and error, so it is often trained in simulation, and a badly specified reward can be gamed: an agent rewarded for score may loop forever collecting points instead of finishing the race. Designing the reward is a safety question, the subject of AI alignment.

unit-17.5vwtwunzgf: A language model assigns probabilities to text: given the words so far, how likely is each possible next word? Predictive text on your phone is one. The simplest is an n-gram model, counting how often each word follows the previous n - 1 words in a large body of text; a bigram (n = 2) model estimates P(next | previous) = count(previous, next) / count(previous). This is a Markov chain over words (Lesson 17.3). To generate text, repeatedly sample the next word from this distribution, or always take the most likely one (greedy decoding). The output is locally plausible but quickly loses the thread, because the model sees only one or two words of context.
unit-17.1u98f514n4m: We judge a language model by perplexity: roughly, how many equally likely words the model is torn between at each step; formally, the exponential of the average negative log-probability of the real text, exp(-(1/N) Σ log P(wᵢ | context)). Lower is better. A model that spreads probability over 100 words evenly has perplexity 100. Words never seen after a given context get probability zero, which would make perplexity infinite, so we smooth (Lesson 17.3) or back off to shorter contexts. Neural language models replace counting with a network that reads a long context and can generalise to word combinations it has never seen.
unit-17.1207dgt1k6z: Models do not read letters or words directly but tokens, pieces of text drawn from a fixed vocabulary of tens of thousands of items. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) builds the vocabulary from data: start with single characters, then repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols and merge it into a new symbol. Common words become single tokens ("the"), common pieces become tokens ("ing", "un"), and rare words are spelled from smaller parts, so any text can be encoded. Tokens are then mapped to integers.
unit-17.2dtxf5tr76z: Each token is turned into an embedding: a list of numbers (a vector, perhaps 768 or 12,000 long) learned during training so that tokens used in similar contexts get similar vectors. "Cat" and "dog" end up near each other, far from "algebra". Similarity is measured by the cosine of the angle between vectors: cos(a, b) = a·b / (|a| |b|), which is 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated (perpendicular) and -1 for opposite. Embeddings capture regularities as directions: the famous example is that the vector for "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands near "queen". The same idea embeds sentences, images and users, and powers semantic search (find documents whose embeddings are close to the query's) and recommendation.
unit-17.e9bqik5u3z: Attention, transformers and large language models
unit-17.yi4pst6ev1: To use context well a model must decide which earlier words matter for the current one: in "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big", what does "it" refer to? Attention computes this. Each position produces a query vector q, a key vector k and a value vector v. A position compares its query with every key by dot product, divides by √d (d is the vector length, to keep numbers well behaved), turns the scores into weights with softmax (Lesson 17.7), and returns the weighted average of the values: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V. High weight means "this word is relevant to me". The transformer (Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", 2017) stacks many layers of attention and ordinary feed-forward networks, runs several attention "heads" in parallel, and, unlike recurrent networks, processes all positions at once, which suits GPUs and allowed training at enormous scale.
unit-17.2cgjbi5c2xe: A large language model (LLM) is a transformer with billions of parameters trained on a huge part of the public text to predict the next token. This pre-training is self-supervised: the text supplies its own labels. The base model is then fine-tuned on examples of following instructions, and often refined with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where people rank answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the LLM is trained (Lesson 17.8) to produce preferred answers. At use time the model generates one token at a time, sampling from its predicted distribution; a temperature setting controls randomness (low is more predictable, high is more varied). LLMs can write, summarise, translate and write code, but they have limits you must understand: they can hallucinate (state falsehoods fluently, because they model what text looks like, not what is true), reflect biases in their training text, have a fixed context window, may leak or memorise training data, and can be manipulated by prompt injection (hidden instructions in the text they read, an injection attack like those in Unit 16). Treat their output as a draft to verify, not as an authority.
unit-17.2e4ph63mozr: Learning systems act on real people, so building them carries obligations. Bias: a model trained on historical data copies its patterns. Hiring tools trained on past hires have downgraded women, face recognition has been far less accurate on darker skin, and risk scores have flagged some groups more often. Bias enters through unrepresentative data, labels that encode human prejudice, proxy features (a postcode can stand in for race), and how the problem is framed. Fairness has several measurable meanings that cannot all hold at once: demographic parity (the same share of each group receives the positive outcome), equal opportunity (the same true-positive rate for each group among those who truly qualify), and calibration (a predicted 70% means 70% in every group). Choosing among them is a judgement about values, not just mathematics. We audit by computing metrics per group (Lesson 17.4) and by examining errors.
unit-17.1q4b5w6vdv2: Other concerns. Privacy: models can memorise and reveal personal data, and training sets scraped from the web raise consent and copyright questions; techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning help (Lesson 16.9). Security: adversarial examples are inputs altered by tiny, often invisible changes that flip a model's answer, data poisoning corrupts training data, and model extraction steals a model through queries. Transparency and explainability: for high-stakes decisions people deserve reasons, so use simple models or tools that show which features drove a prediction. Accountability and human oversight: keep a person responsible, test before deploying, monitor afterwards, and be honest about error rates. Safety and alignment: ensure systems pursue the goals we actually intend (Lesson 17.8). Wider effects: energy use, labour, misinformation and deepfakes, concentration of power, and laws such as the EU AI Act that regulate by level of risk. The professional codes mentioned in Lesson 16.9 apply: avoid harm, be honest, respect privacy, and think about who is affected before you build, not only after something goes wrong.

unit-18.1v01gss593l: Unit 18 is where you put everything together. Before you write a line of a large project you need to decide what you are building, in what order, and how you will know it works. This lesson gives you the planning toolkit: requirements and user stories, a minimum viable product, estimates with uncertainty, a prioritised backlog, task dependencies and the critical path, conventional commits and changelogs, and a README that explains your work.
unit-18.1j3cv4qgrm: By the end you will be able to:
unit-18.1ikfeqm9i69: Turn an idea into requirements, user stories and a minimum viable product
unit-18.1k8yk9f9jcz: Estimate effort with three-point (PERT) estimates and combine uncertainty
unit-18.1rc5r13lrl1: Prioritise a backlog and plan an iteration within a capacity
