unit-18.1ybfkp1sms0: Write conventional commit messages, generate a changelog and check a README
unit-18.1thw2otg4l8: A capstone is a project big enough that you can fail at it by building the wrong thing, building too much, or building things in the wrong order. Professional teams guard against all three with a little planning, which Unit 14 introduced (process, git, testing, design, teams). This unit applies it for real, so we start by rehearsing it.
unit-18.hsvyd6k102: Begin with the problem and the user: who will use this, and what do they need to be able to do? Capture needs as requirements. Functional requirements say what the system does ("a user can add a note"); non-functional requirements say how well ("responds within 100 ms", "rejects unauthorised access", "runs in a browser"). A handy format is the user story: "As a role, I want goal, so that benefit", with acceptance criteria: concrete checks that tell you the story is done ("given a note owned by Ana, when Bo requests it, then the response is 403"). Good acceptance criteria become automated tests, which means your project is defined by tests you can run, exactly as the exercises and projects in this course are.
unit-18.1ewvpqyt953: Then decide the minimum viable product (MVP): the smallest thing that is still useful and demonstrates the idea. Everything else goes on a list for later. Beginners over-scope; a smaller project that works, is tested and is explained well is worth far more than a huge one that is half-finished. A useful rule: build a thin working slice end-to-end first (input to output, even if crude), then thicken it, instead of finishing one layer perfectly before the next exists.
unit-18.27hp1l6t33l: Estimates are always uncertain, and software estimates are famously optimistic. A better habit than a single number is a three-point estimate: an optimistic time o, a most likely time m and a pessimistic time p. The PERT formula gives an expected duration (o + 4m + p) / 6 (a weighted mean that leans toward the most likely value) and a standard deviation (p - o) / 6. For several independent tasks, the expected times add, and the variances add (so the combined standard deviation is the square root of the sum of the squared ones). That is why the total of many uncertain tasks is relatively less uncertain than each one, but also why you should add a buffer.
unit-18.6bb9cih8u1: A backlog is the to-do list of features and fixes. Each item gets a priority (what matters most to users or to risk reduction) and a size estimate (often story points, a relative measure). A priority queue (Unit 7) always hands back the most important item. An iteration (sprint) takes the top items that fit within the capacity of the time you have, and you deliver working software at the end of each one. Tackle the riskiest or most uncertain things early: a surprise on day 2 is cheap, on the last day it is fatal.
unit-18.1t4rozv12n2: Tasks depend on one another: you cannot test a feature before you write it, or write it before the data model exists. These dependencies form a directed acyclic graph (Unit 7). A topological order lists tasks so that every task comes after the ones it needs, and a cycle means the plan is impossible. If tasks have durations, the longest chain of dependent tasks is the critical path: it fixes the minimum total time, and delaying any task on it delays the whole project, while tasks off it have slack. Parallel work on a team can overlap non-critical tasks.
unit-18.2ssqu5yc4r: Keep the project under version control from the first day (Unit 14): commit small, working steps with clear messages, use a branch for each feature, and merge when the tests pass. A widely used convention for messages is Conventional Commits: type(scope): description, where type is feat (new feature), fix, docs, test, refactor, perf or chore, the optional scope names the part touched, and a ! before the colon marks a breaking change (feat(api)!: remove v1 routes). The format makes history readable and lets tools generate a changelog and choose the next semantic version (Lesson 16.8): breaking change means a major bump, feat a minor one, fix a patch.
unit-18.20wntsg2kvs: Write the README early; it is both your plan and your documentation. A good one has: a title and one-sentence purpose, how to install it, how to use it with an example, how to run the tests, a short design note (what the main parts are and why), known limitations, and the license. Add tests that are runnable by a stranger, and a short demo: a few commands or a screenshot showing it work. Ask yourself, "Could a classmate pick this up in an afternoon?" Lesson 18.8 returns to presenting your work.
unit-18.1mtr2565z4c: The capstone lessons that follow are each a self-contained project spec: the problem, the design, a series of milestones that you implement and test one at a time, and extension ideas. Each milestone is an exercise whose tests define done. Work through them in order, run the tests, and then use the extensions to make the project your own.

unit-18.24byd58invs: Every programming language you have used was built by programs, and the first big idea of this capstone is that an interpreter is just a program that reads a program. The classic pipeline has four stages (Units 9 and 15 met each of them): source text is split into tokens by a tokenizer (or lexer): numbers, names, keywords and symbols; the tokens are arranged into a syntax tree (an abstract syntax tree, AST) by a parser, which also rejects ill-formed programs; and an evaluator walks the tree and carries out what it says. A compiler would instead translate the tree to another language or to bytecode (Unit 10's virtual machine); an interpreter just does the work directly.
unit-18.25or19rmvb3: MiniScript is deliberately small. Programs are sequences of statements ending in ;: let x = 3 + 4; creates a variable, x = x * 2; changes it, print x; shows it. Blocks are in braces: if x > 5 { ... } else { ... }, while i < 10 { ... }. Functions are fn name(a, b) { return a + b; }, and values are numbers (integers and decimals). Comparisons return 1 (true) or 0 (false), and any non-zero value counts as true in a condition. Comments start with #.
unit-18.2eyquk84g75: Our plan has five milestones, one per exercise: (1) the tokenizer, (2) an expression parser and evaluator, (3) a statement parser, (4) an interpreter with scopes and functions, and (5) writing real programs in the language you have built.
unit-18.2ddqcmv71j5: A grammar (Unit 15) describes which token sequences are valid. For expressions, we write one rule per level of precedence, from the loosest-binding operator to the tightest:
unit-18.xj08tq6ahh: In a recursive-descent parser each rule becomes a function that calls the function for the next-tighter rule. Because term is called from inside sum, multiplication binds tighter than addition, so 1 + 2 * 3 parses as 1 + (2 * 3). The loop (... term)* makes operators left-associative: 10 - 4 - 3 becomes (10 - 4) - 3. A parenthesised expression restarts at the top rule, which is how parentheses override precedence. Each parse function takes the token list and a position and returns the tree it built along with the position after it, so the caller can carry on. When the tokens do not fit the grammar, the parser raises a clear error rather than guessing.
unit-18.b7vkwicoeg: The result is a tree such as ("bin", "+", ("num", 1), ("bin", "*", ("num", 2), ("num", 3))). The evaluator is then a short recursive function with one case per node type, the same idea as the expression trees of Unit 7. Statements get their own grammar: let name = expression ;, name = expression ;, print expression ;, if expression block [else block], while expression block, fn name ( params ) block, return expression ;, and an expression followed by ;.
unit-18.1jx8shb9arq: Variables need a home. An environment maps names to values. Blocks and function calls create a new scope whose parent is the scope around it, so a lookup that fails locally continues outward; this is the scope chain (Unit 4). let always creates a variable in the current scope, while assignment x = ... changes the nearest existing x and is an error if there is none.
unit-18.1pfr3cgwiql: A function is a stored parameter list and body, plus the scope where it was defined. Calling it creates a fresh scope whose parent is that defining scope, binds the parameters to the argument values, and runs the body. Remembering the defining scope makes the function a closure: fn make(n) { fn add(x) { return x + n; } return add; } returns a function that still sees n after make has finished. We implement return with an exception that unwinds the Python stack back to the call (Unit 5), and functions are stored in the environment as ordinary callable values, which also lets us add built-in functions written in Python. Recursion works automatically because each call has its own scope.
unit-18.m60ya547ik: Finally, safety (Unit 16). An interpreter runs code you did not write, so it must defend itself. An accidental or malicious while 1 { } would loop forever, so we count executed statements and stop at a step limit; unbounded recursion would exhaust the Python stack, so we count the call depth; and every failure becomes a clean LangError with a message instead of a crash. These same limits are how online code runners (and this course's own browser runner) protect themselves.
unit-18.tkyxrpkgc8: The tokenizer splits text into (kind, value) pairs and throws away whitespace and comments.
unit-18.1av66v4z3nk: A tiny recursive-descent parser shows how rule order gives precedence and left-associativity.
unit-18.2g5jzv1065d: One function with a case per node type. The environment is a plain dictionary here.
unit-18.2erjsj4uycy: Each block gets an Env whose parent is the enclosing scope. Lookups walk outward; let defines locally; assignment changes the nearest existing variable.
unit-18.gfc2ti0x8f: Putting the pipeline together: run MiniScript source and see recursion, a closure and an error.
unit-18.1p8hogm95za: Parsing operators in the wrong order
unit-18.236bjn3py2u: Precedence comes from which function calls which. The loosest operators belong in the outermost function.

unit-18.yy7980os23: Blocks and calls need their own child scope, with the parent link for lookups.
unit-18.1bymqms8ung: No limits on loops and recursion
unit-18.4p4qv0tosl: An interpreter must protect itself from runaway programs: count steps and depth.
unit-18.1hduy1k2udt: An interpreter pipeline: tokenizer, parser (syntax tree), evaluator.
unit-18.1o15aj1sb40: Recursive descent turns each grammar rule into a function; call order gives precedence and loops give left-associativity.
unit-18.283umrj317: Environments are chains of scopes; functions that remember their defining scope are closures.
unit-18.1j9wy9cp0mp: Return can be implemented with an exception; resource limits and clear errors make the interpreter safe.

unit-18.fah4ufts96: Build the heart of a database: a log-structured key-value store that survives crashes. You will design a checksummed record format, replay a write-ahead log to rebuild state, add atomic transactions with commit and rollback, detect and survive damaged logs, and compact the log to reclaim space. This capstone brings together Units 7, 10, 12, 14 and 16.
unit-18.1o43mfsu4lg: Explain durability, write-ahead logging and why appending is a good way to write
unit-18.mzmmnkz5jg: Design a record format with checksums that detects corruption
unit-18.6qt8532r3m: Rebuild a data store by replaying a log, including after a crash
unit-18.141hbpl70q: Implement atomic transactions with commit markers and rollback
unit-18.1q4pp5htujn: Compact a log and reason about space, speed and recovery trade-offs
unit-18.w43y7ffh58: What a storage engine must do
unit-18.1o4kynwxy3w: A database is more than a dictionary. A Python dict lives in memory and vanishes when the program ends, so a real storage engine adds durability (data survives restarts and crashes), integrity (damage is detected, not silently used), and atomicity (a group of changes either happens completely or not at all). Units 10 and 12 met these ideas as the ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) and as journalling in file systems. Here you build them yourself.
unit-18.1lsh6t9lr88: The simplest design that survives crashes is a write-ahead log (WAL): before changing anything, append a record describing the change to the end of a file; to rebuild the state after a restart, replay the log from the start. Appending is the cheapest write there is (no seeking, no overwriting existing data, so a half-finished write damages only the tail). Many real systems are built this way: databases keep a WAL for recovery, Kafka is a distributed log, and Git's object store and an LSM-tree database (LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra) are descendants of the idea. The state in memory is then just a cache of the log, a dictionary giving fast reads, and the log is the truth.
unit-18.o86f4kppi1: Our KVStore keeps the "file" as a list of text lines so that it runs in the browser: log_text() is what would be written to disk, and KVStore(text) is what you would do when the program starts again. Each line is one record: put (set a key), del (delete a key), and the markers begin and commit that bracket a transaction.
unit-18.19acb1mogw8: Disks fail, power is lost halfway through a write, and files get edited by mistake or on purpose (Unit 16), so every record carries a checksum: the first 8 hex digits of the SHA-256 hash of its body. When we read a line back we recompute the hash; a mismatch means the line is damaged (or tampered with, though for tamper-proofing against an attacker you would use an HMAC with a secret key, Lesson 16.3). Records are written with json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True) so the same record always produces the same bytes, and any JSON-compatible value can be stored.
unit-18.agjloa710x: Recovery replays the log line by line. Plain put and del records are applied immediately. Our policy for damage is conservative: stop at the first damaged line and ignore everything after it, because after a torn write you cannot trust what follows. This is how real WALs behave, since a crash only ever damages the end.
unit-18.bv87xwtznn: Transactions make several changes atomic. Inside a transaction we do not touch the log or the data: writes go to a buffer, reads look in the buffer first (a transaction sees its own writes), and rollback simply throws the buffer away. On commit we append begin, then the records, then commit. During replay, records between begin and commit are held back and applied only when the commit marker is reached. If the log ends in the middle of a group, the power failed before the commit was written, so the whole group is discarded: this is how a money transfer ("subtract from Alice, add to Bob") can never be half applied. The commit marker is the atomic moment. Real systems add isolation (concurrent transactions not seeing each other's changes), usually with locks or versions, which is a natural extension.
unit-18.zzcyhrh5h4: An append-only log grows forever: a counter updated a million times leaves a million records for one live value. Compaction rewrites the log keeping only what is needed, one put per live key (in a real system it writes a new file and then atomically swaps it in, so a crash during compaction leaves the old log intact). The ratio of wasted records to live ones measures how worthwhile compaction is; databases run it in the background when the ratio gets high.
unit-18.2amgozpph8m: Every design has trade-offs worth being able to state. Writes are fast (append only), but reads need the in-memory dictionary, which must fit in RAM, and recovery time grows with the log (hence snapshots and compaction). A secondary index, a second dictionary from a field's value to the keys that have it, makes queries like "all users in Oslo" fast but must be updated on every write and rebuilt on recovery. Range scans need sorted keys (we sort on demand; real engines keep sorted structures such as B-trees or sorted string tables). Concurrency, replication and encryption at rest are other layers you could add.
unit-18.ge88mjyoyr: Security notes for your own version: validate keys and values (we reject empty or non-string keys), never put secrets into logs in plain text, keep the log file's permissions tight, and treat a log from outside as untrusted input: our parser never evaluates it, it only parses JSON.
unit-18.1m25z1u7if3: Each record is one line: a checksum, a space and canonical JSON. Changing a single character is detected.
unit-18.2bovhs4ovvq: The state is rebuilt by applying records in order. A torn write stops the replay.
unit-18.ytta1o8z8h: A transfer between two accounts is written as one begin...commit group. Cut the log at any point and the transfer is either fully there or fully absent.
unit-18.xkpqyb8tuq: 300 updates to 3 counters leave only 3 live values.
unit-18.1p52m3tphj4: A second dictionary from city to keys, kept up to date on every write and rebuilt from the log on start-up.
unit-18.3cvk481kbo: Changing the data before the log record is safe
unit-18.8tweenwa7i: Write-ahead means the log comes first, so a crash can always be recovered.
unit-18.113qnidxrpw: Applying a transaction's records before the commit marker
unit-18.1wqiw5vu285: Recovery would then apply half a transaction.
unit-18.liu35cyl51: Continuing to read after a damaged line
unit-18.nqvpvjfi9t: After a torn write you cannot know what the rest means. Stop and discard.
unit-18.fyz032m38y: Reject bad keys at the door; stored data becomes tomorrow's input.
unit-18.pwbwr7enof: The log and the recovery time grow without limit.
unit-18.1oqrh6cgkky: A write-ahead log makes changes durable by appending records first; the in-memory dictionary is a cache rebuilt by replay.
unit-18.10uydrhatl8: Checksums detect corruption; recovery stops at the first damaged line.
unit-18.4ahftd94hp: Transactions buffer writes and become atomic through a commit marker in the log.
unit-18.1j4iplb1yd4: Compaction keeps one put per live key; the garbage ratio says when it is worthwhile.
unit-18.1p25fmjtnmn: Secondary indexes speed queries at the cost of extra work on every write and on recovery.
unit-18.15rv7k36pgk: Build the core of a web framework from scratch: a router with path parameters, JSON handlers with correct status codes, a middleware chain, signed-token authentication, rate limiting, input validation and security headers. You will see exactly what frameworks such as Flask and Express do for you. This capstone brings together Units 9, 11, 14 and 16.
unit-18.1eaabwslx1u: Explain the request/response cycle and choose correct HTTP status codes
unit-18.wqss6ookyu: Route requests to handlers using patterns with typed path parameters
unit-18.2bf08qkqx3r: Compose middleware so that cross-cutting concerns wrap every handler
unit-18.2lii8az8vi: Authenticate requests with signed, expiring tokens and limit request rates
unit-18.1isp3g9honq: Validate untrusted input and add security headers and CORS rules
unit-18.eqt6xuk715: What a web framework really does
unit-18.2cn48g5emp8: A web server receives a request (a method such as GET or POST, a path, headers and sometimes a body) and must send back a response (a status code, headers and a body). A web framework is the code that turns that raw exchange into something pleasant to program against. Inside, it is smaller than you might expect: a router decides which function handles a request, handlers are plain functions that return data, and middleware wraps every request with shared behaviour such as logging or authentication.
unit-18.i3ksxzujtv: Our framework is deliberately pure Python and runs entirely in the browser: App.handle(raw) takes a dictionary describing a request and returns a dictionary describing the response. Real servers do the same job after reading bytes from a network socket (Unit 11), so everything you build here carries over to Flask, FastAPI, Express or Spring.
unit-18.1gqeq720c8j: Good status codes are part of a good API: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content (success with no body), 400 Bad Request (the client sent something unreadable), 401 Unauthorized (who are you?), 403 Forbidden (I know who you are, and the answer is no), 404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 422 Unprocessable Entity (readable but invalid), 429 Too Many Requests and 500 Internal Server Error.
unit-18.1dnrcso6s69: Routing, handlers and the middleware chain
unit-18.1htrdfc69k5: The router stores (method, pattern, handler) triples. A pattern such as /notes/<id:int> has path parameters in angle brackets; <id:int> only matches digits and hands the handler an int. Matching has three outcomes that map directly to status codes: a match (200), a path that exists but not for this method (405, with an Allow header listing what is allowed), and no path at all (404).
unit-18.k3kzzouhbj: Handlers stay simple: they receive the request and return data. A dictionary means 200; a (status, data) tuple chooses the status; None means 204. To fail on purpose a handler raises HTTPError(status, message). The framework turns that into a JSON error, and it turns any other exception into a generic 500 that does not reveal the exception text, since error details help attackers (Unit 16).
unit-18.8yubaehusy: Middleware is a function (request, next_handler) -> response. It can act before calling next_handler, after it returns, or instead of it. build_chain nests them like the layers of an onion: the first middleware added is the outermost, so it sees the request first and the response last. Authentication, rate limiting, logging and security headers all fit this one shape, and because they wrap the router itself, they also apply to 404 responses.
unit-18.1rjxrhoaxtg: Authentication, limits and defensive input handling
unit-18.2g7h5ve9gsb: Tokens. After login, the server gives the client a bearer token and the client sends it back in Authorization: Bearer <token>. Ours is payload.mac: the payload is base64url-encoded JSON {"sub": user, "exp": expiry}, and the MAC is an HMAC-SHA256 of the payload with a secret that only the server knows. Anyone can read the payload, but nobody can change it without the secret, so the server can trust what it verifies (this is the idea behind JWTs, which you saw in Unit 16). Always compare MACs with hmac.compare_digest, which takes the same time however many characters match, and always check the expiry.
unit-18.10fl65z7mqt: Rate limiting protects against brute-forcing and overload. Ours keeps the recent request times for each client and answers 429 with a Retry-After header when a client exceeds its budget in a sliding window. Rejected requests are not recorded, so waiting is always enough.
unit-18.ksb950bmxf: Validation. Everything in a request body is untrusted. A schema states the allowed fields, their types, ranges, lengths and choices; validate returns a list of precise messages, and the handler turns a non-empty list into a 422. Reject unknown fields (they hide mass-assignment bugs) and remember that in Python True is an int, so it needs an explicit check.
unit-18.25tftzyvmd1: Headers. Security headers tell browsers to be careful: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, a strict Content-Security-Policy. CORS controls which other websites may call your API from a browser: echo back only origins on an allow-list, never * for an authenticated API, and add Vary: Origin so caches do not mix responses up.
unit-18.cs8tprxk31: The router distinguishes a match, a wrong method (405) and an unknown path (404). Typed parameters only match what they should.
unit-18.2o8gfisezu: Handlers return plain data. Status codes come from what they return or raise.
unit-18.6n93zu6ege: The first middleware is the outermost: it enters first and leaves last.
unit-18.1rn47kdpklg: A token that is expired, forged or signed with another key is rejected. Missing or malformed credentials give 401.
unit-18.281omsbgs9w: Every problem is reported at once, and only allow-listed origins receive CORS headers.
unit-18.1gollb3je87: Leaking exception text in a 500 response
unit-18.bkpr6s3xw1: Stack traces and messages help attackers. Log them privately and return a generic message.
unit-18.28ozo0iewhb: 401 means the client has not proved who it is; 403 means it is known and not allowed.
unit-18.ebv70po0a4: Use hmac.compare_digest, which does not leak how many characters matched.
unit-18.1p1dhx0hoyq: Trusting a token's payload before verifying its MAC
unit-18.12phh9zsb5f: The payload is readable by anyone; only a valid signature makes it trustworthy.
unit-18.1ok55fukrz4: Allowing * as a CORS origin on an authenticated API
unit-18.ktzi3qw34u: Echo only origins from an allow-list.
unit-18.1yh17rxcd72: Forgetting that True is an int
unit-18.1218vofnxyu: Validate booleans explicitly or {"priority": true} passes an integer check.
unit-18.11rrbl5g0i6: A web framework is a router, handlers and middleware around a request and response.
unit-18.1l3ouyu0sl4: Routes map (method, pattern) to a handler; mismatches give 404 or 405 with an Allow header.
unit-18.q2yoec3ww2: Handlers return data or raise HTTPError; unexpected errors become a generic 500.
unit-18.21ajflgxjfh: Middleware wraps handlers like an onion: authentication, rate limits, logging and headers.
unit-18.xlplce6uo9: Signed expiring tokens, validated input and strict headers are the web's basic defences.
unit-18.diuidtfbdz: Build a complete turn-based grid game: levels as data, shortest-path guards, a pure step function for the rules, safe save files and seeded random level generation that is guaranteed solvable. This capstone brings together Units 5, 6, 8, 12, 14 and 16.
unit-18.2a1qfftp2kp: Separate game data, rules and drawing so each can be tested on its own
unit-18.gxuc9nzwx0: Parse and validate levels from text
unit-18.zb7s9q1vxp: Use breadth-first search to give enemies a smart, deterministic chase
unit-18.28uro7qc779: Write a pure step function that returns a new state instead of changing the old one
unit-18.231bkdzy4l4: Treat save files as untrusted input and generate levels reproducibly from a seed
unit-18.tzhquznahh: Games feel like a pile of special cases, but good ones are built from three separate parts. Data says what exists: the map, where things are, the score. Rules say how the data changes when something happens: one move, one tick. Presentation turns data into something a player can see. In this lesson the whole engine is pure logic with no drawing and no input; the game shown in your browser or terminal is just render(state) printing characters.
unit-18.1srbnj4iyij: That separation is what makes the engine testable. Our central function is step(state, action). It takes the current state and a player action and returns a new state, never changing the old one. Functions like this are called pure (Unit 6) and have wonderful properties: you can undo a move by keeping the previous state, replay a whole game from a list of moves, run thousands of random games to find bugs, and save a game by writing the state to a file.
unit-18.1u37kq56vxk: The state is a plain dictionary: level (the unchanging map), player, guards, the remaining coins, score, turns and status (playing, won or lost). The level is parsed once from ASCII art such as # for wall, @ start, X exit, $ coin and g guard, and any malformed level is refused with a clear ValueError at the door.
unit-18.1o6ba5bjwai: Guards need to chase the player around walls. The classic tool is breadth-first search (BFS) (Unit 8): explore outward from the start one step at a time, remembering for every cell where you came from. The first time you reach the goal you have found a shortest path, and following the "came from" links backwards gives the route.
unit-18.1optlufc8bd: Our BFS visits neighbours in a fixed order (up, down, left, right). That makes the game deterministic: the same moves always produce the same game. Determinism is a feature to protect, because it is what lets a bug report say "start a new game and make these ten moves" and lets tests assert exact positions.
unit-18.1jqpra8grmo: Each turn, after the player moves, every guard asks BFS for the shortest path to the player's new cell and takes the first step. A guard with no path simply waits (a sealed-off guard is harmless). Notice the careful rule order in step: moving onto a guard loses immediately, reaching the exit wins before the guards get to move, and only then do the guards move and possibly catch you. Game design is mostly choosing these small rules and writing them down precisely.
unit-18.1rj45uhxip1: A save file is data that outlives your program, so it is untrusted input (Unit 16). Players edit files, files get damaged, and old versions linger. load_state therefore checks everything: it parses JSON inside try, demands exactly the expected fields, checks types (remembering that True is an int in Python), re-parses the map, and verifies that every position is a legal floor cell, that coins are a subset of the level's coins and that the guard count matches. Anything wrong raises SaveError instead of producing a corrupt game. Validation catches impossible data, not plausible cheating: a player can still raise their own score. To detect that you would sign the file with an HMAC and a secret (Unit 16, and the token code in the web-service capstone) or keep scores on a server. A version field lets future versions of the game change the format safely.
unit-18.1lfv0kj12f8: Procedural generation makes levels from an algorithm. We use random.Random(seed), so the same seed always gives the same level: players can share seeds, tests can replay failures, and nothing needs storing. Random walls alone can seal the exit, so the generator first carves a guaranteed route from start to exit and only then scatters coins and guards on the remaining free cells (guards far from the start so that the first turn is fair). "Generate, then guarantee a property by construction" is more reliable than "generate, then test and retry".
unit-18.112wsg0rqhf: ASCII art becomes a level dictionary. Bad levels are refused with a message that says what is wrong.
unit-18.segc2h5jau: BFS finds a shortest route through a maze and returns None when the goal cannot be reached.
unit-18.1hho4vtl24q: The guard chases the player through the level; each move produces a new state. Reaching the exit ends the game before the guard can move again.
unit-18.1b9ugu40xq: A save file is plain JSON. Impossible or damaged data is refused, but a plausible edit such as a higher score passes validation: stopping that needs a signature (Unit 16) or a server.
unit-18.5c323ius1m: The same seed gives the same level, and carving a route first makes every level solvable, even with many walls.
unit-18.hi9lwlyrtm: Changing the old state inside step
unit-18.1jens20bjtj: Return a new state; otherwise undo, replay and tests all break.
unit-18.16oqds6mhhc: Letting dictionary or set order decide the game
unit-18.2di3yjkzlt0: Iterate in a fixed order so the same moves always give the same game.
unit-18.1iwv50jeonq: Checking the rules in the wrong order
unit-18.2ajeoz4loay: Win, loss and guard movement interact; write the order down and test every combination.
unit-18.kcj4b2vtr8: Validate types, ranges and relationships; True is also an int in Python.
unit-18.1n1bao0nbif: Create random.Random(seed) so generation is reproducible and does not disturb other code.
unit-18.26anjji0b2b: Hoping a random level is solvable
unit-18.el2iqcd95c: Carve the guaranteed route first and add the randomness around it.
unit-18.eqqsit5sp9: Keep data, rules and drawing apart; the engine is pure logic that tests can drive.
unit-18.1iufo37p9cu: A pure step function returns a new state, which gives undo, replay and easy saving for free.
unit-18.216dduhgy3h: Breadth-first search with a fixed neighbour order gives deterministic shortest-path guards.
unit-18.haixypihb1: Save files are untrusted input: validate every field and raise one clear error type.
unit-18.1ousjo7g1z1: Seeded generators are reproducible; construct the guarantees you need instead of hoping.
unit-18.2pvw8al787: Build a complete, honest machine-learning pipeline from raw CSV text to a fairness report: a quote-aware CSV parser, cleaning with imputation, a reproducible train/test split, leak-free scaling and one-hot encoding, logistic regression trained from scratch, evaluation metrics and a per-group audit. This capstone brings together Units 4, 9, 13, 14, 16 and 17.
unit-18.24h5rm4os7g: Parse real-world CSV, including quoted commas, quotes and line breaks
unit-18.1ase2szw4q1: Clean data reproducibly and report exactly what was changed
unit-18.49icpssi7x: Split data and fit scalers and encoders on training data only, to avoid leakage
unit-18.2dbiesa3s8n: Train and evaluate a logistic regression classifier and read precision, recall and F1
unit-18.1fd89f2zo7z: Audit a model for group differences and explain what such numbers can and cannot show
unit-18.20yel0jpktd: From raw text to a trustworthy dataset
unit-18.1yijropk6g8: Most of a data project is not modelling. Real files are messy: numbers are blank or say NA or n/a, text has stray capitals and spaces, a field contains a comma inside quotes, and a few rows have no answer at all. A pipeline is a fixed sequence of steps that turns such raw text into something a model can learn from, written as ordinary functions so that every step can be tested and re-run.
unit-18.1p26w2twc1j: CSV looks trivial and is not: "Smith, Ann" is one field, "" inside quotes means a literal quote, and a quoted field may contain a line break. A correct parser is a small state machine (Unit 12) that remembers whether it is inside quotes. Splitting on commas is the classic bug.
unit-18.1k2hcglco9k: Cleaning makes decisions, and every decision should be visible. We drop rows with no valid target (the answer we want to predict), replace missing numbers by the median (robust to outliers), mark missing categories as unknown, and return a report of how many rows were dropped and values imputed. Silent cleaning hides problems; a report lets you notice that 40% of one column was missing.
unit-18.22p69ywzbz7: A model must be judged on data it has never seen, so we split the cleaned rows into a training set (to learn from) and a test set (to grade on). The split uses random.Random(seed), so it is shuffled but reproducible.
unit-18.2ck5yviijjf: The most common serious mistake is data leakage: letting information from the test set influence training. If you compute the mean and standard deviation for scaling from all rows, the test set has already shaped your features. So fit_scaler and fit_encoder run on the training rows only, and the same fitted scaler and encoder are then applied to the test rows. Categories seen only in the test set simply become all zeros.
unit-18.m1ttxsj2nn: Standardising (subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation) puts income in dollars and age in years on a common scale so gradient descent behaves. One-hot encoding turns a category into one 0/1 column per value. Logistic regression (Unit 17) multiplies features by weights, adds a bias and squeezes the result through the sigmoid to get a probability; training minimises log loss by gradient descent. Our sigmoid is written carefully so that a huge negative or positive input cannot overflow.
unit-18.ez25c8i6rl: Always compare with a baseline: a model that always predicts the majority class. If 95% of cases are negative, 95% accuracy means nothing. That is why we also read precision (of the ones we flagged, how many were right), recall (of the real positives, how many we found) and F1 (their harmonic mean), all from the confusion matrix of true and false positives and negatives.
unit-18.psh516oxkq: A model that approves loans, ranks job candidates or flags students affects real people, so accuracy is not enough. A group report computes the same statistics separately for each group: the selection rate (share of the group that the model says yes to) and the true positive rate (share of the group's genuinely qualified people who get a yes). The largest difference between groups is the demographic parity gap (for selection rate) or the equal opportunity gap (for true positive rate).
unit-18.klzxcxq4rq: Our synthetic data contains a historical bias: at the same income and debt, group b was approved less often. A model trained on those labels learns the pattern, and when it can see the group column its selection gap grows. Removing the sensitive column does not make a model fair: other columns can act as proxies, and here the gap stayed small without it only because this toy data has no strong proxy for the group. These numbers come from invented data and one random split; on a real project you would use far more data, check confidence intervals and ask whether the labels themselves are the problem.
unit-18.hzkxyfgofe: Different fairness definitions can contradict one another, so choosing one is a human and legal decision, not a computation. What engineers can do: measure, report honestly, keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions, document the data and its limits, and be willing to not ship a model (Unit 16's security mindset applies here as well: assume inputs and incentives are not all benign).

unit-18.omnaxllny3: Build a miniature search engine: text normalisation and stemming, an inverted index you can update, boolean, phrase and exclusion queries, TF-IDF ranking, autocomplete and spelling suggestions, plus safe highlighting of results. This capstone brings together Units 5, 8, 9, 12, 14 and 16.
unit-18.14fftvjntrh: Normalise text into terms with case folding, accent removal, stop words and stemming
unit-18.2a9i1pbcjsj: Build and maintain an inverted index with positions
unit-18.4p8ray4y3g: Answer word, phrase and exclusion queries using set operations
unit-18.x47ldkcfmf: Rank results with TF-IDF and explain why rare words matter
unit-18.2babs4wxmtc: Offer autocomplete and spelling suggestions with binary search and edit distance
unit-18.27av09cdaus: The simplest search reads every document and checks whether it contains the word. That is linear in the size of the collection: fine for ten notes, hopeless for ten million web pages. Search engines do the work in advance: they build an inverted index, a dictionary from each term to a postings list of the documents (and positions) that contain it, just like the index at the back of a book. Answering a query becomes a few dictionary lookups and set operations (Unit 5) instead of a scan.
unit-18.2exv87mls4y: Before indexing, text must be normalised so that Searching, searches and SEARCH meet at the same term. We lower-case, remove accents, split into words, drop stop words (very common words such as the and of that carry little meaning) and stem each word by stripping common endings. Our stemmer is tiny and approximate: its stems (engin, whal) need not be real words, as long as related words reduce to the same stem. Real systems use better stemmers (Porter, Snowball) or lemmatisers and language-specific rules.
unit-18.v3ko8t82mf: Each posting stores the positions of the term in the document. Positions cost memory, but they make phrase queries possible: "search engine" matches only where engine comes directly after search. (Because stop words are removed before positions are counted, state of the art and state art look alike. A real engine would keep stop-word positions.)
unit-18.m3fztzgmxj: Our tiny query language has three kinds of parts: plain words (all must appear: set intersection), "quoted phrases" (positions must be adjacent) and a leading minus such as -linked (exclude: set difference). search_any uses set union for "at least one of these words".
unit-18.7sd5keck58: Finding matches is not enough, because a search for search may match thousands of documents. Ranking puts the best first. TF-IDF combines two ideas. Term frequency (TF) says a document that uses a word more often is probably more about it, but with diminishing returns: we use 1 + ln(tf), so ten occurrences count about 3.3 times, not 10. Inverse document frequency (IDF) says a word that appears in few documents is more informative than one that appears everywhere: ln((N + 1) / (df + 1)) + 1. A document's score is the sum of TF x IDF over the query's words, divided by the square root of its length so that long documents do not win simply by having more words. This is a simplified cousin of the BM25 formula used by many production engines.
unit-18.yb3t4q80g7: Scores are only comparable within one query, and the ordering of ties must be deterministic (here: by document id), otherwise results flicker between runs.
unit-18.1mwv5a32st3: Autocomplete finds the index terms that start with what the user has typed. Keep the terms in a sorted list and use binary search (bisect_left, Unit 8) to jump to the first match, then walk forward while the prefix still fits. Offer the most common terms first.
unit-18.1l6y9oc09n: Spelling suggestions use edit distance (Levenshtein distance): the fewest single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one word into another. It is computed with dynamic programming (Unit 8), keeping only the previous row of the table. For serch the nearest term is search at distance 1. Comparing a typo with every term is slow for big vocabularies, so real engines first narrow the candidates (by length, by shared character n-grams, or with a trie), which is why our code skips terms whose length differs too much.
unit-18.hyjoaw7m8v: Finally, showing results safely: highlighting a match means putting HTML around part of a document, and document text is untrusted. In highlight every piece of text goes through html.escape before the <mark> tags are added, so a document containing <script> shows up as harmless text instead of running (Unit 16: cross-site scripting).
unit-18.23koefv2wtg: Case, accents, punctuation, stop words and word endings are all handled before indexing. A sentence made only of stop words disappears.
unit-18.5zk87l8euc: Each term maps to the documents and positions where it occurs. Removing a document updates every term it used.
unit-18.1e65hi4vpn8: All words, any word, phrases, exclusions and a query nobody can answer.
unit-18.10oam8djw0g: Rarer words have a higher IDF, so matching engine is worth more than matching search.

unit-18.254er8j0to1: Normalisation (case, accents, stop words, stemming) decides what counts as the same word.

unit-18.1x8t9cx06iw: Finish like a professional: generate API documentation from code, keep documentation honest with runnable examples, publish a portfolio page safely, audit dependencies for known vulnerabilities and licences, and gate a release on objective checks. Then think about ethics, your portfolio and where to go next. This capstone brings together Units 1, 14, 15 and 16.

unit-18.2c1acbksb4z: Work is finished when others can use it
unit-18.ru4cgq30qg: A project that only runs on your machine, with no explanation, is not finished. People who use or review your work judge it by what they can see in a few minutes: a README that says what it does and how to run it (you built a linter for one in the planning capstone), documentation of its public functions, examples that actually work and a changelog of what changed between versions.
unit-18.15pwo4acdon: Documentation that is written by hand drifts away from the code. Two habits keep it honest. First, generate what you can: with the ast module (Unit 14) a program can read your source code, find every public function and class, and write the reference for you, so a renamed parameter shows up in the docs automatically. Second, test the documentation itself: examples in docs that start with >>> can be run and compared with the output they claim. Python's own doctest module works this way, and our run_examples is a miniature of it. An example that stops working fails the build, so the text cannot quietly become wrong.
unit-18.1g6ropes2n9: A good demo is rehearsed and short: say what problem it solves, show the core flow once with prepared data, then show one thing that can go wrong and how the program handles it. Prepared inputs and fixed random seeds (as in the game and search capstones) make demos repeatable.
unit-18.8xmcwwlhqp: Supply chain, safety and the release gate
unit-18.ip5gaeej31: Modern programs are mostly other people's code. Every dependency brings its own bugs, its licence terms and its own dependencies. The software supply chain is a real attack surface: a vulnerable old version, a hijacked package or a package with a similar name can all end up inside your program (Unit 16). Good habits: pin versions, keep dependencies few, read the licence, and audit regularly. An audit compares each name and version with a list of advisories (published vulnerabilities such as CVEs) that say which versions are affected, and also checks that every licence is acceptable for your use. For that you need to compare versions properly: 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.9, which is true for tuples of numbers but false for the strings.
unit-18.16ibxw9jmfy: Before shipping, teams use a release gate: a written, automated list of conditions that must hold, such as "no failing tests, coverage of at least 80%, no high or critical vulnerabilities, README, changelog and licence present". The gate removes argument and wishful thinking at the worst possible moment (a deadline). Our gate reports every reason it says no, not just the first, and treats missing information as a failure, because "we did not measure coverage" is not the same as "coverage is fine".
unit-18.1hox8wjh30s: When you publish a portfolio page you are putting your work in front of strangers' browsers, so the same rules apply as for any web page: escape every piece of text, and only create links for http and https addresses, because a javascript: URL in an href can run code when clicked.
unit-18.1an2vzt5zn2: Software affects people, often people who never chose to use it. Responsible computing is not a separate subject, it is a set of habits in every project: collect only the data you need and protect it (Unit 16), say plainly what your system can and cannot do, test with people unlike yourself, make interfaces accessible (keyboard use, contrast, text alternatives), credit other people's work and respect licences, and measure whether your models treat groups differently (the machine-learning capstone). When asked to build something that you believe will cause harm, "I was told to" is not a defence, and professional bodies such as the ACM publish codes of ethics worth reading.
unit-18.1pgukazgnw0: For your portfolio, quality beats quantity. Choose three to five projects, such as the interpreter, the database, the web service, the game, the ML pipeline and the search engine you built here. For each, write: the problem, what you built, one hard decision you made and why, how you tested it, what you would improve, and a link to the code. Honest limitations ("the stemmer is approximate") read as maturity, not weakness. Keep the code runnable, the README accurate and the history of commits readable.
unit-18.c37sjidzcj: Where next? This curriculum gives you a map of the whole field, but depth comes from building. Choose a direction that draws you (systems, web and mobile, data and AI, security, graphics and games, embedded) and build something real in it. Read code written by others, contribute a small fix to an open-source project, solve problems regularly, and write about what you learn. Classic books such as Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, Introduction to Algorithms, Designing Data-Intensive Applications and Code Complete reward patient reading once you have your own experience to connect them to. Be kind to your future self and to the next reader of your code, and keep going.

unit-19.ibgwcbwi6q: Meet vectors as both arrows and lists of numbers, and learn the operations that all of linear algebra is built on: addition, scaling, the dot product, length, angles, projection and the cross product. Every operation is built from scratch in Python so you see exactly how libraries such as NumPy work inside.
unit-19.1j3cv4qgrm: By the end you will be able to:
unit-19.qzi6ykryih: Describe a vector as a list of numbers and as an arrow, and add and scale vectors
unit-19.2e4qzshpsey: Compute dot products, lengths and distances and say what they mean geometrically
unit-19.12um8v6mdmf: Find the angle between two vectors and use cosine similarity to compare data
unit-19.eukwwqreou: Split a vector into a part along another vector and a perpendicular part
unit-19.1kcy9habl9f: Use the cross product in three dimensions to find perpendicular directions and areas
unit-19.2b55oseiymm: A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [2, 1] or [3.5, -1, 4]. It can be read in two ways, and a great deal of mathematics comes from switching between them. As an arrow, [2, 1] means "go 2 to the right and 1 up"; the list says how far to move along each axis. As a point, it names a position. As data, it can hold anything you measure: the height, weight and age of a person; the pixels of an image; how often each word appears in a document.
unit-19.5es9kjeime: Two operations are available for every vector. Addition works entry by entry: [2, 1] + [1, 3] = [3, 4], and as arrows it means "do one trip, then the other". Scaling multiplies every entry by a number (a scalar): 3 * [2, 1] = [6, 3] is an arrow three times as long, and a negative scalar flips the direction. Together these two operations obey the familiar rules of algebra (order does not matter for addition, scalars distribute over sums), and any set of objects that obeys them is called a vector space. That idea returns in lesson 6.
unit-19.qzi6lafol8: In code a vector is just a Python list, and the number of entries is its dimension. Adding vectors of different dimensions is meaningless, so our functions raise ValueError instead of silently using zip to cut the longer one short; quiet truncation would hide a real bug.
unit-19.18b4arkexyj: The dot product, length and angle
unit-19.1if4rnhnqvf: The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up: [1, 2, 3] . [4, 5, 6] = 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32. It looks like bookkeeping, but it measures how much two vectors point the same way. The dot product of a vector with itself is the sum of its squared entries, so the length (or norm) of a vector is sqrt(v . v). This is the Pythagorean theorem in any dimension: [3, 4] has length 5. The distance between two points is the length of their difference.
unit-19.pnl9iuwbw4: The geometric formula is u . v = |u| |v| cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the arrows. Solving for the angle gives cos(theta) = u . v / (|u| |v|), called the cosine similarity. It is 1 for vectors pointing the same way, 0 for perpendicular (orthogonal) ones and -1 for opposite directions. Because it ignores length, it is a favourite way to compare documents, songs or shoppers: describe each by a vector of word counts or ratings and a high cosine similarity means "similar taste, whatever the size". Search engines (Unit 18) and recommendation systems rely on it.
unit-19.1ns4ts8e5rh: Floating-point arithmetic needs care. Rounding can make a cosine come out as 1.0000000000000002, which makes acos fail, so we clamp the value to the range -1 to 1. Likewise, testing "perpendicular" with == 0 will fail for harmless rounding errors, so we compare with a small tolerance.
unit-19.1m731jeg9is: Often we want to split a vector into a part along a direction and a part across it. A wind of [3, 4] over a road that runs east [1, 0] pushes the car along the road with [3, 0] and sideways with [0, 4]. The projection of u onto w is (u . w / w . w) * w: first measure how much of u points along w, then scale w by that amount. What is left over, u - projection, is the rejection and is always perpendicular to w. Projection is the key to the shortest distance from a point to a line, and in lesson 8 it will solve the least-squares problem behind every line of best fit.
unit-19.2ef43i318dt: In three dimensions there is one more product. The cross product u x v is a new vector perpendicular to both u and v; its length is the area of the parallelogram they span, so half of it is the area of a triangle. Unlike the dot product it is not commutative: v x u = -(u x v), which is the right-hand rule. Graphics programs use it to find which way a surface faces and to light it correctly.
unit-19.24gf8gronq3: Finally, the centroid of a set of points is their average (add them as vectors, then scale by 1/n): the balance point of the shape. Notice that every tool in this lesson was assembled from the same few operations, which is how linear algebra works throughout.
unit-19.hsgoyo88ge: Vector arithmetic works entry by entry and follows the usual laws of algebra.
unit-19.xgjwawfezf: Here is some code. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-19.1veeiiq3gyb: The norm is the Pythagorean theorem in any dimension. The coordinates here are latitude and longitude, so these are rough distances in degrees, not kilometres.
unit-19.q1mehhrinb: Documents described by word counts: the query is most similar to the document it points nearest to.

unit-19.uy0x9n7vy5: Learn what a matrix is, how to multiply matrices (and why the rule looks strange), and how one idea, a matrix as a machine that transforms vectors, explains rotations in graphics, counting paths in a network, Markov chains and even Fibonacci numbers.
unit-19.2533dbqlksx: Describe a matrix as a grid of numbers and name its rows, columns and shape
unit-19.2bcgip18jy0: Add, scale, transpose and multiply matrices, and check that shapes fit
unit-19.1ayyan1u6n: Explain why matrix multiplication is not commutative but is associative
unit-19.w0jlinatt3: Use matrices to rotate and stretch shapes and to compose transformations
unit-19.1vpg1yykuab: Use matrix powers to count walks in a graph, evolve a Markov chain and compute Fibonacci numbers fast
unit-19.zebengrya8: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers
unit-19.2f5538t2ak3: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows (going across) and columns (going down). In Python we store it as a list of rows: [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] has two rows and three columns. Its shape is written rows x columns, so this one is 2x3. A grid with one column is basically a vector, which is why vectors and matrices fit together so well.
unit-19.1zb1phuszgm: Three simple operations come first. You can add two matrices of the same shape by adding matching entries, and scale a matrix by multiplying every entry by a number. The transpose flips the matrix over its diagonal so rows become columns: a 2x3 matrix becomes 3x2. A special square matrix called the identity matrix has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere; it does nothing when you multiply by it, like the number 1 does for ordinary multiplication.
unit-19.21ikuzgviy3: Notice how often we check shapes. In linear algebra, the shapes tell you whether an operation even makes sense, exactly as types do in a program. A function that quietly accepts mismatched shapes hides bugs, so ours raise ValueError with a clear message.
unit-19.1hesj5i4zgb: Multiplying a matrix by a vector is the heart of the subject. To compute M v, take each row of M, form its dot product with v (lesson 1), and collect the results as a new vector. A 2x3 matrix times a vector of length 3 gives a vector of length 2: the matrix is a machine that takes a 3-dimensional input and produces a 2-dimensional output.
unit-19.ayni3kjz9g: To multiply two matrices A B, apply that rule to each column of B: entry (i, j) of the answer is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. This only works when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B (a 2x3 times a 3x4 is fine and gives a 2x4; a 2x3 times a 2x3 is not). The rule looks odd until you see what it means: A B is the machine that does B first and then A. Because doing things in a different order usually gives a different result, A B is generally not equal to B A (multiplication is not commutative). But grouping does not matter, (A B) C = A (B C) (it is associative), and multiplication distributes over addition. Also (A B) transposed equals B transposed times A transposed, with the order reversed, like taking off your shoes and socks.
unit-19.1qnhhw18iu6: A power M^k means multiplying M by itself k times. Rather than k - 1 multiplications, repeated squaring (Unit 4) uses about log k of them: square the base, and multiply it into the answer whenever the matching bit of k is 1.
unit-19.23f4rwb6fmb: Geometry. In two dimensions, the matrix [[cos t, -sin t], [sin t, cos t]] rotates every point by the angle t, and [[sx, 0], [0, sy]] stretches the x and y directions. Every image on a screen is moved around with matrices like these. To do several steps, multiply the matrices once and then apply the single result to every point: compose(rotate, stretch) stretches first and rotates after. The order matters, as you will see in the examples.
unit-19.jaii8pxx44: Networks. Write a graph (Unit 6) as an adjacency matrix: entry (i, j) is 1 if there is an edge from i to j. Then A^k has in position (i, j) the number of walks of exactly k steps from i to j. Multiplying matrices is counting paths!
unit-19.j0wjjuhacv: Chance. A Markov chain describes something that moves between states with fixed probabilities, such as the weather changing from sunny to rainy. Its transition matrix has the probability of going from state i to j in row i. Multiplying a distribution of probabilities by the transposed matrix gives tomorrow's distribution. Repeating this for many days often settles to a steady state: here, in the long run it is sunny 2/3 of the time. This idea powers PageRank (the first Google ranking) and many ML models.
unit-19.1betusuq4jo: Fast formulas. The Fibonacci recurrence F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) is a matrix multiplication in disguise: [[1, 1], [1, 0]] raised to the power n contains F(n). With repeated squaring, a number with hundreds of digits takes only a few dozen multiplications.
unit-19.1gbuq3dr5it: A matrix is a list of rows. The shape is rows by columns, and a ragged list is not a matrix.

unit-19.2boqsa9cyaw: Learn Gaussian elimination, the most used algorithm in scientific computing: turn a system of linear equations into a matrix, simplify it with three row operations, and read off the answer. You will also see when a system has no solution or infinitely many, and why real solvers swap rows.
unit-19.30sb7iho8l: Write a system of linear equations as an augmented matrix
unit-19.1jlkycjqwku: Use the three row operations and explain why they keep the solutions unchanged

unit-19.1bjz8zafx57: A linear equation is one like 2x + y = 5: each unknown is multiplied by a number and the results are added, with no squares, products of unknowns or other curves. A system is several such equations that must all be true at once, for example
unit-19.n9mhnpypwc: Each equation is a line in the plane, and solving the system means finding where the lines cross (here x = 1, y = 2). With three unknowns each equation is a plane in space; with a thousand unknowns nobody can draw it, but the algebra is the same. Systems like this appear everywhere: balancing chemical equations, electrical circuits, fitting curves to data, computer graphics, economics and the training of machine-learning models.
unit-19.22lzt03x0qb: We only need the numbers, so we store the system as a matrix. The coefficient matrix A holds the multipliers, the vector b holds the right-hand sides, and the system is the single equation A x = b (matrix times vector, lesson 2). Gluing b on as an extra column gives the augmented matrix [[1, 1, 3], [2, -1, 0]], where every row is one equation.
unit-19.vhkhwrln4m: Three row operations change the matrix without changing the solutions: swap two rows (the order of equations does not matter), scale a row by a non-zero number (multiply both sides of an equation), and add a multiple of one row to another (add equations together). Scaling by zero is forbidden because it would erase an equation.
unit-19.238ofvl1iov: Gaussian elimination uses these operations with a plan. Work through the columns from left to right. In each column choose a pivot (a non-zero entry) and subtract multiples of its row from the rows below until everything under the pivot is zero. After this forward elimination the matrix is upper triangular: a staircase with zeros below the diagonal. The last equation then has only one unknown, so solve it, substitute the answer into the equation above, and continue upward. This is back substitution.
unit-19.8w43h382g3: For n equations the work grows like n^3 (three nested loops), which is fine for thousands of unknowns and is the reason computers can solve problems no person ever could by hand.
unit-19.29oycpydcx8: One practical detail matters a great deal. If the pivot is zero the method divides by zero, and if it is merely tiny, the floating-point rounding errors (Unit 1) are blown up enormously. Partial pivoting fixes both: before eliminating in a column, swap up the row whose entry in that column is largest in absolute value. Every serious solver does this. Afterwards, check your answer with the residual, the size of A x - b: a tiny residual means the computed x really satisfies the equations.
unit-19.hihmj7pvw0: One solution, none, or infinitely many
unit-19.1v12s6gopix: Two lines in the plane can cross once (one solution), be parallel (no solution) or be the same line (infinitely many solutions). Exactly these three cases, and no others, occur for every linear system of any size.
unit-19.1fzg9ah50mk: To tell them apart, continue eliminating until each pivot is 1 and is the only non-zero entry in its column. This is the reduced row echelon form (RREF), and it is unique: any sequence of row operations leads to the same RREF. To avoid rounding we compute it with Python's exact Fraction type.
unit-19.1ukrwdrv93j: Read the result like this. A row that says 0 0 ... 0 | 1 claims 0 = 1, so the system is inconsistent: no solution. Otherwise, if every unknown has a pivot, there is exactly one solution. If some column has no pivot, that unknown is a free variable which can take any value, giving infinitely many solutions.
unit-19.eiz7m8zx4i: A square matrix that leads to a unique solution for every right-hand side is called invertible (or non-singular); one that does not is singular. Our floating-point solve raises ValueError for singular matrices, because no single answer exists. The next lesson studies invertible matrices and a single number, the determinant, that detects them.

unit-19.2gjywj350cw: Learn the determinant, a single number that tells you how a matrix scales areas and whether it can be undone, and the inverse matrix that undoes it. You will compute both exactly with fractions, solve systems two more ways, and use matrix inverses to build and break a real cipher.

unit-19.151kcp4lev4: Last lesson, some systems had exactly one solution and others did not. Is there a quick test for a square matrix? Yes: the determinant, written det(A). For a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] it is a*d - b*c. For example det([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) = 1*4 - 2*3 = -2.
unit-19.3z3tmr606s: What does the number mean? Think of the matrix as a machine that moves points (lesson 2). Feed it the unit square (area 1) and it produces a parallelogram. The absolute value of the determinant is the area of that parallelogram: stretch x by 2 and y by 3 ([[2, 0], [0, 3]]) and every area becomes 6 times bigger. In three dimensions it is a volume factor. A negative determinant means the machine also flips the picture like a mirror (swapping x and y has determinant -1). And a determinant of 0 means the machine squashes the plane flat onto a line, so information is lost and the action cannot be undone.
unit-19.jotoz5x6de: That is the main fact of this lesson: a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is not 0. Several other statements are equivalent to it: A x = b has exactly one solution for every b, the rows are independent, and the columns are independent.
unit-19.rcq4e4ncvh: For bigger matrices the definition is cofactor expansion: pick the first row, and for each entry multiply it by the determinant of the smaller matrix left after deleting its row and column (the minor), alternating the signs + - + - .... Each of those smaller determinants expands the same way, so the code is a short recursion. The cost is terrible: an n x n matrix needs about n! steps (for n = 20 that is more than a billion billion). It is wonderful for understanding and awful for computing.
unit-19.ddbxb2foge: The fast way uses Gaussian elimination from lesson 3. Three facts make it work: adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the determinant, swapping two rows flips its sign, and the determinant of a triangular matrix is just the product of its diagonal. So eliminate, remember how many swaps you did, multiply the diagonal, and fix the sign. This needs about n^3 steps. If a column has no pivot, the determinant is 0.
unit-19.myn2xw7xxt: The determinant also follows pleasant rules: det(A B) = det(A) * det(B) (scale factors multiply), det(A^T) = det(A), and multiplying one row by c multiplies the determinant by c. We use Python's Fraction so the answers are exact integers or fractions, with no rounding.
unit-19.21szwtnygmn: Inverses, and what they are good for
unit-19.1l19ebv2mbv: The inverse of A, written A^-1, is the matrix that undoes A: A A^-1 = A^-1 A = I (the identity). Like 1/5 for the number 5, it exists only when A is invertible (determinant not 0). To find it, write A next to the identity as [A | I] and apply the elimination of lesson 3 until the left half becomes I; the right half has become A^-1 (Gauss-Jordan elimination). The same row operations that turn A into I turn I into A^-1.
unit-19.1tdoqb6f0r7: With the inverse, A x = b is solved by x = A^-1 b. A different formula is Cramer's rule: x_j = det(A_j) / det(A), where A_j is A with column j replaced by b. Both are lovely on paper and poor in practice: forming an inverse costs more than solving the system directly, and Cramer's rule needs n + 1 determinants. Numerical programmers solve A x = b with elimination and almost never compute inverses explicitly. The inverse is mostly a tool for thinking and for small matrices.
unit-19.1ysgxk4ja6h: One place where inverses are the whole point is cryptography. The Hill cipher (1929) turns letters into numbers 0 to 25, groups them in pairs, multiplies each pair by a secret key matrix and reduces the result modulo 26 (Unit 6). To decrypt you need the inverse of the key matrix modulo 26, which exists only when gcd(det, 26) = 1. For a 2x2 key this is det^-1 * [[d, -b], [-c, a]], with the inverse of the determinant taken modulo 26. The Hill cipher is not secure today (anyone who knows a little plaintext can solve for the key with linear algebra, which is exactly why this lesson belongs to the previous one), but it was the first cipher to use matrices and it shows the idea clearly.

unit-19.1g04iz9ytio: Understand which vectors can be reached by combining others (span), when vectors carry new information (independence), the smallest complete set of directions (a basis), and how rank and the null space measure what a matrix keeps and what it destroys.
unit-19.1uf9772qgyo: Explain span and linear independence in plain words
unit-19.mg1nqwmeox: Compute rank with row reduction and read pivot columns

unit-19.1ooc143igqx: Write a vector in coordinates relative to a basis
unit-19.1t4v6n2zqrs: A linear combination of vectors is what you get by scaling them and adding: 3*(1, 0) + 2*(0, 1) = (3, 2). The span of some vectors is the set of every vector you can reach this way. One vector spans a line, two vectors that point in different directions span a flat plane, and three directions that do not lie in a plane span all of 3D space.
unit-19.fou21361tk: The question "is b in the span of the columns of A?" is exactly the question "does A x = b have a solution?" from lesson 3. Linear algebra keeps reusing the same few ideas in different clothes.
unit-19.2byx68os16v: Vectors are linearly independent if none of them is a combination of the others, so each adds a genuinely new direction. (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1) are dependent because the third is the sum of the first two: it adds nothing. A basis of a space is an independent set of vectors that spans it: enough to reach everything, with nothing wasted. Every basis of the same space has the same number of vectors, called the dimension. The plane has dimension 2, ordinary space 3.
unit-19.5bxeticzin: A basis gives each vector coordinates: the unique numbers c such that c0*b0 + c1*b1 + ... = v. The usual (1,0), (0,1) is just one basis; (1, 1), (1, -1) is another, and the same point has different coordinates in each. Choosing a good basis is one of the main tricks of the rest of this unit (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD).
unit-19.fxnenouapi: The rank of a matrix is the number of independent rows, which always equals the number of independent columns (a surprising and useful fact). Compute it by row reduction: it is the number of pivots. Columns that contain a pivot are the pivot columns; they form a basis for what the matrix can output.
unit-19.17b8ckk8cqr: The null space of A is every x with A x = 0: the directions the matrix flattens to nothing. Find it by solving with the reduced matrix: each free column (one without a pivot) gives one basis vector. The rank-nullity theorem says rank + dimension of null space = number of columns. What the matrix keeps plus what it destroys equals what you started with. A matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is full and its null space is just the zero vector.

unit-19.ix1vdgisbf: See a matrix as a machine that moves every point in the plane or in space: stretch, rotate, shear, reflect, squash. Learn what makes a transformation linear, how to get its matrix from where it sends the basis vectors, and why composing transformations means multiplying matrices in a particular order.
unit-19.2bt9f3mzlpv: Say what makes a function a linear transformation
unit-19.1uy0vhca4uw: Build a matrix from what a transformation does to the basis vectors

unit-19.2978syv0orp: Functions that keep the grid straight
unit-19.1xp0a2xpon3: A transformation is a function that takes a vector and returns a vector, like f(x, y) = (2x, 3y). It is linear if it respects the two operations of linear algebra: f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b) and f(c a) = c f(a). Picture the grid lines on graph paper: a linear transformation keeps them straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and keeps the origin fixed. Stretching, rotating, shearing (slanting like a deck of cards) and reflecting are linear. Shifting by (1, 0) is not (it moves the origin), and neither are squaring or absolute value (they bend lines).
unit-19.1zmkbpir7lo: The deep fact is that every linear transformation is a matrix multiplication. To find the matrix, ask where the basis vectors go. If f(1, 0) = (a, c) and f(0, 1) = (b, d), the matrix is [[a, b], [c, d]], with those results as its columns. Why is that enough? Every vector is x*(1, 0) + y*(0, 1), and linearity says f of that is x*f(1, 0) + y*f(0, 1). Knowing two answers gives you all of them.
unit-19.xd88uz2vwk: A scaling [[k, 0], [0, k]] makes everything k times bigger. A reflection [[1, 0], [0, -1]] flips y, like a mirror along the x-axis. Swapping x and y [[0, 1], [1, 0]] mirrors across the diagonal. A shear [[1, k], [0, 1]] slides each point sideways in proportion to its height. A projection [[1, 0], [0, 0]] throws away y: every point lands on the x-axis, and information is lost, so it has no inverse (rank 1, determinant 0). A rotation by 90 degrees counter-clockwise is [[0, -1], [1, 0]]: the vector (1, 0) goes to (0, 1) and (0, 1) goes to (-1, 0), which are exactly its two columns.
unit-19.28prk93caqe: Computer graphics works this way. A 2D game, a photo editor and a 3D engine all store shapes as lists of corner points and move them by multiplying every corner by a matrix.
unit-19.5hszpzs9p8: Do a shear, then a rotation: multiply the points by the shear matrix, then by the rotation matrix. That equals multiplying once by the product R S (rotation on the left, because it is applied last). So composing transformations is matrix multiplication, and order matters: slide then turn is generally not turn then slide, which matches the fact that A B is usually not B A (lesson 2).
unit-19.3anonqmldl: Finally the determinant gets its meaning: the unit square has area 1 and its image under a matrix is a parallelogram of area |det|. This holds for any shape, not just the square, because every region is built from tiny squares that all scale by the same factor. A determinant of 0 means everything collapses to a line, so the area is zero and no inverse can bring it back.

unit-19.vny48jfmvu: Learn what to do when a system has no exact solution, which is the normal situation with real, noisy data. You will use perpendicular vectors to find the closest possible answer, fit lines and curves through scattered points, and see why a perfect fit can be a bad one.

unit-19.28s4syhiwcp: When there is no exact answer
unit-19.1rxbu9qr8t9: Real measurements are noisy. Suppose you measure a spring five times and get points that almost, but not exactly, lie on a line. The equations a x = b that say "every point is on my line" are overdetermined: more equations than unknowns, and no x satisfies all of them (in the language of lesson 5, b is not in the span of the columns of a). What now? Give up? No: pick the x that makes a x as close as possible to b. This is the least-squares solution, because "close" means the sum of the squares of the errors is as small as possible.
unit-19.1uyo3ia3ocv: Why squares? Squaring makes every error positive, punishes big misses more than small ones, and, best of all, gives a problem with a clean algebraic answer.
unit-19.12wxsznarvj: Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) when their dot product is 0 (lesson 1). The closest point to b in a space is where the leftover residual b - a x meets that space at a right angle, like dropping a plumb line from a ball to the floor. Writing that out, the residual must be orthogonal to every column of a: a^T (b - a x) = 0, which rearranges into the normal equations (a^T a) x = a^T b. That is a square system we already know how to solve exactly. One recipe handles every overdetermined system.
unit-19.13fqafrje6e: Orthogonal vectors are easy to work with, so we want a way to make them. Gram-Schmidt takes vectors one at a time and subtracts from each its projection onto the ones already processed, leaving only the new, perpendicular part. The same idea underlies the QR factorization that professional libraries use instead of normal equations for accuracy.
unit-19.1m1rdn4d6j9: Fitting lines and curves, and overfitting
unit-19.wjrrwz9rl3: To fit the line y = m x + c to points (x_i, y_i), put the x values in one column and 1s in another, and solve for (m, c). To fit a parabola y = c0 + c1 x + c2 x^2, use columns 1, x, x^2. The model is linear in the unknowns even when the curve is not a line, which is why linear algebra does curve fitting. This is the simplest form of machine learning: choose a model, then choose the numbers in it that minimize the error on the data.
unit-19.18dvx20x77a: R squared measures the fit: 1 means all the variation is explained, 0 means you did no better than predicting the average. But beware: with n points, a polynomial of degree n - 1 hits every point exactly and has zero error, yet it wiggles wildly between them and predicts new data badly. That is overfitting: memorizing the noise instead of learning the pattern. Lower error on the data you used is not the same as being right about the data you have not seen.

unit-19.w18ov4tqwh: A matrix usually knocks vectors off their line: send (1, 2) through it and it comes out pointing somewhere new. But some special vectors stay on their own line and only get stretched or flipped. Such a vector is an eigenvector of the matrix (from the German eigen, "own" or "characteristic"), and the stretch factor is its eigenvalue lambda. The defining equation is A v = lambda v, with v not the zero vector.
unit-19.1bnl86mq57f: Example: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Then A (1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3 (1, 1), so (1, 1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. And A (1, -1) = (1, -1), eigenvalue 1. These two directions are the matrix's skeleton: along them it acts like simple multiplication by a number. Every other vector is a mix of the two, so once you know them you understand the whole matrix.
unit-19.298dxkoy54p: Rewrite A v = lambda v as (A - lambda I) v = 0. We want a non-zero v in the null space (lesson 5), which exists only when A - lambda I is singular, meaning its determinant is 0. For a 2x2 matrix this gives the characteristic equation lambda^2 - trace * lambda + det = 0, where the trace is the sum of the diagonal (lesson 2). It is a quadratic, so the quadratic formula solves it. Two handy checks: the eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
unit-19.1tbye4taj11: Sometimes there are no real eigenvalues. A quarter turn [[0, -1], [1, 0]] points every vector in a new direction, so nothing stays on its line (its eigenvalues are the complex numbers i and -i). For each eigenvalue, the eigenvector is any vector in the null space of A - lambda I; for 2x2 that means any vector perpendicular to a non-zero row of it.
unit-19.1r6mm0ptks4: Why do eigenvalues matter? Apply a matrix again and again (a population, a weather chain, a web surfer clicking links). The component along the eigenvector with the biggest eigenvalue grows fastest and soon dominates: after many steps the result points almost exactly along it. That is power iteration: multiply, rescale to keep the numbers manageable, repeat. The Fibonacci matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] has dominant eigenvalue (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2 = 1.618..., the golden ratio, which is why Fibonacci numbers grow by that factor each step.
unit-19.15eqtd9h8w: PageRank, the idea that launched Google, imagines a person clicking random links forever (and, with probability 15 percent, jumping to a random page). The fraction of time spent on each page is that page's score, and it is the dominant eigenvector of the link matrix. Pages linked from important pages become important. Real search engines work with matrices billions of entries wide, but the method is power iteration, exactly as in this lesson.

unit-19.163mexxj2mb: Suppose a table lists the height and weight of five people. Each row is a point in 2D; a table with 1,000 columns (a genome, a document's word counts) is a point in 1,000-dimensional space. We cannot see that, but linear algebra works in any dimension. A first step is centering: subtract each column's average so the cloud sits around the origin. Next the covariance matrix records how features move together: its diagonal holds each feature's variance (spread), and an off-diagonal entry is positive when two features rise together (taller people weigh more) and negative when one rises as the other falls. Entry (i, j) is the sum of centered_i * centered_j divided by n - 1. This matrix is symmetric, and symmetric matrices have wonderfully well-behaved eigenvectors: real eigenvalues and mutually perpendicular eigenvectors.
unit-19.zjkkvo7rj: PCA: the direction of greatest spread
unit-19.1n8xx9rs76h: Principal component analysis (PCA) asks: along which direction does the data vary the most? The answer is the dominant eigenvector of the covariance matrix, and its eigenvalue is the variance along that direction. Project every point onto it and you replace two numbers per person with one, losing as little information as possible. With 1,000 features you might keep the top 10 directions. That is dimensionality reduction, the first step in countless machine-learning pipelines and the way scientists draw pictures of high-dimensional data. We find the direction with power iteration from lesson 8.
unit-19.btzm29m5mg: Any matrix can be written as a sum of simple rank-one pieces sigma * u v^T, ordered from most to least important (the singular value decomposition, SVD). Keep only the largest piece or pieces and you have the best possible lower-rank summary of the table. For a picture, a few pieces carry almost all of the visible structure, so storing u, v and sigma (a few dozen numbers) instead of every pixel is compression. Here we compute the top piece: v is the dominant eigenvector of A^T A, sigma = |A v|, and u = A v / sigma.
unit-19.294zdxfrjcf: Recommendations use the dot product from lesson 1. Treat each user's ratings as a vector. Cosine similarity (the cosine of the angle between two vectors) says how alike two tastes are regardless of how generously each user rates. To predict whether you will like an item you have not tried, average the ratings of other users who did, weighting each by how similar they are to you. Real services use much more sophisticated versions of exactly this idea.
